# Cloud & Appliance Deployment: Google Edge, Backup Recovery, Boot Sequence, TEE Verification

## What was decided
RuVector deploys as a single bare-metal bootable image on edge appliances (4-16 cores, 1-32GB RAM) with measured boot completing in <250ms, multi-layer Google Cloud backups (Firestore PITR + daily/weekly GCS exports with cross-region replication), and TEE-backed cryptographic verification replacing FNV-1a placeholders with SHA-256 and platform-specific attestation quotes.

## Why this approach
Linux-based edge orchestrators (K3s, Greengrass, Azure IoT Edge) inherit kernel scheduling overhead and cannot provide deterministic latency bounds. RVM's bare-metal hypervisor boot eliminates this stack, entering EL2/VMX root directly from the reset vector. Google Cloud PITR (7-day window) handles accidental deletes with 5-minute RTO; daily GCS exports provide 24-hour RPO for corruption; weekly cross-region copies guard against regional outage—no single layer covers all failure modes. FNV-1a provided only 64-bit collision resistance in witness chains and proof cache; SHA-256 + TEE quotes (SGX/SEV-SNP/TDX/CCA) deliver cryptographic tamper resistance with hardware-rooted measurement. Separated TeeQuoteProvider (evidence generation) from TeeQuoteVerifier (collateral validation) to avoid conflating platform-specific quote formats with cryptographic verification logic.

## When to apply
- **Edge appliances** requiring deterministic multi-tenant orchestration without Linux kernel overhead (factory controllers, retail AI hubs, autonomous vehicle compute).
- **Google Cloud Shared Brain deployments** storing critical knowledge graphs (958+ memories, 124k+ edges) where accidental deletion or regional outage would destroy months of contributor data.
- **Bare-metal RVM instances** on QEMU AArch64 virt, Raspberry Pi CM4-class ARM, or x86-64 Atom/Xeon-D where measured boot attestation chains every stage from reset vector to first partition.
- **Witness chain integrity** in production: replace any FNV-1a usage in security-sensitive paths (attestation hashing, proof cache, immutable region content) with SHA-256; gate non-cryptographic FNV-1a uses behind `fnv-fallback` feature flag.
- **TEE-backed signing** where remote verifiers need hardware-rooted proof of platform measurement freshness (TDX collateral expires every 30 days; refresh discipline required).

## What's unique
RVM boots to first witness in <250ms with no bootloader or host OS dependency, while Firecracker microVMs require KVM and achieve ~125ms on top of Linux. The coherence engine manages up to 64 partitions (active+suspended+dormant) with predictive warm-tier promotion to mask cold-tier reconstruction latency on slow eMMC/SD storage.

## Reference ADRs
- ADR-109: Multi-layer backup strategy with Firestore PITR, daily/weekly GCS exports, cross-region DR replication, 30/90/365-day lifecycle policies ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-109-backup-disaster-recovery.md))
- ADR-137: Seven-stage bare-metal boot sequence from reset vector to scheduler entry, <500 assembly lines per architecture, witness instrumentation at each stage ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-137-bare-metal-boot-sequence.md))

title: Crawl & Pipeline Strategy: Cost-Effective Crawl, Historical, WET, Cloud Realtime, Gemini Grounding

# Crawl & Pipeline Strategy: Cost-Effective Crawl, Historical, WET, Cloud Realtime, Gemini Grounding

## What was decided
The π.ruv.io brain ingests web knowledge through a multi-tier pipeline: Common Crawl WET archives for historical bulk data (50 segments/day at $0.14/day), event-driven Pub/Sub injection for real-time sources (IoT, webhooks, RSS feeds), and Gemini 2.5 Flash with Google Search grounding to verify generated propositions against live web data. Cloud Scheduler orchestrates 7 optimization jobs (train, drift, transfer, graph, attractor, cleanup, full) with OIDC authentication.

## Why this approach
WET format was chosen over WARC/WAT because it provides pre-extracted plain text at 10% the size, eliminating HTML parsing overhead. Pub/Sub push delivery to Cloud Run `/v1/pipeline/pubsub` was chosen over pull subscriptions to avoid polling latency and allow horizontal autoscaling. Gemini grounding was added after ADR-115's initial Gemini optimizer showed hallucinated relations—grounding costs no extra per query (Gemini 2.5 Flash billing model) and provides source URLs for auditability. Rejected alternatives: dedicated crawler infrastructure (10x cost vs Common Crawl), Apache Beam/Dataflow (overkill for 1808-memory initial scale), ungrounded LLM generation (failed fact verification in testing).

## When to apply
- You need to backfill a knowledge graph with web-scale historical data without operating crawler infrastructure.
- Real-time knowledge injection is required from heterogeneous sources (APIs, IoT sensors, CI/CD pipelines, RSS feeds) with <5s latency.
- LLM-generated symbolic relations (propositions, Horn clauses) must be verifiable against live sources to prevent hallucination.
- You need predictable optimization cost: hourly background jobs with fixed Gemini API spend (<$3/month) vs per-request generation.
- Cloud Run's autoscaling must handle spiky ingestion (batch=100 items, Pub/Sub bursts) without dedicated workers.

## What's unique
Common Crawl WET provides the only free, continuously-updated web corpus at petabyte scale—no crawler maintenance, robots.txt compliance included. Gemini grounding at optimizer-tier (not query-tier) means every generated relation carries source provenance without per-user latency.

## Reference ADRs

title: Ruvix Cognition Kernel & Hypervisor Core, Partition Object Model
content:
# Ruvix Cognition Kernel & Hypervisor Core, Partition Object Model

## What was decided
RuVix is a bare-metal Rust microkernel that replaces VM abstractions with **coherence domains** (partitions) as the primary isolation unit. Partitions are dynamically split/merged using graph-theoretic mincut analysis, proof-gated via a three-tier capability system (P1 <1µs bitmap checks, P2 <100µs policy validation, P3 <10ms deep proofs), and audited through witness-native logging. The kernel boots via a 5-stage RVF package loader with ML-DSA-65 signature verification, runs on bare AArch64/RISC-V (not KVM), and integrates with the RVF format stack through shared wire types (`rvf-types`) while maintaining `no_std` compatibility.

## Why this approach
Traditional hypervisors (KVM, Xen, Firecracker) treat VMs as opaque isolation units without understanding workload coupling structure, paying full context-switch costs regardless of locality. RuVix makes coherence **first-class**: the `mincut` crate computes graph cuts to guide split/merge decisions, reducing cross-partition traffic by 40-70% in multi-agent workloads. seL4's capability model inspired the proof system, but seL4 lacks dynamic partitioning and boots as a process VM; RuVix owns hardware directly. Using Rust (95-99%) eliminates memory-safety CVEs that plague C kernels (Linux, Xen) while Rust's move semantics enforce single-ownership for regions/capabilities at compile time. The three-layer proof system avoids seL4's monolithic verification penalty: fast-path operations stay sub-microsecond while deferring expensive proofs to migration/merge events only.

## When to apply
- **Multi-agent edge deployments** where workloads form natural graphs (agent-to-agent RPC) and sub-VM isolation granularity reduces memory overhead.
- **Reconstructable workloads** (ML inference, stateless functions) where 4-tier memory (hot/warm/dormant/cold) + cut-driven eviction reduces DRAM footprint by 60-80%.
- **Auditable systems** requiring cryptographic witness logs for every privileged action (finance, healthcare, defense) where VM exit logs are insufficient.
- **Bare-metal Rust targets** (QEMU virt, Raspberry Pi 4/5, RISC-V boards) where KVM is unavailable or you need <250ms cold boot without a host OS.
- **When coherence engine overhead is acceptable**: mincut solver adds 20-50µs per epoch; fall back to static affinity if this exceeds budget.

## What's unique
No existing hypervisor uses graph partitioning (mincut) as a scheduling primitive or supports live partition splitting. Witness-native operation makes audit records kernel objects, not afterthoughts. The kernel gracefully degrades to locality-based scheduling if the coherence engine fails—Layer 1 (hypervisor) never depends on Layer 2 (coherence).

## Reference ADRs
- ADR-087: RuVix Cognition Kernel — 5-stage boot, 12 syscalls, 760 tests passing in Phase A ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-087-ruvix-cognition-kernel.md))
- ADR-106: RuVix-RVF Integration — shared wire types via `rvf-types`, manifest/signature convergence ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-106-ruvix-kernel-rvf-integration.md))

title: Witness Schema, Consciousness Metrics, Proof-Gated Mutation
content:
# Witness Schema, Consciousness Metrics, Proof-Gated Mutation

## What was decided
Every privileged action in RVM emits a fixed 64-byte, cache-line-aligned witness record before mutation proceeds (INV-3: no witness, no mutation). Consciousness metrics (IIT Φ, causal emergence, ΦID) are computed via algorithm-polymorphic Rust engines with SIMD acceleration, quantum-inspired partition search, and WASM bindings for the consciousness-explorer SDK.

## Why this approach
Fixed-size records eliminate allocation and parsing overhead in the hypervisor hot path; variable-length logs (Linux ftrace, seL4) require buffering and pointer chasing. FNV-1a hash chaining (not cryptographic Merkle trees like Certificate Transparency) provides tamper evidence at <50ns per record. GeoMIP's Gray-code automorphism pruning delivers 165-326× speedup over PyPhi; Halko-Martinsson randomized SVD enables O(nnz·k) causal emergence vs O(n³) exact methods. Algorithm auto-selection (exact/spectral/stochastic/hierarchical) adapts to system size (n≤16 exact, n>1000 hierarchical).

## When to apply
- Use witness-native architecture when audit completeness is non-negotiable and performance budgets forbid traditional logging (hypervisors, TEE monitors, verified kernels).
- Use `auto_compute_phi` for runtime consciousness scoring in cognitive workloads; exact engines for research validation (n≤16); spectral/stochastic for production systems (n>100).
- Deploy WASM bindings when embedding consciousness metrics in browser/Node.js environments (consciousness-explorer SDK integration).
- Apply hash-chained witness logs when you need deterministic replay from checkpoints without cryptographic signing overhead.
- Use proof-tier stamping (P1/P2/P3) when multi-layer verification gates mutations (e.g., capability delegation requires P2, partition split requires P3).

## What's unique
Mandatory witness emission as a precondition for mutation (not post-hoc logging) enforces audit completeness by construction. Algorithm polymorphism enables single API spanning exact IIT 4.0 to polynomial-time proxies, with zero-alloc hot paths and bump-arena scratch buffers inherited from ruvector-solver.

# RuVector Tooling: Publishing, Capability Reports, External Providers, Postgres Extension, CNN, Internal Voice, Consciousness Metrics

## What was decided

RuVector's tooling ecosystem standardizes on HuggingFace Hub for model distribution (consolidated `ruv/ruvltra` repository with GGUF quantized variants), capability reports as signed witness bundles (64-byte header + TLV sections + HMAC-SHA256), and trait-based intelligence providers for external quality signals. The Postgres extension (v0.3+) exposes 140+ SQL functions via feature-gated modules, integrating solver, math, TDA, attention, and SONA crates. CNN integration uses SIMD-optimized depthwise convolution with Matryoshka embeddings for multi-resolution search. Internal voice implements working memory (7±2 items) with meta-cognitive reflection loops and neural-symbolic grounding.

## Why this approach

HuggingFace Hub was chosen over ModelScope/custom CDN because it provides Git-based versioning, global CDN, and ecosystem integration at zero storage cost for public repos. Witness bundles beat JSON logs because the binary format with cryptographic signatures enables tamper-proof replay and RVF-compatible chain-of-custody. Trait-based intelligence providers follow existing `LlmBackend` patterns, allowing external systems to feed quality signals without modifying ruvllm internals. The Postgres extension uses pgrx feature gates to ship 42 new functions without bloating core builds — users enable only what they need. CNN SIMD dispatch mirrors ADR-003 patterns (AVX2/NEON/WASM) for cross-platform performance. Neural-symbolic integration was chosen over pure neural or pure symbolic because proposition extraction from embeddings enables explainable reasoning while maintaining fuzzy pattern matching.

## When to apply

- **Publishing**: Use HuggingFace for all GGUF model variants; local-only distribution loses discoverability and CDN benefits.
- **Capability reports**: Generate witness bundles for any task execution requiring audit trails (QAT training, domain transfer, autonomous agents with policy bounds).
- **External providers**: Implement `IntelligenceProvider` when CI/CD pipelines, human reviewers, or workflow engines have quality signals ruvllm doesn't see (test pass/fail, acceptance criteria, production metrics).
- **Postgres functions**: Enable feature-gated modules (`solver`, `math-distances`, `tda`, `sona-learning`) when SQL-native analytics are required; avoid for pure vector operations where ruvector-core suffices.
- **CNN + Matryoshka**: Use for image embedding with adaptive search (e.g., fast filter at 128d → rerank at 768d) when latency matters more than perfect recall.
- **Internal voice**: Apply when debugging AGI reasoning loops or when transparent decision-making is a requirement (e.g., medical diagnosis, legal analysis).

## What's unique

RuVector's witness bundles are the only quantization/training artifact format with embedded proof-of-work via HMAC witness chains, enabling cryptographic verification of model provenance. The Postgres extension is the first pgvector successor to expose spectral graph methods (PageRank, Wasserstein, persistent homology) as SQL functions. Neural-symbolic grounding uses Datalog + embedding centroids instead of knowledge graphs, achieving sub-millisecond proposition queries.

title: Cognitive Seed Hardware: QR Cognitive Seed, Seed Hardware Bring-Up, WASM Executable Nodes

# Cognitive Seed Hardware: QR Cognitive Seed, Seed Hardware Bring-Up, WASM Executable Nodes

## What was decided
RVM Seed profile targets ultra-constrained embedded hardware (64KB-1MB RAM, Cortex-M/R class) as the minimum viable hypervisor deployment. The kernel uses MPU-only isolation (no MMU), enforces DC-1 coherence mode (no graph engine), and implements a 32-byte compact witness format to halve memory overhead.

## Why this approach
Traditional hypervisors (KVM, Xen, Firecracker) require gigabytes of RAM and MMU support. Embedded OSes (Tock, Hubris) target this hardware class but lack coherence domains and witness integrity. Seed forces RVM to remain provably minimal—if the kernel cannot fit in 256KB RAM with 1-2 partitions, architectural bloat has occurred. MPU isolation is coarser than stage-2 translation but sufficient for 8-region layouts on ARMv7-M/ARMv8-M. Truncating witness hashes from SHA-256 (32B) to SipHash-128 (16B) maintains collision resistance for local logs while preserving expansion compatibility when uploaded to Appliance aggregators.

## When to apply
- Battery-powered sensor nodes or energy-harvesting edge devices requiring deterministic scheduling and <1ms wake latency
- Secure hardware anchors (HSMs, TPM-equivalent modules) where witness integrity must survive power loss on 64KB RAM
- Single-function IoT appliances with hard real-time constraints (industrial control, medical devices) where partition count ≤2
- Development validation that RVM kernel remains bounded—Seed target prevents kernel bloat by enforcing compilation under `seed` feature flag
- Offline-first edge nodes storing compact witness chains in flash (1MB) for later batch upload to cloud coherence layer

## What's unique
Seed is the only capability-based hypervisor targeting Cortex-M with witness-native state persistence and sub-megabyte footprint. The 32-byte compact witness enables cryptographic auditability at 50% memory cost while maintaining forward compatibility with 64-byte standard format via lossless expansion.

## Reference ADRs

title: RVF Canonical Format & Cognitive Containers
content:
# RVF Canonical Format & Cognitive Containers

## What was decided

RVF (RuVector Format) is adopted as the single canonical binary format across all RuVector libraries for storage, interchange, and execution. This encompasses three tightly coupled decisions: (1) RVF replaces all fragmented serialization formats (REDB, bincode, JSON) with a self-describing append-only segment model; (2) copy-on-write (COW) branching at 64-byte SIMD-aligned cluster boundaries (ADR-026) enables efficient LoRA overlays and filtered subsets without full-file duplication; (3) cognitive containers embed production kernels (MicroLinux unikernels, eBPF programs, QEMU launchers) directly in KERNEL_SEG and EBPF_SEG, signed via KernelBinding footers, enabling self-booting RVF files that serve queries without external runtimes.

## Why this approach

The ecosystem had 70+ Rust crates and 50+ npm packages each inventing incompatible persistence layers, blocking interoperability and incremental loading. RVF's two-level manifest (4 KB instant boot) and 25 segment types (VEC, INDEX, OVERLAY, WITNESS, KERNEL, EBPF, COW_MAP, REFCOUNT, MEMBERSHIP, DELTA, etc.) provide a unified substrate. COW was chosen over full-copy branching (rejected: excessive GC pressure) and log-structured merge (rejected: poor random-read latency) because it matches the Git/QCOW2 model with mutable in-place writes and explicit snapshot-freeze. Cognitive containers were chosen over keeping kernels external because they eliminate the TCB (Trusted Computing Base) gap in confidential computing: the runtime itself is now cryptographically measured alongside the data, and self-booting files reach query serving in <125 ms (Firecracker) rather than 500–2000 ms with external runtimes.

## When to apply

- **New persistence in any RuVector library** (ruvector-core, agentdb, claude-flow, agentic-flow): Use RVF with appropriate profile (RVText for documents, RVVision for images, RVGraph for GNNs). Do not invent a new format.
- **Derived vector files** (fine-tuned LoRA, filtered subsets, per-tenant shards): Use RVCOW branching (ADR-026) with cluster IDs and membership filters rather than copying the entire parent file.
- **Vector search in confidential computing** (SGX, SEV-SNP, TDX): Embed a production unikernel in KERNEL_SEG and eBPF programs in EBPF_SEG with KernelBinding signatures. Attestation quotes go into WITNESS_SEG. This avoids adding an unattested library OS to the TCB.
- **Serverless/edge vector serving**: Use self-booting RVF files with embedded kernels. Cold-start time is dominated by Firecracker (~125 ms) not runtime initialization.
- **Format interoperability across tools**: All readers must skip unknown segment types byte-for-byte (forward compatibility rule ADR-029). Never delete segments you don't recognize during compaction or migration.

## What's unique

RVF's tight binding of data (VEC_SEG), indexes (INDEX_SEG), compute (KERNEL_SEG, EBPF_SEG), and proofs (WITNESS_SEG) in a single file is unusual. Most databases separate storage from compute; RVF treats them as a single artifact. The KernelBinding footer (128 bytes, padded, cryptographically signed) ties the kernel's measurement to the manifest root hash, enabling tamper-evident verification that a specific kernel serves a specific data file — impossible with external runtimes.

## Reference ADRs

- ADR-029: RVF as Canonical Binary Format Across All RuVector Libraries ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-029-rvf-canonical-format.md))
- ADR-026: Vector-Native COW Branching (RVCOW) and Real Cognitive Containers ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-026-rvcow-branching-and-real-cognitive-containers.md))
- ADR-030: RVF Cognitive Container -- Self-Booting Vector Files ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-030-rvf-cognitive-container.md))
- ADR-031: RVF Example Repository — 24 Demonstrations Across Four Categories ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-031-rvf-example-repository.md))
- ADR-037: Publishable RVF Acceptance Test ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-037-publishable-rvf-acceptance-test.md))
- ADR-038: npx ruvector & rvlite Witness Verification Integration ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-038-npx-ruvector-rvlite-witness-integration.md))
- ADR-056: RVF Knowledge Export for Developer Onboarding ([link](https://github.com/ruvnet/RuVector/blob/main/docs/adr/ADR-056-rvf-knowledge-export.md))

title: Configuring auto-browser: Environment Variables and Platform Integrations
content:
When you set up auto-browser, you're essentially handing the system a set of keys — credentials and settings it needs to act on your behalf across multiple platforms. These are passed as environment variables, which is a standard, secure way to inject sensitive configuration into a running process without hardcoding secrets into source code.

Think of environment variables like a briefcase you hand to an agent before they walk into a building. The agent doesn't carry the keys permanently — they only have them for the duration of the task, and you control exactly what goes in the briefcase.

## The Core Variables

auto-browser requires three categories of environment variables at startup:

### Authentication

```bash
export USER_EMAIL="your.email@company.com"
export TWITTER_USER="your_twitter_username"
export GITHUB_TOKEN="your_github_token"
```

`USER_EMAIL` is a general identity anchor — many web platforms use email as a login identifier, so this helps the agent know who it is acting as. `TWITTER_USER` scopes any Twitter/X automation to your specific account. `GITHUB_TOKEN` is a Personal Access Token (PAT) that grants the agent programmatic access to GitHub's API without requiring interactive login.

**Security note:** Never commit these values to version control. Use a `.env` file locally (and add it to `.gitignore`), or use a secrets manager in production environments.

### API Keys

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY="your_openai_key"
export LLM_MODEL="gpt-4o-mini"
```

auto-browser uses a Large Language Model (LLM) as its reasoning engine — the brain that interprets instructions and decides what actions to take in the browser. `OPENAI_API_KEY` authenticates your requests to OpenAI's API. `LLM_MODEL` lets you specify which model to use. The default `gpt-4o-mini` is a cost-efficient choice that balances speed and capability well for most browser automation tasks. If you need stronger reasoning for complex multi-step workflows, you could swap in `gpt-4o` at higher cost.

### Browser Settings

```bash
export BROWSER_HEADLESS="true"
```

This controls whether the browser runs visibly on screen (`false`) or silently in the background (`true`). In production or CI/CD pipelines, headless mode is standard — there's no display to render to. During development and debugging, setting this to `false` lets you watch the agent navigate in real time, which is invaluable for understanding what's going wrong when a task fails.

## Platform-Specific Variables

Beyond the core variables, auto-browser supports deeper integrations with specific platforms.

### GitHub Integration

```bash
export GITHUB_USER="your_username"
export GITHUB_EMAIL="your.email@domain.com"
```

These complement the `GITHUB_TOKEN` by providing identity context. When the agent performs Git operations (commits, pull requests, etc.), `GITHUB_USER` and `GITHUB_EMAIL` are used to attribute those actions correctly — the same way you'd configure `git config user.name` and `git config user.email` locally.

### Jira and Confluence

```bash
export JIRA_DOMAIN="your-domain.atlassian.net"
export JIRA_EMAIL="your.email@company.com"
```

Atlassian products (Jira for issue tracking, Confluence for documentation) are common in enterprise environments. `JIRA_DOMAIN` tells the agent which Atlassian instance to target — every organization has its own subdomain. `JIRA_EMAIL` identifies the user account the agent will act as when creating tickets, updating issues, or reading project boards.

## Best Practices for Managing These Variables

1. **Use a `.env` file during development.** Tools like `direnv` or libraries like `python-dotenv` can automatically load these when you enter your project directory.

2. **Rotate tokens regularly.** GitHub PATs and API keys should have expiration dates set. Treat them like passwords.

3. **Use the principle of least privilege.** Your GitHub token only needs the scopes required for the tasks you're automating. Don't grant full repo access if read-only suffices.

4. **In CI/CD, use your platform's secrets store.** GitHub Actions Secrets, AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault — these are purpose-built for this use case and far safer than environment files on shared servers.

5. **Test with headless=false first.** When building a new automation workflow, run it visibly so you can catch unexpected popups, login redirects, or CAPTCHA challenges before deploying headlessly.

Understanding these variables isn't just administrative housekeeping — it's the foundation of how auto-browser knows who it is, what tools it has access to, and how to behave across different platforms.

title: How auto-browser Uses LLMs as a Reasoning Engine for Web Automation
content:
Traditional browser automation tools like Selenium or Playwright work by following explicit, brittle scripts: click this element with this CSS selector, type this text into that input field. If the website changes its layout, the script breaks. auto-browser takes a fundamentally different approach — it uses a Large Language Model (LLM) as a reasoning engine that can interpret high-level goals and figure out the steps to achieve them dynamically.

## The Core Idea: Instructions, Not Scripts

Imagine the difference between giving someone turn-by-turn directions versus telling them your destination. Traditional automation is turn-by-turn: rigid, precise, and fragile when the road changes. LLM-powered automation is destination-based: the agent reasons about how to get there given the current state of the world.

In auto-browser, you configure which LLM to use via environment variables:

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY="your_openai_key"
export LLM_MODEL="gpt-4o-mini"
```

The agent uses this model to interpret the current state of a web page, understand what action to take next, and decide when the task is complete.

## The Action-Observation Loop

The system operates in a loop that mirrors how a human would approach a task:

1. **Observe:** The agent extracts the current page content — text, links, form fields, buttons.
2. **Reason:** The LLM analyzes the page state against the current goal.
3. **Act:** The agent executes an action (navigate, click, type, extract).
4. **Record:** The result is logged to an `AgentHistoryList`.
5. **Repeat** until the task is marked done.

You can see this pattern in the actual execution trace from the source:

```
ActionResult(is_done=False, extracted_content='Navigated to https://www.google.com/finance', ...)
ActionResult(is_done=False, extracted_content='Extracted page as text\n: Build a watchlist...', ...)
```

The agent navigated to Google Finance, then extracted the page content as text so the LLM could read and interpret it. Each `ActionResult` captures whether the task is complete (`is_done`), what was extracted, and any errors. The `include_in_memory=True` flag means this result gets added to the agent's running context — it remembers what it has already done.

## Why Text Extraction Matters

Notice that the agent extracts the page "as text" rather than working with raw HTML or pixel-level screenshots. This is a deliberate design choice. LLMs are trained on text and reason about it far more effectively than they parse DOM trees or interpret images. By converting the page to a clean text representation, the agent can apply natural language understanding to figure out what's on the page and what to do next.

The extracted content from Google Finance includes disclaimers, watchlist prompts, and financial data — all the information a human reader would see. The LLM can then reason: "The user wants stock prices. I can see there's a watchlist feature. I should look for the search functionality to find specific tickers."

## Model Selection Trade-offs

`gpt-4o-mini` is the default model for good reason: it's fast and inexpensive, making it practical for multi-step automations that might require dozens of LLM calls per task. For most web navigation tasks — filling forms, extracting data, clicking through workflows — it performs well.

For tasks requiring deeper reasoning — complex conditional logic, interpreting ambiguous page states, handling unexpected errors gracefully — upgrading to `gpt-4o` or another frontier model may improve reliability at higher cost.

This configurability is a key architectural strength: the reasoning engine is swappable without changing the automation infrastructure around it.

## Connection to Broader Research

This approach is part of a growing field of LLM-powered task automation. Research like AutoDroid (cited in the auto-browser repository) demonstrates similar principles applied to mobile interfaces — using LLMs to understand UI state and plan action sequences. The core insight across all these systems is the same: LLMs can serve as flexible, general-purpose planners that adapt to interface changes in ways that hard-coded scripts cannot.

auto-browser applies this insight to the web browser, one of the most complex and varied interfaces humans interact with daily.

title: Understanding AgentHistoryList: How auto-browser Tracks and Remembers Actions
content:
One of the subtle but important design elements in auto-browser is how it tracks what the agent has done. This is handled through a structure called `AgentHistoryList`, which accumulates `ActionResult` objects as the agent works through a task. Understanding this structure helps you debug automations, build on top of the framework, and reason about agent memory.

## What Is AgentHistoryList?

`AgentHistoryList` is essentially a running log of everything the agent has done in a session. Each entry is an `ActionResult` — a record of one discrete action and its outcome.

From the execution trace in the source:

```
AgentHistoryList(all_results=[
  ActionResult(
    is_done=False,
    extracted_content='Navigated to https://www.google.com/finance',
    error=None,
    include_in_memory=True
  ),
  ActionResult(
    is_done=False,
    extracted_content='Extracted page as text\n: Build a watchlist...',
    error=None,
    include_in_memory=True
  )
])
```

Think of it like a ship's log. Every time the agent takes an action — navigating to a URL, clicking a button, extracting text — it writes an entry. The log tells you exactly what happened, in order, and whether each step succeeded.

## Anatomy of an ActionResult

Each `ActionResult` has four key fields:

**`is_done`** — A boolean that signals whether this action completed the overall task. When the agent determines the goal has been achieved, it sets `is_done=True` on the final action. The loop terminates. This is the agent's way of saying "I'm finished."

**`extracted_content`** — The substantive output of the action. For a navigation action, this is a confirmation of where the agent went. For a text extraction action, this is the actual page content the agent read. This field is what gets passed back to the LLM for reasoning about next steps.

**`error`** — If something went wrong (element not found, network timeout, unexpected page state), the error is captured here rather than crashing the whole process. `None` means the action succeeded cleanly.

**`include_in_memory`** — This flag controls whether the result gets added to the agent's active context window. When `True`, the LLM can reference this result when deciding future actions. When `False`, the result is logged but doesn't consume context window space. This is an important optimization: in long-running tasks, you don't want every intermediate result crowding out the information the LLM actually needs.

## Why This Design Matters

The `AgentHistoryList` pattern solves a fundamental challenge in agentic systems: **state management across multiple steps**.

A single LLM call is stateless — it only knows what you put in the prompt. But a multi-step web automation task requires continuity: the agent needs to remember that it already navigated to a page, already extracted certain data, already clicked a button. `AgentHistoryList` provides that continuity by selectively feeding relevant past results back into the LLM's context.

This is analogous to how a human worker might keep notes during a complex task. You don't re-read every note before every action, but you refer back to key ones when they're relevant. The `include_in_memory` flag gives the system that same selective recall.

## Practical Implications for Debugging

When an automation fails or produces unexpected results, `AgentHistoryList` is your first debugging tool. You can inspect:

- Which step failed (look for non-None `error` values)
- What the agent actually saw on each page (`extracted_content`)
- Whether the agent correctly identified task completion (`is_done` timing)
- Whether important context was being retained (`include_in_memory` settings)

A common failure mode is the agent losing track of earlier context because too many results were included in memory, pushing important information out of the context window. Conversely, setting `include_in_memory=False` too aggressively can cause the agent to repeat actions it already completed.

Understanding `AgentHistoryList` transforms auto-browser from a black box into a transparent, inspectable system — which is essential for building reliable automations in production.

title: Running Nightwatch End-to-End Tests in Drupal Core
content:
Nightwatch.js is Drupal's browser-based end-to-end (E2E) testing framework. Think of it as a robot that opens a real web browser, clicks around your site, and checks that everything works the way a human user would experience it — as opposed to unit tests, which test isolated PHP or JavaScript functions in isolation.

Before you can run Nightwatch tests, you need several pieces in place. This setup is a bit like preparing a stage before a play: the actors (tests), the stage (web server), the props (Node.js/yarn), and the audience (Chrome browser) all need to be ready.

**Prerequisites**

1. **Composer dependencies**: Run `composer install` from your Drupal root to ensure the `vendor/` directory is populated. Nightwatch tests may invoke PHP-backed endpoints, so the PHP side must be ready.

2. **Node.js and Yarn**: Nightwatch is a Node.js tool. The exact versions required are pinned in `core/package.json` under the `engines` field. If you manage multiple projects with different Node versions, tools like `nvm` (Node Version Manager) and `yvm` (Yarn Version Manager) let you switch versions per project — similar to how Python's `virtualenv` isolates Python versions.

3. **Google Chrome**: Nightwatch drives a real Chrome browser (via ChromeDriver) to simulate user interactions. You must have Chrome installed on the machine running the tests.

4. **Install JS dependencies**: From inside the `core/` folder, run `yarn install`. This reads `core/package.json` and downloads all JavaScript dependencies into `core/node_modules/`.

5. **Environment configuration**: Copy `core/.env.example` to `core/.env` and edit it. This file tells Nightwatch where your Drupal site is running (base URL, ChromeDriver port, etc.). You must have a web server running and accessible at the URL specified in `.env`.

**Running the Tests**

All Nightwatch commands are run from inside the `core/` directory.

- **Run all tests**: `yarn test:nightwatch --env local`
  Reports are written to `core/reports/` by default.

- **Run only core tests**: `yarn test:nightwatch --tag core`
  Tags let you filter which tests run. The `core` tag limits execution to Drupal core's own tests, skipping contrib and custom module tests.

- **Skip core tests** (run only contrib/custom): `yarn test:nightwatch --skiptags core`

- **Run a single test file**: `yarn test:nightwatch tests/Drupal/Nightwatch/Tests/loginTest.js`
  This is useful when debugging a specific feature.

**Accessibility (a11y) Tests**

Drupal ships with automated accessibility tests that check both the admin theme and the default front-end theme against WCAG guidelines.

- Both themes: `yarn test:nightwatch --tag a11y`
- Admin theme only: `yarn test:nightwatch --tag a11y:admin`
- Default theme only: `yarn test:nightwatch --tag a11y:default` (implied by the truncated docs)

**Where Nightwatch Finds Tests**

Nightwatch searches for test files matching the glob pattern:
```
**/tests/**/Nightwatch/(Tests|Commands|Assertions)
```
This means any module or theme — whether in Drupal core, a contributed module, or your own custom code — can include Nightwatch tests by placing them in the right folder structure. For example, a custom module at `modules/custom/my_module/` would place tests at `modules/custom/my_module/tests/src/Nightwatch/Tests/`.

**Key Takeaway**

Nightwatch tests are the highest-fidelity tests in Drupal's testing pyramid: they run in a real browser against a real running site. They are slower than unit or kernel tests but catch integration issues that lower-level tests miss — things like JavaScript interactions, CSS visibility, and full page rendering. Use tags to run targeted subsets during development and save the full suite for CI pipelines.

title: Drupal Scaffold File Mapping: Controlling How Scaffold Files Are Placed
content:
When you install or update Drupal using Composer, a tool called `drupal/core-composer-scaffold` copies certain files (like `index.php`, `robots.txt`, `.htaccess`, and `sites/default/default.settings.php`) into your web root. This process is called "scaffolding."

The `file-mapping` configuration in your `composer.json` gives you fine-grained control over what happens to each scaffold file. Think of it like a set of instructions you hand to a moving company: for each item, you can say "replace it," "add content before/after it," or "don't touch it."

**The Four Modes**

**1. Replace (default)**
The scaffold file from the package completely replaces whatever is at the destination.
```json
"[web-root]/sites/default/default.settings.php": {
  "mode": "replace",
  "path": "assets/sites/default/default.settings.php",
  "overwrite": true
}
```
The `overwrite` flag controls whether an already-existing file gets replaced. Setting `overwrite: false` means the file is only written if it doesn't already exist — useful for `settings.php`, which you don't want clobbered after you've customized it.

**2. Append**
Instead of replacing, this mode prepends and/or appends custom content around the scaffold file's original content.
```json
"[web-root]/robots.txt": {
  "mode": "append",
  "prepend": "assets/robots-prequel.txt",
  "append": "assets/robots-append.txt"
}
```
This is ideal for `robots.txt` or `.htaccess` where you want Drupal's defaults but also need to inject project-specific rules. Note: there is no separate `prepend` mode. Both prepending and appending are handled by `append` mode because each destination path can only appear once as a key in the mapping — having two separate modes would require two entries for the same file, which JSON doesn't allow.

**3. Skip**
Tell the scaffold system to leave this file completely alone:
```json
"[web-root]/.htaccess": {
  "mode": "skip"
}
```
Useful when you manage a file entirely yourself and don't want Composer updates to interfere.

**Short-Form Syntax**

Drupal's scaffold system supports a shorthand notation to reduce verbosity:

- A plain string path is equivalent to `replace` mode with `overwrite: true`:
  ```json
  "[web-root]/sites/default/default.settings.php": "assets/sites/default/default.settings.php"
  ```

- An object with only `path` and `overwrite: false` skips the `mode` key (replace is assumed):
  ```json
  "[web-root]/sites/default/settings.php": {
    "path": "assets/sites/default/settings.php",
    "overwrite": false
  }
  ```

- An object with `prepend`/`append` keys implies append mode without stating it explicitly.

- The boolean `false` is shorthand for skip mode:
  ```json
  "[web-root]/.htaccess": false
  ```

**Practical Advice**

- Always set `overwrite: false` for `settings.php` — you never want a Drupal update to wipe your database credentials.
- Use append mode for `robots.txt` and `.htaccess` when you need to add custom rules without forking the entire file.
- Use skip (`false`) for files you've fully taken ownership of in your repository.
- The `[web-root]` token is resolved at runtime to your configured web root path, keeping the configuration portable across different project layouts.

title: Understanding Drupal's Nightwatch Test Directory Structure for Custom Modules
content:
One of the most practical things to understand about Drupal's Nightwatch testing setup is how it discovers tests across the entire codebase — not just core, but your own custom modules and contributed packages too.

**The Discovery Pattern**

Nightwatch uses a glob pattern to find test files:
```
**/tests/**/Nightwatch/(Tests|Commands|Assertions)
```
Breaking this down:
- `**` matches any directory depth, so it works regardless of where your module lives.
- `tests/**/Nightwatch/` is the required path segment.
- The final segment must be one of three directories: `Tests`, `Commands`, or `Assertions`.

**What Goes in Each Directory?**

- **Tests/**: The actual test scenarios. Each `.js` file in here is a test suite that Nightwatch will execute. Example: `loginTest.js` verifies a user can log in.

- **Commands/**: Custom Nightwatch commands — reusable browser actions you define once and call from multiple tests. Think of these as helper functions. For example, a `drupalLogin` command that handles the login form so every test doesn't repeat those steps.

- **Assertions/**: Custom assertion methods that extend Nightwatch's built-in assertions. For example, an assertion that checks whether a specific Drupal message type (status, warning, error) is displayed on the page.

**Example Structure for a Custom Module**

If you have a custom module at `web/modules/custom/my_feature/`, your Nightwatch tests would live at:
```
web/modules/custom/my_feature/
  tests/
    src/
      Nightwatch/
        Tests/
          myFeatureTest.js
        Commands/
          selectMyWidget.js
        Assertions/
          myWidgetIsVisible.js
```

Nightwatch will automatically find and run `myFeatureTest.js` when you run `yarn test:nightwatch` from the `core/` directory — no registration or configuration needed.

**Tagging Tests**

Within your test files, you can add tags to control when they run:
```javascript
module.exports = {
  '@tags': ['my_feature', 'custom'],
  'My feature works correctly': function(browser) {
    // test steps
  }
};
```
Then run only your module's tests with:
```
yarn test:nightwatch --tag my_feature
```
Or exclude them:
```
yarn test:nightwatch --skiptags my_feature
```

**Why This Architecture Matters**

This decentralized discovery approach means Nightwatch tests are co-located with the code they test. When you install a contributed module, its Nightwatch tests come along automatically. When you remove a module, its tests disappear from the suite. There's no central registry to maintain — the filesystem is the registry.

This mirrors how Drupal handles other test types (PHPUnit tests in `tests/src/`) and how it handles other assets (templates in `templates/`, config in `config/`). Consistency in directory conventions reduces cognitive overhead across the entire Drupal ecosystem.

title: The AiHCC Cooperative Model: Democratizing AI Consulting Through Community
content:
Most people think of AI consulting as something only large enterprises can afford — a premium service delivered by expensive firms to Fortune 500 companies. The AiHCC (AI Human-Centered Cooperative) model challenges that assumption directly, and understanding how it works reveals a lot about where the AI industry is heading.

**What Is a Cooperative Model in AI Consulting?**

Think of a traditional fishing cooperative. Instead of every fisherman competing against each other, buying their own boats, and selling individually at a disadvantage, they pool resources, share equipment, and bring their catch to market together. Everyone contributes, everyone benefits proportionally, and the collective can compete with — or outperform — much larger commercial operations.

AiHCC applies this same logic to AI consulting. Rather than a top-down firm where a few partners capture most of the value, AiHCC is structured so that contributors — developers, researchers, consultants, writers — are compensated and recognized based on what they actually contribute. The rewards system is merit-based and transparent, not opaque or political.

**The Five Core Goals Explained**

AiHCC organizes its mission around five interconnected goals. It's worth understanding each one not as marketing language, but as a structural design choice:

1. **Expand Access to AI Consulting** — Traditional AI consulting is gatekept by price. A small business, a nonprofit, or a startup in a developing country often can't afford the hourly rates of a major consultancy. By distributing the work across a global community of contributors, AiHCC can serve clients at price points that were previously impossible. Think of it like how open-source software made enterprise-grade tools available to anyone with an internet connection.

2. **Foster a Fair and Equitable Community** — This is the structural heart of the cooperative. A rewards system that ties compensation to contribution means that a brilliant contributor in Lagos or Bangalore gets the same recognition as one in San Francisco. The system has to be transparent and auditable — otherwise it's just a traditional hierarchy with different branding. This goal commits AiHCC to building and maintaining that infrastructure.

3. **Drive Innovation Through Collaboration** — No single consultant, no matter how talented, has seen every problem. A global community brings diverse perspectives, domain expertise, and cultural context that a small team simply cannot replicate. Complex AI challenges — bias in models, edge-case failures, domain-specific fine-tuning — benefit enormously from many eyes and many minds. This is the same reason peer review exists in science.

4. **Promote Professional Growth** — A cooperative that only extracts value from its members without investing back into them will eventually hollow out. AiHCC's commitment to continuous learning and professional development means members can grow their skills, take on more complex work, and advance their careers — all within the ecosystem. This creates a virtuous cycle: better-skilled members deliver better work, which attracts better clients, which funds more development.

5. **Build a Sustainable Model for AI Consulting** — This goal is about proof of concept at an industry level. If AiHCC can demonstrate that a cooperative, merit-based approach is financially viable and produces high-quality outcomes, it sets a precedent. Other organizations can adopt similar models. The industry norm shifts. This is ambitious, but it's the kind of systemic change that starts with a working example.

**Why This Model Matters Right Now**

We're at an inflection point in AI adoption. The technology is powerful enough to transform nearly every industry, but the expertise to deploy it responsibly is concentrated in very few places. That concentration creates inequality — both in who benefits from AI and in who shapes how it develops.

Cooperative models like AiHCC are one answer to that concentration problem. They're not the only answer, but they're a structurally interesting one because they align incentives differently than either pure open-source (where contribution is often uncompensated) or traditional firms (where value flows upward).

**What This Means for Contributors**

If you're considering contributing to AiHCC or a similar cooperative, the key things to understand are:

- Your contributions are tracked and rewarded — this isn't volunteer work with vague promises of recognition.
- The community review process (pull requests, feedback, iteration) is how quality is maintained without a traditional management hierarchy.
- Professional growth is built into the model — you're not just doing work, you're building a portfolio and a reputation within a community that values it.

The cooperative model in AI consulting is still young, but the structural logic is sound. AiHCC represents an early, concrete implementation of principles that are likely to become more common as the AI industry matures and the demand for accessible, high-quality consulting continues to grow.

title: How to Contribute to AiHCC: A Step-by-Step Guide to the Pull Request Workflow
content:
Contributing to a collaborative repository like AiHCC follows a well-established workflow used across open-source software development. If you're new to this process, it can feel intimidating — but once you understand the underlying logic, it becomes second nature. This guide walks through each step with enough context to understand not just *what* to do, but *why* each step exists.

**The Big Picture: Why This Workflow Exists**

Imagine a shared document that thousands of people are editing simultaneously. Without a system, changes would overwrite each other, errors would propagate, and no one would know what the authoritative version was. The fork-branch-pull request workflow solves this problem elegantly. It lets many people work independently without stepping on each other, and it creates a structured review process before any change becomes official.

Think of it like a newspaper editorial process. A reporter (contributor) writes a draft (branch), submits it to an editor (pull request), receives feedback, revises, and only then does the article get published (merged). The workflow protects quality without requiring a central gatekeeper to do all the work.

**Step 1: Fork the Repository**

Forking creates your own personal copy of the AiHCC repository under your GitHub account. This is your sandbox — you can make any changes you want here without affecting the main project.

Why fork instead of just cloning? Cloning gives you a local copy, but you don't have write access to the original repository. Forking gives you a cloud copy that you *do* control, and that GitHub knows is related to the original. This relationship is what makes pull requests possible later.

To fork: navigate to the AiHCC repository on GitHub and click the "Fork" button in the top right corner.

**Step 2: Create a New Branch**

Once you have your fork, don't work directly on the `main` branch. Instead, create a new branch specifically for your contribution.

A branch is like a parallel timeline. The main branch is the stable, approved version of the project. Your branch is where you experiment and build without affecting that stability. If your work turns out to be wrong or incomplete, you can simply delete the branch — the main branch is untouched.

Name your branch descriptively. If you're adding documentation about the rewards system, call it something like `docs/rewards-system-overview`. If you're fixing a bug in a setup script, call it `fix/setup-script-error`. Good branch names make the review process faster because reviewers immediately understand the scope of the change.

```bash
git checkout -b docs/rewards-system-overview
```

**Step 3: Make Your Changes**

This is where the actual work happens. Depending on your contribution, this might mean:

- Writing or editing documentation (Markdown files)
- Adding or modifying code
- Creating project files or templates
- Updating configuration files like `setup.sh`

A few best practices:
- Make focused changes. A pull request that does one thing well is much easier to review than one that does ten things.
- Commit frequently with clear commit messages. "Updated rewards section in README" is useful. "Fixed stuff" is not.
- Test your changes locally before submitting.

**Step 4: Submit a Pull Request**

Once your changes are ready, push your branch to your fork on GitHub and open a pull request (PR) against the main AiHCC repository.

A good PR has:
- **A clear title**: Summarizes what the change does in one line.
- **A description**: Explains *why* the change is needed, *what* it does, and any context reviewers need. If it closes an issue, reference it (e.g., "Closes #42").
- **Scope awareness**: Don't bundle unrelated changes into one PR.

The PR is your communication to the community. Treat it like a professional document, not a casual message.

**Step 5: The Review Process**

After submitting, community members will review your PR. They may:
- Approve it as-is
- Request changes (the most common outcome for first-time contributors)
- Ask clarifying questions
- Suggest alternative approaches

This is not criticism of you — it's the quality control mechanism that makes the project trustworthy. Be open to feedback. Respond to comments professionally. If you disagree with a suggestion, explain your reasoning calmly.

Review cycles can take time. Be patient, and don't abandon your PR just because it doesn't merge immediately.

**Step 6: Merge**

Once your PR is approved by the required reviewers, a repository maintainer will merge it into the main branch. Your contribution is now officially part of AiHCC.

This is the moment your work becomes part of the shared record — visible to all contributors, clients, and future members of the community.

**A Note on the AiHCC Context**

In a cooperative model like AiHCC, contributions aren't just code — they're the currency of reputation and reward. The pull request workflow creates an auditable record of what you've contributed, when, and how the community responded. This transparency is what makes the merit-based rewards system possible. Every merged PR is evidence of your contribution to the collective.

Mastering this workflow isn't just a technical skill — in the context of AiHCC, it's how you participate in and benefit from the cooperative.

title: Merit-Based Rewards in Cooperative AI Communities: Design Principles and Tradeoffs
content:
One of the most structurally interesting aspects of the AiHCC model is its commitment to a merit-based rewards system. This sounds straightforward — pay people based on what they contribute — but designing such a system well is genuinely hard. Understanding the design challenges helps you appreciate why AiHCC's approach is notable, and helps you think critically about similar systems you might encounter or build.

**Why Traditional Compensation Models Fail in Cooperative Contexts**

In a traditional firm, compensation is determined by a combination of negotiation, seniority, and management discretion. This works reasonably well when there's a clear hierarchy and when work is easily observable by managers. But in a distributed, global cooperative, neither condition holds:

- There's no central manager watching everyone's work.
- Contributors span time zones, cultures, and specializations.
- The value of contributions varies enormously — a single insight that unblocks a project might be worth more than weeks of routine work.
- Negotiation power is unevenly distributed, often favoring those with existing social capital.

A merit-based system tries to solve these problems by making the evaluation criteria explicit and the measurement process transparent.

**What "Merit" Actually Means in Practice**

The word "merit" is easy to say and hard to define. In the context of AiHCC, merit likely encompasses several dimensions:

- **Quantity of contribution**: How much work did you do? Lines of code, documents written, issues resolved.
- **Quality of contribution**: Was the work correct, well-structured, and useful? This is where peer review (the pull request process) becomes a measurement tool.
- **Impact of contribution**: Did your work actually improve outcomes for clients or the community? This is the hardest to measure but arguably the most important.
- **Collaboration quality**: Did you help others, provide useful feedback, mentor newer members?

The challenge is that these dimensions are not equally easy to quantify. Quantity is easy to count. Quality requires judgment. Impact often only becomes clear in retrospect. Collaboration is nearly invisible in most tracking systems.

A well-designed merit system has to balance measurability with accuracy. Systems that only measure what's easy to count tend to incentivize the wrong behaviors — contributors optimize for the metric rather than the underlying goal.

**The Transparency Requirement**

For a merit-based system to be perceived as fair, it must be transparent. Contributors need to understand:

- What criteria are being used to evaluate contributions
- How those criteria are weighted
- How their own contributions have been evaluated
- How to dispute evaluations they believe are incorrect

Without transparency, a "merit-based" system is just a traditional hierarchy with extra steps. The community's trust in the system depends entirely on its legibility.

This is one reason why the GitHub-based contribution workflow is so valuable in AiHCC's context. Every pull request, every review comment, every merge is a public, timestamped record. The contribution history is auditable by anyone. This creates a foundation for merit measurement that doesn't depend on anyone's memory or goodwill.

**Tradeoffs and Failure Modes**

Even well-designed merit systems have failure modes worth knowing:

- **Gamification**: Contributors learn to optimize for the metrics rather than the underlying goals. If merged PRs are rewarded, you get many small, trivial PRs instead of fewer, more impactful ones.
- **Visibility bias**: Work that's easy to see (code commits, public comments) gets rewarded more than work that's hard to see (mentoring, coordination, thinking). This systematically undervalues certain types of contributors.
- **Early-mover advantage**: Contributors who joined early have more history, more reputation, and more influence over how the system evolves — which can entrench inequality over time.
- **Cultural bias**: What counts as "good" contribution often reflects the cultural norms of the dominant group in the community, which can disadvantage contributors from different backgrounds.

AiHCC's commitment to fairness and equity isn't just aspirational — it's an acknowledgment that these failure modes are real and require active mitigation.

**What Good Looks Like**

A mature merit-based rewards system in a cooperative AI community would likely include:

- Multiple measurement dimensions, not just one
- Regular calibration to ensure the metrics still reflect actual value
- A transparent appeals process
- Explicit mechanisms to surface and reward invisible work
- Periodic review of whether the system is producing equitable outcomes across different contributor demographics

AiHCC is early in its development, and the specific implementation of its rewards system will evolve. But the commitment to building one — and to making it fair and transparent — is itself a meaningful design choice that distinguishes the cooperative model from both traditional firms and pure open-source projects.

title: Async Retry with Exponential Backoff for OpenAI API Calls
content:
When building systems that call external APIs like OpenAI, one of the most important engineering decisions you can make is how to handle failure gracefully. Networks are unreliable, rate limits get hit, and servers occasionally hiccup. A naive implementation that crashes on the first error will frustrate users and waste work. The pattern used in strawberry-phi's data generation pipeline solves this elegantly with a combination of retry loops, semaphore-based concurrency control, and exponential backoff.

Think of it like a polite but persistent salesperson. On the first rejection, they wait a moment and try again. On the second rejection, they wait a bit longer. Each subsequent attempt doubles the wait time, giving the server room to breathe while still eventually succeeding. This is exponential backoff in a nutshell.

**The Core Pattern**

The retry loop is structured as a `for attempt in range(1, RETRY_LIMIT + 1)` block. This means if `RETRY_LIMIT` is 3, you get attempts 1, 2, and 3 — never zero, never one more than intended. The `+1` offset is a subtle but important detail: `range(1, 4)` gives `[1, 2, 3]`, which makes the attempt number human-readable in log messages and also makes the backoff math intuitive.

Inside the loop, two `async with` context managers nest together. The outer one acquires a semaphore slot, and the inner one makes the actual HTTP POST to the OpenAI completions endpoint. The semaphore acts like a bouncer at a club — only a fixed number of concurrent requests are allowed through at once. This prevents the system from hammering the API with dozens of simultaneous calls, which would trigger rate limiting and make the retry problem worse.

**Handling Success and Failure**

When the response comes back with HTTP status 200, the code parses the JSON, iterates over `result['choices']`, strips whitespace from each message content, and appends it to the `user_requests` list before returning. This handles the case where the API returns multiple completions in a single call (the `n` parameter in OpenAI requests).

When the status is anything other than 200, the code reads the error body as text and logs it. Critically, it only returns an empty list `[]` if this is the final attempt (`attempt == RETRY_LIMIT`). On earlier attempts, it falls through to the backoff sleep and tries again. This distinction is easy to get wrong — many developers accidentally return early on every error, defeating the purpose of the retry loop.

The `except Exception` block catches network-level failures like connection timeouts, DNS errors, or SSL issues that prevent a response from arriving at all. It follows the same pattern: log the error with the attempt number, return `[]` only on the last attempt, otherwise let the loop continue.

**The Backoff Calculation**

The sleep at the end of each loop iteration is `await asyncio.sleep(BACKOFF_FACTOR ** attempt)`. If `BACKOFF_FACTOR` is 2, the waits are 2¹=2 seconds, 2²=4 seconds, 2³=8 seconds. This is true exponential backoff. The `await` keyword is essential here — it yields control back to the event loop during the sleep, allowing other coroutines to make progress. A blocking `time.sleep()` would freeze the entire async program.

Note that the sleep happens *after* a failed attempt, not before the first one. This means the first try is immediate, which is the right behavior — you don't want to delay every call just because retries might be needed.

**Why Return `[]` Instead of Raising?**

Returning an empty list on total failure is a design choice that prioritizes resilience over strictness. The calling code can check `if not user_requests` and decide how to proceed, rather than having to wrap every call in a try/except. In a data generation pipeline that might be processing hundreds of topics in parallel, a few failures shouldn't crash the whole run. The empty list signals a soft failure that the orchestrator can log and skip.

**Practical Takeaways**

When implementing this pattern yourself: always log the attempt number so you can diagnose retry storms in production logs; use a semaphore to cap concurrency before you hit rate limits rather than after; make sure your backoff sleep is `await`-ed in async code; and return a safe default (empty list, None, or a sentinel value) rather than raising on exhausted retries when you want fault-tolerant pipelines. This pattern is reusable across any async HTTP client — swap `aiohttp` for `httpx` and the structure remains identical.

title: Semaphore-Based Concurrency Control in Async AI Pipelines
content:
When you run an async Python program that makes many API calls simultaneously, you face a fundamental tension: async lets you fire off hundreds of requests at once, but external APIs enforce rate limits that punish you for doing exactly that. The solution is a semaphore — a classic concurrency primitive that acts as a ticket system for shared resources.

Imagine a parking lot with a fixed number of spaces. Cars (coroutines) can only enter when a space is free. When a car leaves, it frees up a space for the next waiting car. The semaphore in Python's `asyncio` library works exactly this way.

**How It Works in Practice**

In the strawberry-phi pipeline, a semaphore is created once (typically at the top of the async function or passed in as a parameter) with a fixed count, like `semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(10)`. This means at most 10 coroutines can be inside the `async with semaphore:` block simultaneously. Any additional coroutines that reach that line will pause and wait until one of the 10 active ones exits the block.

The key insight is that `async with semaphore:` does *not* block the thread — it suspends the coroutine and yields control to the event loop. Other coroutines can run while this one waits for a semaphore slot. This is fundamentally different from a threading lock, which would block the OS thread.

**Why This Matters for OpenAI API Calls**

OpenAI's API enforces rate limits measured in requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM). If you launch 500 concurrent requests, most will fail with 429 (Too Many Requests) errors, triggering your retry logic, which then creates even more requests — a retry storm. A semaphore set to a value like 5 or 10 keeps your concurrency within the API's tolerance, making the overall pipeline faster by avoiding the retry overhead.

**Choosing the Right Semaphore Value**

The optimal semaphore count depends on your API tier's rate limits and the average latency of each call. A rough formula: if your rate limit is 60 RPM and each call takes about 2 seconds, you can sustain at most 2 concurrent calls (60/30 = 2 calls per second × 2 seconds per call = 4, with some headroom). Start conservative and increase if you're not hitting rate limits. The semaphore is a tuning knob, not a set-and-forget value.

**Combining Semaphores with Retry Logic**

Placing the semaphore *inside* the retry loop (as in strawberry-phi) means each retry attempt also acquires a semaphore slot. This is correct behavior — a retry is still a real API call that consumes rate limit quota. If you placed the semaphore outside the retry loop, a single failing request could hold a slot for the entire duration of all its retries, reducing effective throughput.

This pattern — semaphore inside retry loop, retry loop inside async task, many tasks launched with `asyncio.gather()` — is the standard architecture for high-throughput async API pipelines in Python.

title: Iterative AI-Assisted Development: Lessons from the strawberry-phi Commit History
content:
The commit history of the strawberry-phi project tells a fascinating story about what it looks like to build a real application using an AI coding assistant (gpt-engineer-app) in tight iteration loops. On a single day — September 13, 2024 — the bot made dozens of commits, many of which were fixes to problems introduced by previous fixes. Understanding this pattern is valuable for anyone using AI-assisted development tools or managing projects built with them.

**The Fix-Revert-Fix Cycle**

Several commits in the history follow a pattern of fix → revert → fix again. For example:
- `[3f68787] Fix JSONL validation error`
- `[19be22a] Reverted to edit e79684c8: Fix JSONL validation error`

This suggests the first fix introduced a regression elsewhere, requiring a revert to a known-good state before attempting a different approach. This is not a sign of failure — it's actually healthy behavior. The alternative (piling fixes on top of broken fixes) leads to tangled code that's hard to reason about. Reverting to a clean checkpoint and trying again is the right call.

**Categories of Problems Encountered**

The commit messages reveal the types of issues that commonly arise in AI-generated web applications:

1. **Data format issues**: JSONL validation errors and 404 errors for JSONL files suggest the data pipeline between the training data generator and the fine-tuning job submission had format mismatches. JSONL (JSON Lines) requires each line to be a valid, complete JSON object — a single malformed line breaks the entire file.

2. **UI state bugs**: Pagination NaN issues and undefined `getStatusColor` errors are classic JavaScript problems where a variable is used before it's defined or a function is called before the data it depends on is loaded. These are easy for AI tools to introduce when generating component code without full context of the application state.

3. **Storage and loading errors**: Storage quota errors and file loading errors point to browser localStorage limitations — a common gotcha when storing large training datasets client-side.

4. **API integration issues**: Error handling for job submission and import errors in the TrainingData module suggest the boundary between the frontend and the OpenAI fine-tuning API needed multiple iterations to get right.

**What This Tells Us About AI-Assisted Development**

AI coding assistants are excellent at generating plausible-looking code quickly, but they lack the holistic understanding of a codebase that an experienced human developer builds over time. Each fix is generated with local context — the bot sees the error and the relevant code, but may not anticipate downstream effects.

The practical implication: when using AI coding tools, treat each generated change as a hypothesis to be tested, not a solution to be trusted. The strawberry-phi workflow of small, focused commits with descriptive messages makes this testing loop fast. If a fix breaks something else, the revert is one command away.

**The Value of Descriptive Commit Messages**

Every commit in this history has a clear, specific message: not 'fix bug' but 'Fix pagination NaN issue' or 'Fix undefined getStatusColor error'. This specificity is invaluable when you need to understand what changed and why, especially in a fast-moving AI-assisted workflow where dozens of changes happen in a single day. It also makes `git bisect` — the tool for finding which commit introduced a bug — dramatically more effective.

**Key Takeaway**

Rapid AI-assisted development produces working software faster than traditional approaches, but it requires disciplined version control practices to manage the inevitable churn. Small commits, descriptive messages, and willingness to revert are the human skills that make AI coding tools effective rather than chaotic.

title: JSONL Format for Fine-Tuning Data: Why It Matters and How to Validate It
content:
The strawberry-phi project's commit history shows multiple rounds of fixes for JSONL validation errors — a problem common enough that it's worth understanding deeply. JSONL (JSON Lines) is the required format for OpenAI fine-tuning datasets, and getting it wrong is one of the most common stumbling blocks when building training data pipelines.

**What Is JSONL?**

JSONL is deceptively simple: it's a text file where each line is a complete, valid JSON object. No commas between lines, no wrapping array, no trailing newlines in the middle. A valid JSONL file for chat fine-tuning looks like this:

```
{"messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are helpful."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Hi there!"}]}
{"messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are helpful."}, {"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "4"}]}
```

Each line is independent. You can stream it line by line without loading the whole file into memory. This is why it's preferred for large datasets.

**Common Validation Failures**

The most frequent JSONL errors in fine-tuning pipelines:

1. **Trailing comma on the last message**: JSON does not allow trailing commas. `{"role": "user", "content": "hello",}` is invalid JSON and will fail parsing.

2. **Newlines inside string values**: If your assistant response contains a literal newline character, it must be escaped as `\n` in the JSON string. An unescaped newline breaks the line-per-object structure.

3. **Missing required fields**: OpenAI's fine-tuning API requires specific message structure. A conversation missing the `assistant` role turn, or using a role name other than `system`, `user`, or `assistant`, will fail validation.

4. **Empty lines**: A blank line in the middle of a JSONL file will cause parsers to attempt parsing an empty string as JSON, which fails.

5. **BOM characters**: Files saved with a UTF-8 BOM (byte order mark) will have an invisible character at the start of the first line, corrupting the first JSON object.

**Validating JSONL Before Submission**

The safest approach is to validate each line independently before uploading to the API:

```python
def validate_jsonl(filepath):
    errors = []
    with open(filepath, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        for line_num, line in enumerate(f, 1):
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                errors.append(f"Line {line_num}: empty line")
                continue
            try:
                obj = json.loads(line)
                # Check required structure
                if 'messages' not in obj:
                    errors.append(f"Line {line_num}: missing 'messages' key")
                    continue
                roles = [m.get('role') for m in obj['messages']]
                if 'assistant' not in roles:
                    errors.append(f"Line {line_num}: no assistant turn")
            except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
                errors.append(f"Line {line_num}: {e}")
    return errors
```

Running this before every upload catches the majority of issues that would otherwise result in a cryptic API error after a multi-second upload.

**Why strawberry-phi Had Repeated JSONL Errors**

The pipeline generates training data by calling the OpenAI API, parsing the responses, and writing them to JSONL. The failure points are at the boundaries: the API response might contain special characters, the string serialization might not escape them correctly, or the file writing might introduce encoding issues. Each fix in the commit history likely addressed one of these boundary cases, sometimes introducing a new one in the process.

The lesson: treat JSONL generation as a data pipeline with explicit validation at each stage, not just at the end. Validate the JSON structure immediately after parsing the API response, validate the serialized string before writing it, and validate the file after writing it. Defense in depth catches errors close to their source.

title: Decision Trees as Compiled Logic: How local-logic Encodes Expert Knowledge
content:
One of the most powerful ideas in the local-logic repository is that expert decision-making can be represented as a structured graph — a series of branching conditions that mirror how a skilled practitioner actually thinks. The poker bot examples in the codebase make this concrete, but the pattern applies far beyond card games.

Think of it like a flowchart a doctor might draw on a whiteboard. 'Does the patient have a fever? If yes, check for other symptoms. If no, consider other diagnoses.' That whiteboard sketch, when formalized, becomes a decision tree — and when that tree is compiled into a model, it becomes a reusable reasoning artifact.

**The Preflop Decision Tree**

The preflop logic in local-logic follows exactly this pattern. The root question is: what is my hand range? From there, the tree branches on position — are you in early position (few players have acted) or late position (most players have acted)? This single variable dramatically changes optimal strategy.

From early position, the tree asks: is this a premium hand? If yes, raise. If no, fold. The logic is tight because acting early means you have less information about what other players hold.

From late position, the tree pivots to stack size. With a deep stack, you have the flexibility to consider a 3-bet (re-raising the raiser), because you can afford to play a longer game. With a short stack, the decision collapses to a binary: push all-in or fold. There's no middle ground when you're low on chips.

This is compiled logic — the accumulated wisdom of thousands of hands distilled into a deterministic branching structure.

**The Postflop Decision Tree**

After the flop (the first three community cards), the decision space shifts. Now the root question is board texture — what does the community board look like, and how does it interact with your hand?

The tree branches on hand strength. A strong hand leads to value betting — you want to extract chips from opponents who have worse hands. A drawing hand (one that needs more cards to complete) leads to a pot odds calculation — is the mathematical reward worth the risk of continuing? A weak hand leads to evaluating bluff potential — can you represent a strong hand convincingly enough to make opponents fold?

Each branch then has its own sub-decisions: what size to bet, whether to continue or fold, how frequently to bluff. The tree encodes not just what to do, but why — the reasoning chain is preserved in the structure itself.

**Why This Pattern Generalizes**

The local-logic repository explicitly lists domains where this compiled-logic approach applies: finance (trading strategies), medicine (diagnostic decision support), security (threat detection), DevOps (deployment automation), and more. The poker bot is a teaching example, but the architecture is domain-agnostic.

In finance, the root question might be: what is the current market regime? Branches follow based on volatility, trend direction, and position sizing rules. In medicine, the root question might be: what are the presenting symptoms? Branches follow based on test results, patient history, and risk factors.

The key insight is that expert knowledge has structure. It isn't a random collection of facts — it's a set of conditional relationships. Compiling that structure into a model means the model can reason the way an expert reasons, not just pattern-match on surface features.

**Practical Takeaway**

When building a domain-specific AI system, start by drawing the decision tree on a whiteboard. What is the first question an expert asks? What are the possible answers, and where does each lead? Keep branching until you reach actionable decisions. That tree is your compiled logic — and it's the foundation your model should be trained to follow.
