**Educational Content Analysis: Turning Video into Study Guides**

Lecture videos are information-dense but hard to skim. By sampling frames from an educational video and prompting the AI with `"Describe what concept is being taught in this slide or diagram"`, you can automatically generate a structured summary of the entire video. Chain the per-frame responses together and you have a rough outline or study guide — without watching a single minute of footage yourself.

This also works for accessibility: generating alt-text descriptions of visual content in educational videos for learners who are visually impaired.

**Content Creation: Automating the Tedious Parts**

Video creators spend significant time reviewing footage to find usable clips, identify key moments, or write descriptions for uploads. Frame-by-frame AI analysis can automate the first pass. Send frames from a long recording with the prompt `"Rate this frame 1-10 for visual interest and explain why"` and you get a rough cut guide. Or use `"Write a one-sentence description of this scene for a video thumbnail caption"` to generate thumbnail text at scale.

**Choosing the Right Sampling Rate**

Not every frame needs analysis. Video at 30 frames per second means 1,800 frames per minute — sending all of them to an AI would be expensive and redundant. The right sampling rate depends on how fast your scene changes:

- **Slow-changing scenes** (a lecture slide, a static camera): sample every 5–30 seconds.
- **Moderate activity** (a retail floor, a construction site): sample every 1–5 seconds.
- **Fast action** (sports, security incidents): sample every 0.5–1 second, or trigger on motion detection.

Motion detection is a smart pre-filter: only send frames to the AI when something has changed, saving both cost and latency.

**Stateless by Design: Scaling Horizontally**

Because each `/process_frame` request is completely self-contained — it carries the image, the prompt, and the API key — there's no shared state between requests. This makes the service trivially easy to scale horizontally. Run multiple instances behind a load balancer and distribute frame analysis across all of them. Each worker is independent. This is the right architecture for bursty workloads, like processing a batch of recorded videos overnight.

**Where This Pattern Falls Short**

Frame-by-frame analysis has blind spots. It doesn't understand motion — it sees a snapshot, not movement. It can't track an object across frames without additional logic on your end. And it's not real-time in the strictest sense: there's network latency and model inference time on every call. For applications requiring sub-second response times or continuous tracking, you'll need to pair this with traditional computer vision techniques or purpose-built video AI models. But for the broad middle ground of monitoring, summarization, and content analysis tasks, the simplicity of this approach is a genuine advantage.

title: Security Considerations When Passing API Keys in Request Bodies
content:
The `ai-video` API accepts an OpenAI API key directly in the JSON body of each `POST /process_frame` request. This design choice is worth examining carefully, because how you handle that key determines whether your application is safe or a liability.

**Why Per-Request Keys Are Used Here**

Passing the API key in the request body makes the server completely stateless. It doesn't need a database of user credentials, a session store, or any key management infrastructure. Each request is self-sufficient. For a simple demo or a single-user local tool, this is perfectly reasonable. The complexity budget stays low.

But this design shifts the responsibility for key security entirely to the caller. The server trusts whatever key it receives and forwards it to OpenAI. If a bad key arrives, OpenAI rejects it. If a stolen key arrives, OpenAI charges the key's owner. The server is indifferent.

**The Client-Side Exposure Problem**

The most dangerous version of this pattern is when the API key lives in browser-side JavaScript. If `script.js` contains your OpenAI key — or if the browser sends it directly to `/process_frame` — anyone who opens DevTools and watches the Network tab will see it in plain text. API keys found this way get scraped by bots within hours. The result is unexpected charges on your OpenAI account and potential abuse of your quota.

The fix is straightforward: never let the API key touch the browser. Instead, store it as an environment variable on the server running `app.py`. The browser sends its request to your backend, the backend injects the key, and then forwards the request to the AI service. The key never appears in any client-visible network traffic.

```
Browser → app.py (injects key from env) → OpenAI API
```

This is called a backend proxy pattern, and it's the standard approach for any application that calls third-party APIs with secret credentials.

**HTTPS Is Non-Negotiable**

Even with a backend proxy, if your server communicates over plain HTTP, the API key is visible to anyone on the network path between the client and your server. Always serve `app.py` behind HTTPS in any non-local deployment. Tools like Let's Encrypt make this free and straightforward. If you're deploying to a cloud platform, TLS termination is usually handled automatically at the load balancer level.

**Rate Limiting and Abuse Prevention**

If you do expose this endpoint to external users — even with their own keys — consider adding rate limiting. A single client sending thousands of frames per minute could exhaust your server's resources even if OpenAI handles the AI costs. A simple rate limiter (e.g., 60 requests per minute per IP) prevents accidental or intentional abuse. Python libraries like `flask-limiter` make this easy to add to `app.py`.

**Validating the Key Format Before Forwarding**

A small defensive measure: validate that the `api_key` field looks like a real OpenAI key before forwarding it. OpenAI keys follow the pattern `sk-...` with a specific length. Rejecting malformed keys early prevents your server from making unnecessary outbound requests and gives callers clearer error messages.

**Summary of Best Practices**

- Store the API key as a server-side environment variable, not in client code.
- Use a backend proxy so the key never appears in browser network traffic.
- Enforce HTTPS for all non-local deployments.
- Add rate limiting to prevent resource exhaustion.
- Validate key format before forwarding to reduce unnecessary API calls.
- Rotate keys immediately if you suspect exposure — OpenAI's dashboard makes this straightforward.

The per-request key design in `ai-video` is a reasonable starting point for a local or demo tool. Graduating it to a production application means wrapping it with these protections. The good news is that none of these measures require significant architectural changes — they're additions to the existing `app.py` layer, not rewrites of the core logic.

title: Agentic Diffusion: Repository Architecture and Module Organization
content:
The agentic-diffusion repository is organized around a clear separation of concerns, making it easier to understand, extend, and test each part of the system independently. Think of it like a well-designed kitchen: there are dedicated stations for prep work, cooking, plating, and cleanup — each with its own tools and responsibilities, but all working together to produce the final dish.

At the top level, the repository splits into several key directories:

**core/** holds the fundamental diffusion model components. This is the engine room — the mathematical machinery that drives the noise-based generation process. Everything else depends on what lives here.

**adaptation/** contains mechanisms that allow the model to adjust its behavior based on task-specific feedback. This is what makes the system 'agentic' rather than static — it can learn and evolve during deployment.

**code_generation/** is a specialized application layer, containing components like `hybrid_llm_diffusion_generator.py`. This module combines a large language model (LLM) with a diffusion model, blending the strengths of both: LLMs excel at understanding intent and structure, while diffusion models excel at iterative refinement and diversity.

**planning/** handles multi-step reasoning and trajectory generation — useful when the system needs to produce sequences of actions rather than a single output.

**api/** exposes clean interfaces for external consumers. The `hybrid_llm_diffusion_api.py` file specifically wraps the hybrid generator behind a stable API surface, decoupling implementation details from callers.

**infrastructure/** and **testing/** round out the operational side, providing shared utilities and a three-tier test suite (unit, integration, and system tests).

The architectural layering follows a deliberate pattern: Applications (code generation, planning, custom apps) sit on top of Core APIs (Generation, Adaptation, Control), which in turn sit on top of the Diffusion Engine (Model Core with denoisers and samplers, plus Adaptation Mechanisms with optimizers and evaluators). This layered design means you can swap out or upgrade any layer without breaking the ones above it — a classic principle of good software architecture.

For developers new to this codebase, the recommended entry point is the `examples/` directory, which demonstrates end-to-end usage patterns. From there, tracing calls down through the API layer into the core gives a natural learning path that mirrors the system's own dependency graph.

title: DiffusionModel and CodeGenerator: Configuration-Driven Initialization in Agentic Diffusion
content:
Both `DiffusionModel` and `CodeGenerator` in agentic-diffusion follow a configuration-driven initialization pattern — a design choice that makes the system highly flexible without requiring code changes for different deployment scenarios. Think of the config object like a recipe card: the same kitchen (codebase) can produce very different dishes (models) just by changing the ingredients list.

**DiffusionModel Configuration**

The base `DiffusionModel` class accepts a dictionary-style config with parameters covering four main concerns:

1. *Model architecture*: `embedding_dim`, `hidden_dim`, `num_layers`, `num_heads`, `dropout` — these control the neural network's capacity and structure.
2. *Diffusion process*: `num_diffusion_steps` (default 1000) and `noise_schedule` (`linear`, `cosine`, or `custom`) — these govern how noise is added and removed during generation. More steps generally means higher quality but slower generation.
3. *Conditioning*: `model_type` can be `conditional` (generation guided by a prompt or task) or `unconditional` (free generation). Conditional is the default and most common for practical applications.
4. *Hardware*: `device` (`cpu` or `cuda`) and `precision` (`fp32`, `fp16`, `bf16`) — these control where and how efficiently the model runs. The device defaults to CUDA if available, falling back to CPU automatically.

The constructor validates the config before doing anything else — a defensive programming practice that surfaces misconfiguration early rather than producing cryptic errors deep in a training loop.

**CodeGenerator Extends with Code-Specific Defaults**

`CodeGenerator` inherits this foundation and adds parameters specific to source code:

- `max_sequence_length` (default 1024): Code can be long; this caps the token window.
- `supported_languages`: A list of programming languages the generator handles.
- `token_vocabulary_size`: The size of the token dictionary, which must match the tokenizer used.
- `use_syntax_constraints`: A boolean flag that, when enabled, applies grammar-aware constraints during generation to reduce syntactically invalid outputs.

Notably, `CodeGenerator` sets sensible defaults for any missing keys rather than raising errors — a more permissive approach than the base class. This reflects a practical tradeoff: the base model needs strict validation because wrong architecture parameters cause silent failures, while code-generation parameters have safe defaults that work for most use cases.

**Key Takeaway**

When instantiating either class, always provide at minimum the architecture and diffusion process parameters. Hardware parameters can be omitted safely. For `CodeGenerator`, specifying `supported_languages` and `use_syntax_constraints` is strongly recommended for production use, as they significantly affect output quality and validity.

title: AdaptDiffuserModel: Self-Evolving Diffusion for Planning Tasks
content:
The `AdaptDiffuserModel` class represents one of the most sophisticated components in agentic-diffusion: a diffusion model that doesn't just generate outputs, but actively adapts to task-specific feedback over time. If a standard diffusion model is like a skilled craftsperson who always works the same way, `AdaptDiffuserModel` is like an apprentice who watches the results of their work and adjusts their technique accordingly.

**Core Components**

The model is initialized with four key collaborators:

- **`noise_pred_net`**: A neural network responsible for predicting the noise component at each diffusion step. This is the heart of the denoising process — at each timestep, it estimates what noise was added so the model can subtract it and recover a cleaner signal.
- **`noise_scheduler`**: Controls how much noise exists at each timestep. The scheduler defines the 'trajectory' from pure noise back to a coherent output. Different schedules (linear, cosine) produce different quality/speed tradeoffs.
- **`reward_model`**: An optional component that scores generated trajectories for task-specific quality. This is what enables adaptation — the model can use reward signals to bias future generation toward higher-quality outputs.
- **`adaptation_rate`**: A scalar (default 0.1) controlling how aggressively the model updates based on reward feedback. Too high and the model overfits to recent tasks; too low and it adapts too slowly to be useful.

**The Forward Pass**

The `forward` method takes a noisy trajectory `x`, a timestep tensor `t`, and an optional `task` identifier. The task can be either a string label or a pre-computed embedding tensor, giving callers flexibility in how they specify what they want the model to do. The output is the predicted noise — which the sampler then uses to iteratively denoise toward a final trajectory.

**The Sample Method**

The `sample` method generates complete trajectories from scratch given a target shape and optional task specification. Internally, it runs the full reverse diffusion process: starting from random noise and repeatedly applying the denoising network guided by the noise scheduler, until a coherent trajectory emerges.

**Why This Matters for Planning**

Planning tasks require generating sequences of actions or states, not just single outputs. Diffusion models are well-suited here because they naturally produce diverse, high-quality sequences through iterative refinement. The adaptation mechanism adds a crucial capability: the model can specialize to specific planning domains (robot navigation, task scheduling, game playing) without full retraining, by using reward signals to guide generation toward domain-appropriate trajectories.

This makes `AdaptDiffuserModel` particularly valuable in agentic systems where the environment changes and the model must continuously improve its planning quality based on observed outcomes.

title: Agentic Robotics Framework: Layered Architecture Overview
content:
The Agentic Robotics framework is built like a well-organized kitchen: each layer has a specific job, and they work together without stepping on each other's toes. Understanding the layers helps you know where to look when something goes wrong — or where to plug in new capabilities.

## The Four Layers

**Application Layer (Rust / TypeScript)**
This is where your code lives. You write robot behaviors, decision logic, and integrations here. The framework supports both Rust (for performance-critical paths) and TypeScript (for rapid development and AI tooling). Think of this as the chef — it gives the orders.

**agentic-robotics-rt (Real-Time Runtime)**
This layer handles timing guarantees. It runs a dual executor: one for high-priority tasks (like motor control or collision avoidance) and one for low-priority tasks (like logging or telemetry). Deadline scheduling ensures that critical operations complete within their time windows. Priority isolation means a slow background task can never starve a fast safety-critical one. Think of this as the kitchen timer — it makes sure nothing burns.

**agentic-robotics-core (Messaging)**
This is the communication backbone. It implements a publish/subscribe model with named topics, so different parts of your system can talk without being directly connected. It uses CDR/DDS serialization (the same standard used in ROS2) and lock-free channels for high-throughput, low-latency message passing. Think of this as the restaurant's order tickets — structured, fast, and decoupled.

**Middleware Layer (Zenoh)**
Zenoh handles pub/sub discovery across the network. When a new robot or sensor comes online, Zenoh helps it find the right topics automatically. This is the maitre d' — routing messages to the right table without you having to manage seating charts manually.

## Why This Layering Matters

Each layer has a single responsibility. The real-time runtime doesn't care about serialization formats. The messaging core doesn't care about scheduling priorities. This separation means you can swap out or upgrade one layer without breaking the others — a key property for long-lived robotics systems that evolve over time.

## Getting Started

To run the framework locally:
```bash
npm install
npm run build:ts
node examples/01-hello-robot.ts
```
The `01-hello-robot.ts` example is the best starting point — it exercises the messaging layer and shows how topics are published and subscribed in practice.

title: Agentic Robotics Package Ecosystem: Choosing the Right Install
content:
Agentic Robotics follows a modular philosophy: you only install what you need. This keeps your deployment lean and your dependency surface small. Here's a practical guide to the four packages and when to reach for each one.

## The Packages at a Glance

| Package | What It Does | When to Use It |
|---|---|---|
| `agentic-robotics` | Meta-package, pulls in everything | Prototyping, full-stack projects |
| `@agentic-robotics/core` | Node.js bindings to the Rust runtime | Production apps needing the runtime |
| `@agentic-robotics/cli` | Command-line tools | Debugging, introspection, scripting |
| `@agentic-robotics/mcp` | MCP server with 21 AI tools | AI-integrated or LLM-driven robots |

## Package Deep Dives

**`agentic-robotics` (12.6 KB)**
This is the convenience package. It re-exports everything from the other packages so you don't have to manage multiple installs during development. Use it when you're exploring or building a monolith. Avoid it in production microservices where you want minimal footprint.

```bash
npm install agentic-robotics
```

**`@agentic-robotics/core` (5.3 KB)**
This is the heart of the system — the Node.js bindings that connect your TypeScript code to the underlying Rust real-time runtime and messaging core. If you're building a production robot controller, this is the one package you definitely need. Everything else is optional.

```bash
npm install @agentic-robotics/core
```

**`@agentic-robotics/cli` (2.2 KB)**
A lightweight toolset for working with the framework from the command line. Useful for inspecting topic traffic, triggering test messages, or scripting deployment tasks. Install it globally or as a dev dependency.

```bash
npm install @agentic-robotics/cli
```

**`@agentic-robotics/mcp` (26.1 KB)**
This is the AI integration layer. MCP stands for Model Context Protocol — it exposes 21 tools that AI models (like Claude or GPT-4) can call to interact with your robot swarm. If you're building an LLM-driven robot or an agentic system where a language model issues commands, this package is what bridges the gap between natural language and robot actions.

```bash
npm install @agentic-robotics/mcp
```

## Decision Rule of Thumb

- **Just exploring?** → `agentic-robotics`
- **Building a robot controller?** → `@agentic-robotics/core`
- **Adding AI/LLM control?** → `@agentic-robotics/core` + `@agentic-robotics/mcp`
- **Need CLI debugging tools?** → add `@agentic-robotics/cli` as a dev dependency

The modular design means you can start small and add packages as your system grows, without refactoring your existing code.

title: Performance Validation and Adaptive Resource Management in Agentic Robotics
content:
Running a robot swarm at scale means constantly answering two questions: 'Is the system performing within acceptable bounds?' and 'What resources will it need next?' Agentic Robotics addresses both with a layered performance system that combines real-time profiling, ML-based prediction, and automated validation.

## Performance Profiling: Knowing What's Happening Now

The `PerformanceProfiler` class runs five profilers concurrently — CPU, memory, I/O, network, and application-level metrics. Running them in parallel (via `Promise.all`) means you get a complete snapshot of the system at a single moment in time, rather than sequential measurements that might miss correlated bottlenecks.

After collecting profiles, the `ProfileAnalyzer` looks for patterns — is CPU spiking at the same time as network I/O? Is memory growing monotonically (a leak) or oscillating (normal GC)? The `PerformanceOptimizer` then turns those patterns into concrete recommendations.

Think of this like a doctor running a full panel of blood tests simultaneously rather than one at a time — you see the whole picture, not just one dimension.

## Predictive Scaling: Knowing What's Coming

The `PredictiveScaler` uses an ensemble of ML models to forecast resource needs before they become problems:

- **LSTM Time Series Model**: Good at capturing periodic patterns (e.g., a robot swarm that gets busier every morning)
- **Random Forest Regressor**: Good at handling non-linear relationships between features
- **Isolation Forest**: Detects anomalies — situations that don't fit any learned pattern
- **Ensemble Predictor**: Combines all three for higher confidence

The system collects historical data, engineers features from it (extracting trends, seasonality, lag values), trains or updates the models, and then generates a scaling plan with a confidence interval. You specify a time horizon (e.g., 3600 seconds ahead) and a confidence threshold (e.g., 95%), and the system tells you what resources to provision.

This is the difference between reactive scaling (adding robots after you're already overloaded) and proactive scaling (having resources ready before demand peaks).

## Performance Validation: Knowing If You're Within Bounds

The `PerformanceValidator` runs five validators in parallel against your test results:

- **SLA Validator**: Are you meeting your service-level agreements?
- **Regression Validator**: Is this release slower than the last?
- **Scalability Validator**: Does performance degrade gracefully as load increases?
- **Reliability Validator**: Are there failure modes under stress?
- **Efficiency Validator**: Are you using resources well, or wasting capacity?

Violations from any validator bubble up into a unified `overall` result with a list of specific violations and recommendations. This makes it easy to fail a CI/CD pipeline on a performance regression without writing custom threshold logic.

## Automated Test Campaigns

The `AutomatedPerformanceTester` orchestrates six test suite types — load, stress, volume, endurance, spike, and configuration — according to a schedule and set of constraints. Results are validated in real-time as each test completes, so a catastrophic failure in an early test can halt the campaign before wasting time on later tests.

Together, these systems form a closed loop: profile what's happening, predict what's coming, validate that you're within bounds, and test continuously to catch regressions before they reach production.

title: ACP Session Identity: How ACPX Tracks Agent Sessions Across the Runtime
content:
When you run an AI agent through ACPX, one of the trickiest problems is keeping track of *which session is which* — especially when multiple agents are running concurrently, adapters are spawning subprocesses, and the system needs to correlate events back to the right conversation thread. This is what ACP session identity solves.

**What is a session identity?**

Think of a session identity like a wristband at a concert. Everyone who enters gets one, and every interaction — buying a drink, entering a VIP area — is tied back to that wristband. In ACPX, the session identity is a single canonical key called `agentSessionId`. Every message, event, and error that flows through the runtime carries this identifier so the system always knows which agent conversation it belongs to.

Earlier versions of the codebase used a more ambiguous field called `_meta.sessionId`. This was a looser convention — adapters could pass it in different ways, and the runtime had to guess or reconcile. The refactor (commits `3594524` and `b522ac8`) formalized this: `_meta.sessionId` is now explicitly mapped to `agentSessionId` at the session layer, and the ACP protocol layer enforces that only this single canonical key is accepted. The CLI was also updated (`cfefbc2`) to emit only these canonical keys, removing any legacy aliases that could cause ambiguity downstream.

**Why does this matter in practice?**

Imagine an orchestration system running five parallel agent tasks. Each task fires off tool calls, streams partial results, and may encounter errors. Without a reliable session identity, correlating a tool error back to the right agent task is guesswork. With `agentSessionId` enforced at every layer — from ACP metadata passthrough (`22a1ce7`) to CLI output — the runtime can route, log, and debug with confidence.

The session identity also flows *through* the system rather than being generated at each layer. When an ACP message arrives carrying a `sessionId` in its metadata, ACPX passes that value through as the `agentSessionId` rather than minting a new one. This means external orchestrators that assign their own session IDs retain traceability end-to-end.

**The detached warm session owner pattern**

One architectural subtlety introduced alongside session identity hardening is the concept of a *detached warm session owner*. Normally you might assume the component that *starts* a session (the prompt caller) is also the one responsible for *keeping it alive*. ACPX separates these concerns.

The warm session owner is detached from the prompt caller (`e62f01d`). This means a session can be pre-warmed and held open by one part of the runtime while a completely different caller sends prompts into it. Think of it like a restaurant that pre-heats ovens before customers arrive — the kitchen (warm session owner) and the waiter taking orders (prompt caller) are independent. This improves latency for repeated interactions and makes the architecture more resilient: if a prompt caller disconnects, the warm session doesn't immediately tear down.

**Key takeaways**

- `agentSessionId` is the single source of truth for session identity in ACPX; all other aliases are deprecated.
- Session IDs originating from ACP metadata are passed through rather than replaced, preserving external traceability.
- The warm session owner is architecturally separate from the prompt caller, enabling pre-warming and resilience.
- These changes collectively make multi-agent, concurrent workloads far easier to debug and operate.

title: ACPX Error Strategy: Handling Failures Gracefully in ACP-Aligned Agent Pipelines
content:
Error handling in agent systems is deceptively hard. An agent might fail because a tool timed out, because the underlying model returned something unparseable, or because the user's input triggered a policy violation. Each of these failure modes deserves a different response — and getting it wrong means either silently swallowing errors or crashing the entire pipeline unnecessarily.

ACPX addresses this with a two-tier error strategy that separates *general* errors from *permanent* errors, both aligned to how the ACP protocol itself thinks about failures.

**General errors: recoverable and retryable**

The general error strategy (`8b673f2`) covers the broad class of failures that are transient or context-dependent. Network hiccups, adapter startup delays, tool call timeouts — these are errors where retrying or falling back makes sense. ACPX models these in a way that's compatible with ACP's own error semantics, so errors surfaced to an ACP client carry the right structure and codes for the client to make intelligent retry decisions.

A key refinement here is how errors interact with queued operations. If multiple tool calls are queued and one fails, earlier versions of ACPX could emit duplicate error events — once when the failure was detected and again when the queue was drained. Commit `c948a6f` specifically addresses this: queued failures are deduplicated so a downstream consumer sees exactly one error event per failure, not a confusing burst.

Error metadata is also preserved through the pipeline (`2111ae0`). When a prompt error is queued (for example, because the system is in a non-interactive mode and can't ask the user for clarification), the original error context travels with it. This means when the error is finally emitted, it carries enough information to diagnose the root cause rather than just reporting a generic failure.

**Permanent errors: fail fast and clearly**

Some errors are not worth retrying. A malformed skill configuration, an adapter that fundamentally doesn't support a requested capability, or a protocol violation — these are *permanent* errors. Retrying them wastes time and can mask the real problem.

ACPX splits permanent error handling into its own strategy (`1efef5f`). Permanent errors are surfaced immediately and distinctly, with clear signals that no retry should be attempted. This is especially important in CI/CD pipelines where ACPX runs in `json-strict` mode — a mode designed for machine consumption where every output must be valid JSON and errors must be unambiguous.

**json-strict mode and interactive prompts**

One subtle challenge: some errors in ACPX would normally trigger an interactive prompt asking the user what to do. In `json-strict` mode (used in CI and automated pipelines), there's no user to ask. ACPX handles this with a non-interactive fail policy (`e1a8ebc`): if a local tool prompt would normally pause for user input, the system instead applies the configured fail policy automatically — typically failing fast with a structured error.

At the same time, commit `e33e521` ensures that *legitimate* interactive prompts (like setup wizards) are still preserved even when json-strict mode is active for other output. The system distinguishes between prompts that are part of the user experience and errors that need structured handling.

**Practical guidance**

- In automated pipelines, always run ACPX in `json-strict` mode and configure a non-interactive fail policy to avoid hangs.
- Expect exactly one error event per failure — deduplication is handled internally.
- Distinguish between transient failures (worth retrying) and permanent failures (fix the configuration) using the error codes ACPX emits.
- Error metadata is preserved end-to-end, so structured logs will contain full diagnostic context.

title: Getting Started with ACPX: Installation, Skill Setup, and the Setup Prompt
content:
ACPX is an ACP-compatible agent execution layer that sits between your orchestration logic and the underlying AI adapters (like Claude or OpenCode). Getting it running involves a few distinct steps: installing the CLI, configuring skills, and understanding how the setup prompt guides you through initial configuration.

**Installation**

The recommended way to run ACPX without committing to a global install is via `npx`:

```
npx acpx@latest
```

Using `@latest` ensures you always pull the most recent published version rather than a cached older copy. This is especially important during the current alpha phase, where the API and configuration format are still evolving. If you prefer a persistent global install (useful for frequent local development), the setup prompt also exposes that option (`6abd2e9`) — but for CI environments, `npx acpx@latest` is the safer default since it's reproducible and version-pinned by your pipeline.

**Alpha status**

ACPX is currently in alpha. The documentation explicitly carries an alpha disclaimer (`08728dc`), which means the public API, configuration schema, and adapter contracts may change between releases. If you're building on top of ACPX, pin to a specific version in production and review the changelog before upgrading.

**Installing skills**

Skills are the capability modules that ACPX loads to extend what an agent can do — think of them as plugins that teach the agent new tools or behaviors. The skill installation command has been simplified to:

```
acpx --skill install
```

This replaces earlier, more verbose invocation patterns (`3c464fe`). When you run this command, ACPX launches an interactive skillflag wizard (`9ede3d5`) that walks you through selecting and configuring the skills appropriate for your use case. The wizard asks questions about your environment and desired capabilities, then writes the appropriate configuration flags — you don't need to know the exact flag names upfront.

**Adapter registration**

ACPX supports multiple underlying AI adapters. Two notable ones are Claude and OpenCode:

- The **Claude adapter** is launched via `npx -y` (`3637248`), meaning ACPX will automatically accept the npx prompt to install the adapter package if it isn't already present. This makes first-run setup frictionless.
- The **OpenCode adapter** runs in ACP mode (`dc87fab`), meaning it communicates with ACPX using the standard ACP protocol rather than a custom integration. This is significant because it means OpenCode benefits from all of ACPX's ACP-layer features — session identity tracking, structured error handling, and metadata passthrough — without any adapter-specific special-casing.

**OpenClaw integration**

ACPX also has a planned integration with OpenClaw (`b999903`), an open-source tool orchestration layer. The integration plan positions OpenClaw as a way to extend ACPX's local tool execution capabilities, particularly for complex multi-step tool chains. Details are still being finalized given the alpha status, but the architecture is designed so OpenClaw slots in as another adapter rather than requiring changes to the core runtime.

**Quick reference**

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Run without installing | `npx acpx@latest` |
| Install globally | `npm install -g acpx` |
| Install a skill | `acpx --skill install` |
| Check version | `acpx --version` |

For CI pipelines, combine `npx acpx@latest` with `json-strict` mode and a non-interactive fail policy to get fully automated, machine-readable output with no interactive prompts blocking your build.

title: Vibium v1.5: What's New in Browser Automation (February 2026)
content:
Vibium's v1.5 release cycle (culminating in the 26.2 release notes) brought a significant wave of new capabilities across its JavaScript client, Python client, CLI, and MCP (Model Context Protocol) interfaces. Understanding what shipped helps you choose the right tools and patterns for your browser automation workflows.

**Selector Strategies: More Ways to Find Elements**

One of the most practical additions is expanded selector strategy support. Beyond CSS selectors and basic IDs, Vibium now supports XPath, test IDs (`data-testid` attributes), placeholder text, alt text, title attributes, and label text as first-class ways to locate elements. Think of these as different ways to describe a person to a stranger — you might say their name, their job title, or what they're wearing. Similarly, you can now find a button by its visible label, an image by its alt text, or an input by its placeholder. This makes tests more readable and resilient to DOM structure changes.

**Semantic Find Locators in MCP and CLI**

The `map` command gained a `--selector` flag for scoped element discovery, letting you narrow the search to a subtree of the page rather than scanning everything. Paired with semantic find locators now available in both the MCP and CLI interfaces, this means AI agents and automation scripts can describe what they're looking for in human terms and let Vibium resolve the actual element.

**Window and Viewport Control**

New `vibium window` and `set-window` CLI commands (plus matching MCP tools) give you programmatic control over browser window size and position. The `page.scroll()` method landed in both the JS and Python sync APIs, rounding out the set of viewport interactions. Tests covering viewport and window behavior were added across all four interfaces (JS sync, Python sync, MCP, CLI), so you can trust these features are well-exercised.

**Downloads API**

Handling file downloads in browser automation has historically been awkward. Vibium's new sync download API adds `path` and `saveAs`/`save_as` parameters, letting you specify exactly where downloaded files land on disk. Tutorial documentation and tests for both JS and Python were added alongside the feature, making it straightforward to integrate download handling into your test suites.

**Actionability Checks**

Borrowing a concept from Playwright, Vibium's proxy interaction functions now include actionability checks. Before clicking or typing, Vibium verifies that the target element is visible, enabled, and stable — not hidden behind a spinner or disabled by JavaScript. This catches a whole class of flaky test failures where automation tries to interact with an element that isn't ready yet. A community fix (PR #69) also ensured the actionability reason field is correctly propagated rather than silently dropped.

**Architecture: Features Package Removed**

Internally, the `features` package was removed and all consumers migrated to the proxy layer. This is an architectural consolidation — rather than having two places where browser capabilities were managed, everything now flows through a single proxy. Users shouldn't notice this change directly, but it simplifies the codebase and reduces the surface area for bugs.

**Tracing and BiDi Recording**

For debugging and observability, action-level tracing was added alongside opt-in BiDi (WebDriver BiDi protocol) command recording. Tracing lets you see exactly what Vibium did and when, which is invaluable when a test fails intermittently. BiDi recording captures the raw protocol commands, useful for advanced debugging or building tooling on top of Vibium's browser communication layer.

title: Debugging Vibium: Process Leaks, Fork Bombs, and Windows Access Errors
content:
Browser automation tools sit at the intersection of process management, network communication, and OS-level permissions — which means when things go wrong, the failures can be surprising. Vibium's February 2026 bug fixes addressed several real-world issues that users encountered. Understanding these bugs helps you diagnose similar problems and appreciate the safeguards now in place.

**Chrome Process Leaks**

Two separate Chrome process leak bugs were fixed. The first: Chrome processes were surviving Python REPL exits. When you use Vibium interactively in a Python REPL and close the session (or hit Ctrl+C), the browser should shut down cleanly. Before the fix, the Chrome process would linger in the background, consuming memory and potentially interfering with subsequent runs. The second leak occurred on explicit browser close — calling the close method didn't always terminate the underlying Chrome process. Both are now fixed, meaning Vibium properly cleans up after itself.

If you're on an older version and notice Chrome processes accumulating (check with `ps aux | grep chrome` on Linux/macOS or Task Manager on Windows), upgrading to the patched version is the right move.

**The Fork Bomb: A Subtle Python Packaging Hazard**

This one is worth understanding in depth because it's a non-obvious failure mode. Vibium ships a Python client that wraps a CLI binary. When the Python client needs to invoke the CLI, it uses `shutil.which()` to find the binary on the system PATH. The bug: if the Python client's own wrapper script was named `vibium` and appeared on the PATH before the actual binary, `shutil.which('vibium')` would return the Python wrapper itself. The wrapper would then call itself, which would call itself again — a fork bomb, spawning processes until the system ran out of resources.

The fix involves making the Python client smarter about distinguishing the real binary from its own wrapper. The lesson for anyone building similar tools: when a Python package wraps an external binary, be explicit about the binary's location rather than relying on PATH resolution, which can be ambiguous in environments where the package itself installs a same-named script.

**Windows: "Access is Denied (0x5)"**

Windows users encountered an `Access is denied (0x5)` error, which has been documented in the debugging guide. This error code (0x5 = ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED) typically surfaces when Vibium tries to launch or communicate with a browser process and Windows security policy blocks the operation. Common causes include:

- Running Vibium in a restricted user context without permission to spawn child processes
- Antivirus or endpoint protection software intercepting the browser launch
- Chrome being installed in a location the current user can't execute from
- Named pipe or socket permission issues when Vibium tries to connect to the browser's debugging port

The debugging documentation now covers this scenario with specific remediation steps. If you hit this error, check whether running as administrator resolves it (to isolate permission issues), then work backward to grant the minimum necessary permissions rather than running elevated permanently.

**Documentation Fixes**

A few documentation issues were also corrected: method names in the BiDi data collector docs were wrong (a particularly frustrating kind of bug — the code works but the docs send you in the wrong direction), the getting-started guide was split into JS-specific and Python-specific versions to reduce confusion, and CONTRIBUTING.md examples were updated to use `./vibium` (the local binary) rather than a globally installed command.

These fixes reflect a maturing project: the core functionality is solid enough that documentation accuracy and edge-case process management become the priority.

title: Vibium's Multi-Interface Architecture: CLI, MCP, JS, and Python Working Together
content:
One of Vibium's distinguishing design choices is that it exposes the same browser automation capabilities through four distinct interfaces: a JavaScript (sync) client, a Python (sync) client, a CLI (command-line interface), and MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools. Understanding why this architecture exists and how the interfaces relate helps you pick the right one for your use case — and understand why features tend to land across all four simultaneously.

**Why Four Interfaces?**

Different consumers have different needs. A developer writing a Node.js test suite wants a JavaScript API that feels native to their ecosystem. A data scientist automating browser tasks in a Jupyter notebook wants Python. A DevOps engineer running automation in a shell script wants CLI commands. An AI agent orchestrating browser actions through a tool-calling protocol wants MCP. Rather than forcing everyone into one paradigm, Vibium maintains all four.

The tradeoff is maintenance burden — every new feature needs to be implemented and tested in four places. You can see this in the commit history: viewport/window tests were added "across JS sync, Python sync, MCP, and CLI" in a single commit, and semantic find locators landed in "MCP and CLI" together. The team treats the four interfaces as a unit.

**The Proxy as the Unifying Layer**

The recent removal of the `features` package and migration of all consumers to the proxy layer reveals the underlying architecture. There's a central proxy that handles the actual browser communication (likely via WebDriver BiDi or Chrome DevTools Protocol). The four client interfaces are all thin layers on top of this proxy — they translate their respective idioms (Python method calls, CLI flags, MCP tool invocations) into proxy calls, and translate proxy responses back into their respective formats.

This is analogous to how a restaurant kitchen (the proxy) serves the same food regardless of whether the order came in through a waiter, a phone call, a mobile app, or a drive-through window. The interfaces differ; the core operation is the same.

**MCP: The AI Agent Interface**

MCP (Model Context Protocol) deserves special attention because it's the newest and least familiar interface for most developers. MCP is a protocol for exposing tools to AI agents — think of it as a standardized way for a language model to say "I want to click this button" and have Vibium execute it. The `vibium window`, `set-window`, and semantic find locator tools added to MCP mean AI agents can now control browser window state and find elements by description, not just by CSS selector.

This positions Vibium as infrastructure for agentic browser automation — not just human-written test scripts, but AI systems that navigate the web autonomously.

**Actionability Checks: Consistency Across Interfaces**

The Playwright-style actionability checks added to the proxy interaction functions benefit all four interfaces simultaneously. Because the check happens at the proxy layer (before the action is dispatched to the browser), every interface gets the same guarantee: Vibium won't try to click a hidden or disabled element. This is the architectural payoff of the unified proxy approach — cross-cutting concerns like actionability, tracing, and BiDi recording can be implemented once and apply everywhere.

**Choosing the Right Interface**

- **JavaScript client**: Best for Node.js test suites, CI pipelines in JS ecosystems, and when you want tight integration with frameworks like Mocha or Jest.
- **Python client**: Best for data workflows, Jupyter notebooks, and teams already using Python testing tools like pytest.
- **CLI**: Best for shell scripts, quick one-off automation, and composing Vibium with other Unix tools via pipes.
- **MCP**: Best for AI agent workflows where a language model needs to control the browser as part of a larger task.

All four are first-class citizens in Vibium's development — when a feature ships, it ships everywhere.

title: How ClaWHub Handles Proxy Environments and HTTP Networking Fixes
content:
When you run a CLI tool or server-side application inside a corporate network, a Docker container, or a CI/CD pipeline, your outbound HTTP requests often need to travel through a proxy. Proxies act like a post office: instead of your application sending a letter directly to the recipient, it hands the letter to the post office, which forwards it on your behalf. If your application doesn't know the post office exists, the letter never arrives.

ClaWHub went through a multi-step process to get this right, and understanding that journey teaches you a lot about how proxy support actually works in Node.js.

**Step 1: Recognizing the environment variables**

The standard way to tell a Unix-style application about a proxy is through the `HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` environment variables. These are set by system administrators or CI platforms and are supposed to be automatically respected by well-behaved HTTP clients. The first fix (commit `8b5f242`) made ClaWHub read these variables at all — previously, the application was ignoring them entirely, meaning any deployment behind a proxy would silently fail to reach external services.

**Step 2: Using the right HTTP agent**

Reading the environment variable is only half the battle. You also need to pass that proxy configuration into your HTTP client in a way it understands. Commit `ed961e4` switched ClaWHub to use `EnvHttpProxyAgent` from the Undici library. Think of an HTTP agent as the driver who actually knows the road rules. `EnvHttpProxyAgent` is a specialized driver that automatically reads `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` from the environment and routes traffic accordingly — you don't have to manually wire the variable into every request.

**Step 3: Removing HTTP/2 conflicts**

A separate but related networking fix addressed a `fetch failed` error on Node.js 22+. The culprit was the `allowH2` flag on the Undici agent. HTTP/2 is a newer, faster protocol, but it doesn't play well with all proxy configurations and introduced incompatibilities in newer Node.js versions. Removing `allowH2` restored reliable HTTP/1.1 behavior — sometimes the older, simpler road is the one that actually gets you there.

**Step 4: Finalizing and testing**

Commit `6ea7a07` finalized the proxy support and added changelog credits, while `bc37ec7` completed a related registry-URL migration with full test coverage. This pattern — fix the behavior, then lock it in with tests — is the right way to handle infrastructure-level changes where silent regressions are especially painful.

**The lesson for your own projects**

When building any networked application, proxy support is easy to overlook because it works fine on your laptop but breaks in production. The checklist is: (1) read `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` from the environment, (2) pass those values into your HTTP client's agent or transport layer, (3) avoid protocol features like HTTP/2 that may conflict with proxy infrastructure, and (4) write integration tests that simulate proxy conditions. ClaWHub's commit history is a clean example of fixing each layer in turn.

title: VirusTotal Verdict Lifecycle: How ClaWHub Manages Security Scan State
content:
When ClaWHub receives an uploaded skill package, it doesn't just store it immediately — it routes the file through VirusTotal for malware scanning. Managing the state of that scan over time turns out to be surprisingly tricky, and the fixes in ClaWHub's history illustrate a classic problem in distributed systems: how do you keep a piece of data's status accurate when the underlying truth can change?

**The three-state problem**

A VirusTotal verdict isn't binary. A file can be `clean`, `suspicious`, or `flagged`. The complication is that these states can transition in both directions. A file initially flagged as suspicious might later be re-analyzed and come back clean — perhaps because a virus definition was updated, or because the initial detection was a false positive. ClaWHub needs to reflect that improvement accurately.

Think of it like a credit score. Your score can go up or down over time, and any system that caches your score needs to update it when the underlying data changes — not just when it gets worse.

**Bug 1: Stale suspicious flags**

Commit `8343f0b` fixed a case where a file's `suspicious` flag was never cleared even after VirusTotal returned a clean verdict. The flag was being set correctly when a problem was detected, but the code path that handled an improved verdict didn't include a step to remove the old flag. The fix was straightforward: when a clean verdict arrives, explicitly clear any previously set suspicious marker. The lesson here is that state machines need to handle all valid transitions, not just the ones you thought about first.

**Bug 2: The `alreadyFlagged` gate blocking clean verdicts**

Commit `311bf1a` fixed a more subtle issue. There was a guard in the de-escalation logic that checked whether a file was `alreadyFlagged` before allowing a status downgrade. The intent was to prevent unnecessary writes, but the condition was written in a way that also blocked legitimate clean verdicts from being applied. A file that had ever been flagged could never be marked clean, even if VirusTotal said it was safe.

This is a common class of bug: a guard clause meant to optimize or protect one scenario inadvertently blocks a valid code path. The fix added a proper check on the actual current status before deciding whether de-escalation should proceed.

**Bug 3: Race conditions in scan sync**

The changelog also notes fixes for scan sync race conditions and retry behavior in scan and backfill paths. Race conditions in scanning happen when multiple processes try to update the same file's verdict simultaneously — for example, a real-time scan and a background backfill job both finishing at nearly the same time. Without coordination, you can end up with inconsistent state: one process writes `clean`, the other writes `suspicious`, and the final value depends on which write lands last.

The fix involves ensuring that verdict updates are applied with proper ordering guarantees — typically by using atomic operations or by structuring the update logic so that a newer, more authoritative verdict always wins.

**What this teaches about security state management**

Security verdicts are not append-only logs — they are mutable state that must be kept consistent with an external source of truth. When designing similar systems, always model all possible state transitions explicitly, ensure that improvement paths (not just degradation paths) are handled, guard against race conditions in async scan workflows, and write tests that simulate verdict changes over time rather than just initial scan results.

title: Rate Limiting, Download Deduplication, and the 429 Retry-After Pattern
content:
Two related but distinct rate-limiting problems appear in ClaWHub's recent fix history, and together they form a complete picture of how a well-behaved API citizen handles traffic constraints — both as a consumer of external APIs and as a provider of its own.

**Being a good API consumer: the Retry-After header**

When an external service is overwhelmed, it responds with HTTP status `429 Too Many Requests` and often includes a `Retry-After` header telling you how long to wait before trying again. Commit `3956ca7` fixed how ClaWHub interprets this header.

The bug was using an absolute timestamp interpretation instead of a relative delay. The `Retry-After` header can be expressed in two ways: as a number of seconds to wait (relative), or as an HTTP date string (absolute). If your code always treats the value as absolute but the server sends a relative value like `30` (meaning "wait 30 seconds"), you might calculate a retry time in the distant past or far future, causing either immediate hammering or indefinite waiting.

The fix ensures ClaWHub uses a relative delay calculation when the header value is a plain number. This is the correct behavior per the HTTP specification and makes ClaWHub a polite API consumer that backs off appropriately when upstream services are under load.

The analogy: if a restaurant tells you "your table will be ready in 20 minutes," you wait 20 minutes from now — you don't try to interpret that as a clock time.

**Being a good API provider: download rate limiting and deduplication**

On the other side of the equation, ClaWHub also needed to protect its own download endpoints from abuse. The changelog describes adding download rate limiting with per-IP/day deduplication and scheduled deduplication pruning.

Here's why deduplication matters alongside rate limiting: a naive rate limiter counts every request. But if you're tracking download counts for analytics or billing, you don't want a single user refreshing a page 50 times to inflate your numbers. Deduplication means that if the same IP downloads the same file multiple times in a day, only the first counts as a unique download event.

The scheduled pruning step is equally important. Deduplication records accumulate over time and need to be cleaned up periodically — otherwise your database grows indefinitely with stale tracking data. A scheduled job that removes records older than the deduplication window (one day, in this case) keeps storage bounded.

The fix also notes that moderation gating and deterministic zips are preserved. Deterministic zips mean that the same input files always produce the same zip archive byte-for-byte, which matters for integrity checking and caching — if the zip changes on every request, you can't reliably cache or verify downloads.

**The GitHub API rate limit case**

A third rate-limiting scenario appears in the upload gate: handling GitHub API rate limits during package validation. The fix adds support for an optional authenticated lookup token. GitHub's API allows 60 unauthenticated requests per hour but 5,000 authenticated ones. By optionally accepting a token, ClaWHub can dramatically increase its headroom for GitHub lookups without requiring authentication for every user.

**The unified lesson**

Rate limiting appears at every layer of a distributed system. As a consumer, respect `Retry-After` headers and back off correctly. As a provider, combine rate limiting with deduplication to get accurate metrics and protect your infrastructure. Always plan for cleanup of the state your rate limiter accumulates, and use authentication to expand your own API quotas when talking to third-party services.

title: Structuring a GenAI Project: Separation of Concerns in Practice
content:
One of the most important skills in building production-ready GenAI systems is knowing how to organize your code so that each piece has a single, clear responsibility. The GenAI-Superstream project is a good case study in this principle, sometimes called 'separation of concerns.'

Think of it like a well-run restaurant. The kitchen (model training and prediction) doesn't take orders directly from customers. The waitstaff (server/client layer) handles communication. The pantry (data module) manages ingredients. The manager's office (config and utils) keeps everything coordinated. Each role is distinct, and swapping out one chef doesn't require retraining the waitstaff.

The project's `src/` directory reflects this cleanly:

- **data/**: `loader.py` and `preprocessor.py` handle getting raw data into a usable shape. Nothing else in the system needs to know where the data came from or how it was cleaned.
- **model/**: `trainer.py` and `predictor.py` are purely concerned with machine learning logic — fitting a model and making predictions. They receive preprocessed data; they don't fetch it.
- **server/**: `mcp_server.py` and `interface.py` expose the model's capabilities to the outside world via MCP (Model Context Protocol) and Gradio. The server doesn't know how the model was trained.
- **client/**: `mcp_client.py` and `interface.py` consume the server's exposed tools. The client doesn't care about model internals.
- **utils/**: `logger.py`, `config.py`, and `validators.py` are cross-cutting concerns — things every layer needs but that shouldn't live in any single layer.

This structure has a practical payoff. When the `DataPreprocessor` class supports a `scaling_strategy` parameter (like `'standard'` or `'minmax'`), you can swap scaling strategies without touching the model or server code. When the `MCPServer` changes its port or host, only the server module cares. The `ConfigManager` uses a singleton pattern — one shared configuration object for the whole application — so configuration changes propagate everywhere without passing config objects through every function call.

The `advanced/` subdirectory shows what this looks like at larger scale, adding a `perplexity/` integration layer (for PerplexityAI), a `db/` layer (DuckDB for analytics), and an `analytics/` layer for metrics and visualizations. Each new capability gets its own subdirectory rather than being bolted onto existing files.

The takeaway: before writing a single line of GenAI code, sketch out which layer owns which responsibility. Data wrangling, model logic, serving, and configuration are almost always worth separating. The cost is a few extra files; the benefit is a codebase where you can change one thing without breaking everything else.

title: Exposing ML Models as MCP Tools via Gradio
content:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an emerging standard that lets AI agents call external tools in a structured, discoverable way. One practical pattern in the GenAI-Superstream project is using Gradio as the bridge between a trained ML model and an MCP-compatible interface — essentially turning a Python function into a tool that any MCP-aware agent can invoke.

Here's the core idea. Gradio can launch a web interface with `mcp_server=True`, which causes it to automatically expose your Python functions as MCP tools. The tool's name, description, and parameter schema are derived from the function's docstring and type annotations. This means writing a good docstring isn't just documentation hygiene — it's literally the API contract that agents will use to discover and call your tool.

The `MCPServer` class in the project encapsulates this pattern:

1. **Initialization**: The server takes a `predictor` instance (the trained model wrapper), a `host`, and a `port`. It doesn't train the model — it receives an already-trained predictor, keeping concerns separated.
2. **Setup**: A `setup()` method creates a Gradio `Blocks` interface wrapping the predictor. This is where the visual UI and the MCP tool surface are configured together.
3. **Tool exposure**: An `expose_prediction_tool()` method defines the function that gets registered as an MCP tool. The docstring on this function is critical — MCP clients read it to understand what the tool does, what inputs it expects, and what it returns.

A concrete analogy: imagine a vending machine (the MCP server). The buttons on the front are the tools. Each button has a label (the function name), a description (the docstring), and accepts specific input (typed parameters). An agent browsing available tools is like someone reading the vending machine's panel to decide what to press.

The default configuration in `ConfigManager` shows the expected server settings: host `0.0.0.0`, port `7860`, and `mcp_server: True`. Port 7860 is Gradio's default, which means the same server simultaneously serves a human-readable web UI and a machine-readable MCP endpoint — two audiences, one deployment.

For the `DataPreprocessor`, the `validate_feature_vector()` method acts as a gatekeeper before any prediction is made. In an MCP context this matters because agents may pass malformed inputs. Validation at the tool boundary prevents bad data from reaching the model and produces clear error messages that agents can interpret and retry.

Key lessons for building MCP-exposed ML tools:
- Write precise, complete docstrings — they become your tool's API documentation for agents.
- Validate inputs at the server boundary, not deep inside model code.
- Use a configuration singleton so host/port changes don't require hunting through multiple files.
- Keep the predictor stateless with respect to the server — the server should be restartable without retraining the model.

title: The Singleton Pattern in GenAI Configuration Management
content:
Configuration management sounds boring until you've spent an afternoon debugging why two parts of your application are using different API keys or different server ports. The GenAI-Superstream project addresses this with a classic software pattern: the singleton.

A singleton is a class that guarantees only one instance of itself ever exists in a running program. Think of it like the thermostat in a building — there's exactly one, everyone reads from it, and changing it affects the whole building. If every room had its own thermostat with its own settings, coordinating temperature would be chaos.

The `ConfigManager` class implements this using Python's `__new__` method:

```python
class ConfigManager:
    _instance = None
    
    def __new__(cls, config_file=None):
        if cls._instance is None:
            cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
        return cls._instance
```

The first time you call `ConfigManager()`, Python creates a new instance and stores it in `_instance`. Every subsequent call returns that same stored instance. The `__init__` method guards against re-initialization by checking for a sentinel attribute (`initialized`), so the config file is only loaded once even if `ConfigManager()` is called multiple times across different modules.

The default configuration reveals the system's expected shape:
- **model**: type (`logistic_regression`) and hyperparameters (`max_iter: 200`)
- **server**: host, port, and whether to enable MCP (`mcp_server: True`)
- **client**: the server URL the client should connect to

This structure means that when the `MCPServer` reads its host and port, and when the `mcp_client` reads its server URL, they're both reading from the same object with the same values. There's no risk of the server binding to port 7860 while the client tries to connect to port 8080 because someone passed different arguments to two different config constructors.

The `advanced/config.py` module in the project extends this pattern for a more complex application with database connections, API keys (loaded from `.env` files), and analytics settings. The `.env.sample` file documents which environment variables are expected — a good practice that makes the configuration contract explicit for new developers.

Practical guidelines for GenAI config management:
- Use a singleton for application-wide settings that multiple components share.
- Separate default values (in code or a YAML file) from environment-specific overrides (in `.env` files). Never commit secrets.
- Load configuration once at startup, not on every function call — reading files repeatedly is slow and introduces race conditions.
- Document every configuration key, its type, its default, and what happens if it's missing. The `.env.sample` pattern is a lightweight way to do this.

The singleton pattern is one of the simplest architectural decisions you can make that pays dividends immediately in a multi-module GenAI project.

title: Power Prompt: Taking Manual Control of ChatGPT's API Parameters
content:
When you use ChatGPT through the standard web interface, you're essentially driving a car with an automatic transmission — it makes a lot of decisions for you behind the scenes. Power Prompt is a Chrome extension that hands you a manual gearbox. It exposes the underlying API parameters — model selection, temperature, token limits, and prompt length — directly inside the chat interface, so you can tune how the model behaves without touching a dashboard or writing API calls.

Think of it this way: OpenAI's API is like a professional kitchen with dozens of dials and knobs. The standard ChatGPT web interface gives you a single 'cook' button. Power Prompt gives you access to the actual stove.

## The Four Knobs You're Controlling

**Model Selection**
OpenAI offers multiple models (GPT-3, GPT-3 Sandbox, and others), each with different capability and cost profiles. In the Power Prompt options page, a dropdown labeled 'Model' lets you switch between them. This matters if your account has access to several models and you want to use a lighter, faster model for simple tasks and a more capable one for complex reasoning — without navigating away from the chat window. Note: available models depend on your OpenAI account type and may require additional permissions or credits.

**Temperature**
Temperature controls how 'random' or 'creative' the model's output is. Picture a spectrum from a strict librarian to a free-associating poet. A low temperature (closer to 0) produces conservative, predictable, consistent output — ideal for factual summaries, legal drafts, or code generation where you want reliable results. A high temperature (closer to 1 or above) produces more varied, surprising, creative output — useful for brainstorming, creative writing, or generating diverse options. Most users never touch this setting in the standard interface; Power Prompt makes it a first-class control.

**Tokens**
Tokens are roughly equivalent to words or word fragments — 'ChatGPT' is one token, 'unbelievable' might be two. The token parameter sets the maximum number of tokens the API will generate in its response. If you're generating short summaries, capping tokens prevents the model from rambling. If you need long-form output, you raise the ceiling. Controlling this before the API processes your request is more efficient than hoping the model self-regulates.

**Prompt Length**
Separate from output tokens, prompt length controls the maximum size of the input text you send to the API. This sets a ceiling on how long your input can be, which matters when you're working with large documents or complex multi-part instructions.

## Who Should Use This

Power Prompt is most valuable for people who use ChatGPT in a structured, repeatable way:

- **Domain specialists** (legal, marketing, engineering) who run the same prompt structures repeatedly and want to save them as templates rather than retyping
- **Researchers or analysts** who need to experiment with temperature to find the right creativity-consistency balance for a specific task
- **Developers** who want to prototype API behavior without writing code
- **Power users** on accounts with multiple model access who want to switch models fluidly

If you only use ChatGPT casually for one-off questions, the standard interface is probably sufficient. Power Prompt adds value when you're doing systematic, repeated, or parameter-sensitive work.

## A Word on Security

As with any browser extension, install Power Prompt only from trusted, verified sources. Extensions have access to browser activity, so vetting the source before installation is standard practice — not paranoia.

title: Prompt Templates in Power Prompt: Saving and Reusing Structured Inputs
content:
One of the most underrated time sinks in working with ChatGPT is retyping the same prompt scaffolding over and over. If you draft legal summaries, generate code in a specific style, or write marketing copy with a consistent structure, you're probably rebuilding the same prompt skeleton from scratch every session. Power Prompt's prompt template feature solves this directly.

## What a Prompt Template Is

A prompt template is a pre-written, pre-formatted block of text that you store inside Power Prompt and reuse as input to the OpenAI API. Think of it like a form letter with blanks you fill in — the structure, tone, and instructions are fixed; only the specific details change.

For example, a legal professional might save a template like:

> 'Summarize the following contract clause in plain English, identify any ambiguous terms, and flag potential liability risks. Clause: [INSERT CLAUSE HERE]'

Instead of typing that instruction set every time, they load the template, drop in the clause, and send. The structure is consistent; the variable content changes.

## Why This Matters Beyond Convenience

Templates aren't just about saving keystrokes. They enforce consistency. When you're generating outputs that feed into a workflow — reports, code snippets, structured data — having the same prompt structure each time means the model receives the same instructions each time. That reduces variance in output quality and makes results more predictable and comparable.

This is especially important in team settings or regulated industries where prompt drift (gradually changing how you phrase requests) can introduce inconsistency in outputs that downstream processes depend on.

## Combining Templates with Parameter Control

The real power comes from pairing templates with Power Prompt's parameter controls. You might have:

- A 'brainstorm' template with high temperature (more creative, varied output) and a high token limit
- A 'factual summary' template with low temperature (conservative, consistent output) and a capped token count
- A 'code generation' template locked to a specific model with medium temperature

Each template can be designed for a specific use case, and when you load it, you're not just loading the text — you're loading the right configuration for that task.

## Practical Setup

To use prompt templates in Power Prompt, navigate to the extension's options page. From there you can create, name, save, and load templates. When you're ready to use one, load it into the input field, make any variable substitutions, adjust parameters if needed, and send.

The workflow becomes: load template → fill in variables → confirm parameters → send. That's a significant reduction in cognitive overhead compared to rebuilding context from scratch each session.

## When Templates Are Most Valuable

- **High-frequency tasks**: Any prompt you run more than a few times per week is a candidate for templating
- **Multi-step instructions**: Complex prompts with several conditions or constraints benefit most from being saved — they're the hardest to reconstruct accurately from memory
- **Collaborative workflows**: Shared templates ensure everyone on a team is sending equivalent instructions, making outputs more comparable
- **Regulated or auditable outputs**: Saved templates create a record of what instructions were used to generate a given output

If you've ever spent five minutes trying to remember exactly how you phrased a prompt that worked really well last week, prompt templates are the direct solution to that problem.

title: Understanding Temperature and Tokens: The Two Most Important LLM Output Controls
content:
When you interact with a language model through an API, two parameters have more impact on output quality than almost anything else: temperature and token count. Most users never see these controls in standard chat interfaces. Tools like Power Prompt expose them directly, which makes understanding what they actually do essential.

## Temperature: The Creativity Dial

Temperature is one of those terms that sounds technical but maps cleanly to an intuitive concept: how surprising should the next word be?

Language models generate text by predicting the probability of each possible next token given everything that came before. Temperature modifies how those probabilities are weighted before the model makes its selection.

- **Low temperature (e.g., 0.1–0.3)**: The model heavily favors the highest-probability tokens. Output is predictable, consistent, and conservative. The model essentially takes the 'safest' path through the probability space. Good for: factual Q&A, legal summaries, structured data extraction, code generation where correctness matters more than novelty.

- **High temperature (e.g., 0.8–1.2)**: The model spreads probability weight more evenly across options, making lower-probability tokens more likely to be selected. Output becomes more varied, surprising, and creative — but also more prone to errors or tangents. Good for: brainstorming, creative writing, generating diverse options, exploring unconventional angles.

A useful analogy: low temperature is a cautious editor who always picks the most conventional word. High temperature is a poet who deliberately reaches for the unexpected one. Neither is universally better — the right setting depends on what you're trying to produce.

A common practical pattern: start a brainstorming session at high temperature to generate diverse ideas, then drop the temperature when you shift to refining or summarizing those ideas.

## Tokens: The Length Budget

Tokens are the unit of text that language models process. A token is roughly 0.75 words in English — so 100 tokens is approximately 75 words. 'ChatGPT' is one token. 'Unbelievable' might be two.

The token parameter in Power Prompt sets the maximum number of tokens the model will generate in its response. This is a hard ceiling, not a target — the model will stop when it hits the limit, even mid-sentence if necessary.

**Why you'd want to control this:**

- **Cost control**: API calls are priced per token. Capping output length prevents runaway costs on tasks where you only need a short answer.
- **Format enforcement**: If you need a one-paragraph summary, setting a token limit prevents the model from producing a five-paragraph essay.
- **Pipeline compatibility**: If downstream systems expect output of a certain size, token limits help enforce that constraint at the source.

Setting tokens too low truncates output mid-thought. Setting them too high on simple tasks wastes API budget. The right value depends on the expected output length for your specific use case.

## Prompt Length: The Input Budget

Separate from output tokens, prompt length controls the maximum size of the text you send *to* the model. This matters when you're feeding in large documents, long conversation histories, or complex multi-part instructions. Models have a combined context window (input + output tokens combined), so managing prompt length helps ensure you have room for the output you need.

## Putting It Together

These three parameters — temperature, output tokens, prompt length — form a basic configuration profile for any given task. A well-configured profile for 'legal clause summarization' looks very different from one for 'creative story generation.' Power Prompt lets you set these per session and save them alongside prompt templates, so your configuration travels with your use case rather than being reset to defaults every time.

title: Markov Chains as a Foundation for Prompt Engineering Libraries
content:
Markov chains are one of the oldest and most elegant ideas in probability theory, and they turn out to be surprisingly relevant to modern prompt engineering. Understanding why requires stepping back and thinking about what a Markov chain actually is.

Imagine you are walking through a city, and at every intersection you flip a coin to decide which way to turn. Your next position depends only on where you are right now — not on the entire history of how you got there. That memoryless property is the defining characteristic of a Markov chain. Mathematically, the probability of moving to the next state depends solely on the current state, not on the sequence of states that preceded it.

This simple idea has enormous practical power. Text generation, for example, can be modeled as a Markov process: given the current word (or sequence of words), what is the probability distribution over the next word? Early chatbots and autocomplete systems were built almost entirely on this principle. You train a model by counting how often word B follows word A in a large corpus, and then at generation time you sample from those learned probabilities.

Modern large language models are far more sophisticated, but they inherit this probabilistic, sequential structure. The attention mechanism in a transformer can be thought of as a learned, high-dimensional generalization of the Markov transition matrix. Instead of looking only at the immediately preceding token, transformers look at all previous tokens — but they still produce a probability distribution over the next token at each step.

This is where prompt engineering enters the picture. When you craft a prompt, you are essentially steering the Markov-like process of the language model.
