You are placing the model at a particular starting state — a particular point in the high-dimensional space of possible continuations — and hoping that the probability distributions it has learned will carry it toward the output you want. A well-engineered prompt is one that places the model in a region of that space where the desired behavior is highly probable.

A library built around Markov chains for prompt engineering can offer several concrete benefits. First, it can provide interpretable baselines. Before deploying a complex LLM-based pipeline, you can prototype with a simple Markov text model to verify that your data pipeline, evaluation metrics, and output parsing logic all work correctly. Markov models are fast, deterministic given a fixed seed, and easy to debug.

Second, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods — a family of algorithms that use Markov chains to sample from complex probability distributions — are directly applicable to prompt optimization. You can treat the space of possible prompts as a distribution you want to sample from, where the probability of a prompt is proportional to how well it performs on your task. MCMC gives you a principled way to explore that space without exhaustively trying every possibility.

Third, understanding the Markov structure of language models helps you reason about failure modes. When a model gets stuck repeating itself, that is analogous to a Markov chain entering an absorbing state — a state from which it cannot escape. When a model drifts off topic over a long conversation, that is analogous to the chain diffusing away from the region of state space you wanted it to stay in. Recognizing these patterns by name gives you a vocabulary for diagnosing and fixing them.

For practitioners getting started with a Markov-chain-based prompt engineering library, the recommended path is to first read the installation documentation carefully, then experiment with the provided examples before attempting to integrate the library into a production project. The CLI options — including those implemented in the initial release commits — give you a quick way to test the library's capabilities without writing any code.

Looking ahead, the most exciting frontier for this kind of library is combining classical Markov chain theory with neural approaches. Hybrid systems that use learned neural embeddings to define the state space, but classical Markov transition logic to navigate it, can offer the best of both worlds: the expressiveness of neural representations and the interpretability and mathematical guarantees of Markov models. This is an active area of research, and libraries that build a solid Markov foundation today are well positioned to incorporate these advances as they mature.

title: Building and Using a CLI-Driven Prompt Engineering Workflow
content:
Command-line interfaces often get overlooked in favor of notebooks and web UIs, but for prompt engineering work a well-designed CLI is one of the most powerful tools you can have. It composes naturally with shell scripts, plays well with version control, and makes it easy to run reproducible experiments. The markov-chains library takes this approach seriously, with CLI options implemented as a first-class feature from the initial release.

The core idea behind a CLI-driven prompt engineering workflow is that every experiment should be expressible as a single command that can be logged, replicated, and diffed. When you run a prompt through a web UI and copy the output into a document, you lose the exact parameters you used, the version of the model, and the random seed. When you run the same experiment through a CLI, all of that information lives in your shell history, your CI logs, or a simple wrapper script.

Here is how to think about structuring such a workflow. At the outermost layer, you have shell scripts or Makefiles that define named experiments. Each experiment calls the CLI with a specific set of flags — the prompt template, the model parameters, the output format, and the evaluation criteria. These scripts live in version control alongside your code, so you always know exactly what you ran to produce a given result.

At the next layer down, the CLI itself handles argument parsing, configuration loading, and dispatching to the appropriate library functions. A well-implemented CLI will support both positional arguments for the most common use cases and named flags for everything else. It will read defaults from a configuration file so that you do not have to repeat yourself across experiments, but allow any default to be overridden on the command line.

The library's CLI options cover the key dimensions of a prompt engineering experiment: specifying the input text or template, controlling generation parameters like temperature and maximum length, selecting the output format, and optionally running evaluation against a reference output. Each of these dimensions corresponds to a knob you will want to turn as you iterate on your prompts.

One practical tip: use the CLI's output formatting options to produce structured output — JSON or CSV rather than plain text — even when you are just exploring. Structured output is trivially parseable by downstream tools, so you can pipe it into jq, awk, or a Python script without any fragile text parsing. This habit pays dividends when you want to aggregate results across many experiments.

For teams, the CLI approach also simplifies onboarding. A new team member can clone the repository, follow the installation instructions, and immediately run the same experiments that produced your existing results. There is no need to share notebook state or explain which cells to run in which order. The CLI is the interface, and the documentation tells you how to use it.

As the library evolves, expect the CLI to gain additional options that expose more sophisticated prompt engineering capabilities — things like chain-of-thought scaffolding, few-shot example management, and automated prompt optimization. Building your workflow around the CLI now means you will be able to adopt these features incrementally, adding new flags to your existing scripts rather than rearchitecting your entire pipeline.

title: Setting Up Cline in VS Code for AI-Assisted Development
content:
Cline is an AI coding assistant that lives inside VS Code, giving you a conversational interface to write, test, and refactor code without leaving your editor. Think of it like having a senior developer sitting next to you who can read your entire project structure and respond to multi-step instructions — what the federated-mcp project calls 'multi-hop prompts.'

## What You Need Before Starting

Before installing Cline, make sure you have:
- VS Code installed
- An account with an API provider such as OpenRouter, Anthropic, or OpenAI
- Deno installed (required for the federated-mcp demo environment)

## Step-by-Step Installation

**1. Install the Cline Extension**

Open VS Code and navigate to the Extensions marketplace, or go directly to:
https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=saoudrizwan.claude-dev

Search for "Cline" and click Install.

**2. Open Cline in a New Tab**

Once installed, open the command palette with `CMD + Shift + P` (Mac) or `CTRL + Shift + P` (Windows/Linux). Type and select:

```
Cline: Open In New Tab
```

This gives Cline its own workspace panel, keeping it visible alongside your code.

**3. Configure Your API Provider**

Cline needs a backend language model to function. In the Cline settings panel, link it to your preferred API provider. OpenRouter is recommended for the federated-mcp workflow because it gives you access to multiple models through a single API key, letting you switch between Claude, GPT-4, and others without reconfiguring.

**4. Set the Project Root Directory**

This step is critical and often overlooked. Tell Cline where your project lives by setting the root directory. This gives Cline visibility into your file structure, imports, and dependencies — without it, Cline is essentially working blind, unable to understand how your files relate to each other.

Think of this like giving a new contractor a map of the building before asking them to fix the plumbing. Context is everything.

**5. Install Deno for the Demo Environment**

The federated-mcp project uses Deno as its runtime for edge functions and the MCP server. Install it with:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://deno.land/x/install/install.sh | sh
```

Deno is a modern JavaScript/TypeScript runtime that, unlike Node.js, has built-in TypeScript support and a permission-based security model — meaning scripts can't access your filesystem or network unless you explicitly allow it.

## Why This Setup Matters for the RUV Bounce Method

The RUV Bounce Method uses Cline to run sequences of prompts that build on each other — writing a test first, then implementing the function that passes it, then refactoring. This test-driven loop works best when Cline has full project context, which is why steps 4 and 5 above are non-negotiable.

With everything configured, you can give Cline instructions like "write a failing test for the federation proxy auth handler" and it will understand your existing code structure well enough to produce something immediately useful rather than generic boilerplate.

title: Connecting Supabase to the Federated MCP Project
content:
The federated-mcp project uses Supabase as its backend infrastructure — handling database storage, edge function hosting, and authentication. If you've never used Supabase before, think of it as Firebase but built on PostgreSQL, with a strong emphasis on open standards and self-hosting options.

This guide walks you through linking your local federated-mcp project to a live Supabase instance.

## What You're Connecting

The federated-mcp architecture deploys edge functions (small serverless functions that run close to the user) through Supabase. These functions handle things like intent detection, webhook processing, and meeting information retrieval. To deploy and manage them, your local environment needs to know which Supabase project to talk to and have permission to do so.

You'll need two pieces of information: your **Project ID** and an **Access Token**.

## Getting Your Project ID

1. Log into your Supabase dashboard at https://supabase.com
2. Open your project
3. Navigate to **Settings → API**
4. Copy the value labeled **Project ID**

This ID is a unique identifier for your Supabase project — like a postal address for your backend.

## Generating an Access Token

1. Go to https://supabase.com/dashboard/account/tokens
2. Click **Generate new token**
3. Give it a descriptive name (e.g., `federated-mcp-dev`)
4. Copy the token immediately — Supabase will not show it again

The access token is your credential. Guard it like a password. Anyone with this token can manage your Supabase project.

## Adding Credentials to Your Environment

Create or open the `.env` file in your project root and add:

```env
SUPABASE_PROJECT_ID=your_project_id
SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN=your_access_token
```

Never commit this file to version control. Add `.env` to your `.gitignore` if it isn't already there.

## Initializing and Linking Supabase Locally

With credentials in place, run these two commands:

```bash
supabase init
```

This creates a `supabase/` directory in your project with configuration files for local development, migrations, and edge function definitions.

```bash
supabase link --project-ref your_project_id
```

This connects your local Supabase CLI to your remote project. After this, commands like `supabase functions deploy` will push your edge functions to the correct project.

## What Happens After Linking

Once linked, the federated-mcp project can deploy its edge functions — including the intent detection and webhook handlers — directly to Supabase's global edge network. The Deno runtime powers these functions, which is why the Deno installation step in the Cline setup guide is a prerequisite.

A useful mental model: Supabase is the cloud infrastructure, Deno is the engine running your functions on that infrastructure, and the Supabase CLI is the control panel you use from your laptop to manage both.

title: How the Federated MCP Project Was Built: A Commit History Walkthrough
content:
One of the best ways to understand a codebase is to read its commit history in order — it tells the story of how the project came to life, decision by decision. The federated-mcp project was built rapidly in a single day (November 26, 2024) using AI-assisted development with Cline and aider. Here's what that progression reveals about how federated AI systems get assembled.

## The Build Sequence

**Foundation First: Types and Auth**

The first meaningful commit (`9326107`) established core types and an auth manager. This is the right instinct — before writing any logic, define the data shapes and security boundaries your system will operate within. Types are the skeleton; everything else hangs off them.

**Transport Layer: WebSocket and HTTP**

Next (`c4ba6de`) came the core MCP server with WebSocket and HTTP handling. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) needs to communicate in real time, which is why WebSocket support is included alongside standard HTTP. WebSockets keep a persistent connection open — useful when an AI agent needs to stream responses or receive push updates from a federation of servers.

**The Deno Runtime and Federation Proxy**

Commit `848580a` implemented the Deno MCP server, federation proxy, and an initial test suite together. Notice that tests came in the same commit as the implementation — this reflects the test-driven approach encouraged by the RUV Bounce Method. The federation proxy is the component that routes requests between multiple MCP servers, which is the core architectural idea of the project.

**Node.js Compatibility**

Commit `d573a87` added a `package.json` for Node.js compatibility, followed by `b07104e` which converted Deno tests to Jest. This dual-runtime support (Deno and Node.js) reflects a practical reality: different deployment environments favor different runtimes, and a federated system needs to be portable.

**Official SDK Integration**

Commit `5ae6818` integrated the official MCP TypeScript SDK. This is a maturity signal — early in development you might implement protocol handling yourself to understand it, then swap in the official library once the design stabilizes.

**Edge Functions**

Commit `807c06e` added the first edge functions: intent detection, meeting info retrieval, and webhook handling. These are the actual capabilities the federation exposes — the "what can this system do" layer built on top of the "how does this system communicate" infrastructure established earlier.

**Operational Tooling**

The final commits added keyboard input handling for interactive server management (`3df2b76`), enhanced logging and status display (`efa268a`), and installation/startup scripts (`3448fd1`). This is a common pattern: build the core system first, then add the operational tooling that makes it livable to run and debug.

## What This Pattern Teaches

The build order — types → transport → proxy → tests → SDK → edge functions → ops tooling — is a reusable template for building federated AI infrastructure. Each layer depends on the one below it, and skipping steps creates technical debt that compounds quickly. The fact that this entire stack was assembled in one day using AI-assisted tools demonstrates both the power of that workflow and the importance of having a clear architectural sequence before you start.

title: ARCADIA Engine Architecture: How AI, Vectors, and Game Logic Stack Together
content:
ARCADIA is a Rust-based game engine framework built around the idea that modern games need more than physics and rendering — they need adaptive, learning AI baked into the foundation. Understanding its architecture means understanding how several specialized subsystems cooperate in layers, much like how a city has utilities (power, water, roads) running beneath the buildings people actually see.

At the very bottom sits the **Core Game Engine**, which handles the fundamentals: an Entity Component System (ECS) for managing game objects, a World state, AI primitives, and procedural generation. Think of this as the city's infrastructure — it exists to support everything above it.

One layer up is the **Performance Layer**, composed of three modules: Cache, Memory, and Metrics. These are the engine's nervous system for efficiency. The cache prevents redundant computation, the memory manager controls allocation lifecycles, and metrics provide observability into what's actually happening at runtime. Without this layer, the AI systems above it would be powerful but sluggish.

Above the performance layer live three major AI subsystems — **VIVIAN**, **PARIS**, and **aiTOML** — each with a distinct responsibility:

- **VIVIAN** (Vector Index Virtual Infrastructure for Autonomous Networks) handles how knowledge is stored and retrieved. It uses vector index data structures to enable semantic search across game state, agent memory, and world data. If PARIS is the brain that learns, VIVIAN is the long-term memory that brain draws from.
- **PARIS** is the adaptive intelligence engine. It processes player actions through a pipeline: feedback collection → pattern detection → model updates → hyperparameter tuning → strategy selection → new model generation. This is a full online learning loop embedded directly in the game runtime.
- **aiTOML** manages workflow configuration, allowing AI behaviors and pipelines to be defined declaratively rather than hardcoded.

Finally, at the top of the stack sits the **integration layer**, which connects ARCADIA to external engines like Unreal Engine 5 or Unity. ARCADIA doesn't replace these engines — it augments them with its AI and vector infrastructure.

The source tree reflects this layering cleanly. Under `src/`, you'll find `ai/` (7 AI systems plus integration), `agentdb/` (persistent learning storage), `vivian/` (5 vector infrastructure modules), and `paris/` (5 adaptive intelligence modules). Standalone files like `vector_index.rs`, `cache.rs`, `memory.rs`, and `code_dna.rs` (procedural generation) fill in the cross-cutting concerns.

The key architectural insight is **separation of concerns with tight coupling at defined interfaces**. VIVIAN doesn't know about PARIS's learning algorithms; PARIS doesn't manage memory directly. Each layer exposes a clean API (unified in `lib.rs`) and depends only on the layer beneath it. This is what makes the system testable (6 integration test files), benchmarkable (10 benchmark files), and deployable across multiple platforms per `DEPLOYMENT.md`.

For developers integrating ARCADIA, the practical entry point is `lib.rs` — the public API surface — combined with the tutorials and integration docs. The `.claude/` directory (113 configuration files) also reveals that the project uses Claude Flow for AI-assisted development workflows, meaning the tooling itself is AI-augmented.

title: VIVIAN: Vector Infrastructure as the Memory Backbone of AI Game Agents
content:
Most game AI systems are stateless — an NPC makes a decision, acts on it, and forgets everything. VIVIAN (Vector Index Virtual Infrastructure for Autonomous Networks) is ARCADIA's answer to that limitation. It provides the persistent, searchable memory layer that allows AI agents to store experiences, retrieve relevant context, and make decisions informed by history rather than just the current frame.

The core idea behind VIVIAN is **vector indexing**. When an agent has an experience — say, a player outflanked it using a particular route — that experience isn't stored as a rigid database row. Instead, it's converted into a high-dimensional vector (an embedding) that captures the *semantic meaning* of the event. Later, when a similar situation arises, the agent can query its memory not by exact match but by similarity: "What past experiences are most like what I'm seeing right now?"

This is analogous to how human memory works. You don't remember every detail of every meal you've eaten, but if someone asks you about a time you had bad seafood, your brain retrieves semantically related memories efficiently. VIVIAN does the same for game agents, but with mathematical precision.

VIVIAN is described as **decentralized**, which matters for scalability. In a large game world with hundreds of agents, a centralized memory store becomes a bottleneck. A decentralized design means each agent (or cluster of agents) can maintain its own vector index, with coordination happening only when needed. This keeps the system robust — no single point of failure — and scalable as the number of agents grows.

In the ARCADIA source tree, VIVIAN occupies 5 modules under `src/vivian/`. It works in close coordination with `vector_index.rs` (the core semantic search implementation) and `agentdb/` (the persistent learning storage layer with 6 modules). Together, these form the full memory stack: VIVIAN provides the indexing and retrieval logic, AgentDB provides the durable storage, and `vector_index.rs` provides the low-level similarity search primitives.

The connection to PARIS (the adaptive learning system) is critical. PARIS generates embeddings at the end of its learning pipeline — these embeddings are what VIVIAN indexes. So the flow is: player action → PARIS learns from it → PARIS generates an embedding → VIVIAN stores and indexes that embedding → future queries retrieve it. VIVIAN is the persistence layer that makes PARIS's learning durable across sessions.

For developers building on ARCADIA, VIVIAN is the component to reach for when you need agents that remember, adapt over time, or share learned knowledge across a game world. Its vector-based approach means you get fuzzy, context-aware retrieval rather than brittle exact-match lookups — which is exactly what believable, adaptive game AI requires.

title: PARIS: The Online Learning Loop That Makes ARCADIA Agents Adapt in Real Time
content:
Most game AI is designed once and shipped. Behavior trees, finite state machines, scripted responses — these are authored by developers and remain static after launch. PARIS (the adaptive intelligence subsystem in ARCADIA) takes a fundamentally different approach: it learns from player behavior continuously, updating its models while the game is running.

Understanding PARIS means understanding its **pipeline** — a sequence of managers that each handle one stage of the learning loop.

**Stage 1: Feedback Manager**
Every player action triggers an event that flows into the Feedback Manager. This component captures raw signals: what did the player do, what was the game state, what was the outcome? Think of it as a stenographer that records everything without judgment.

**Stage 2: Feedback Aggregation**
Raw events are noisy. A player might spam a button accidentally, or a single action might generate dozens of low-level events. The aggregation step consolidates these into meaningful signals — filtering noise and grouping related events into coherent behavioral episodes.

**Stage 3: Learning Manager**
This is where pattern detection happens. The Learning Manager analyzes aggregated feedback to identify recurring patterns: Does this player always approach from the left? Do they prefer stealth over combat? Pattern detection feeds directly into model updates — the internal representations PARIS uses to predict and respond to player behavior.

**Stage 4: Optimization Manager**
Once patterns are detected and models updated, the Optimization Manager tunes the system's parameters. This includes hyperparameter tuning (adjusting learning rates, thresholds, weights) and strategy selection (choosing which behavioral strategy best fits the detected player profile). This stage is what separates PARIS from a simple rule-updater — it's doing genuine optimization, not just bookkeeping.

**Stage 5: Layers Manager**
The final stage applies the optimized changes to PARIS's actual model layers, potentially introducing new models entirely. It then generates embeddings — vector representations of the learned patterns — which are handed off to VIVIAN for persistent storage.

The full loop is: **observe → aggregate → detect patterns → optimize → update models → store embeddings**. This cycle runs continuously during gameplay, meaning agents become measurably better at responding to a specific player the longer that player plays.

This architecture has important practical implications. Because each stage is a discrete manager with defined inputs and outputs, the pipeline is testable in isolation. You can unit-test the Learning Manager without running the full game loop. You can benchmark the Optimization Manager independently. The 10 benchmark files and 6 integration test files in ARCADIA's repository reflect exactly this kind of staged testability.

For game designers, PARIS means AI difficulty and behavior can self-calibrate without manual tuning. For developers, it means the AI system is observable (each manager can emit metrics to the Performance Layer) and extensible (new managers can be inserted into the pipeline). The combination of PARIS's learning with VIVIAN's memory storage is what gives ARCADIA agents genuine long-term adaptability.

title: How the Agent Name Service (ANS) Works: A DNS for AI Agents
content:
When you type a website address into your browser, a system called DNS quietly translates that human-readable name into a numeric IP address your computer can actually use. The Agent Name Service (ANS) does something analogous for AI agents: it gives each agent a stable, verifiable identity that other agents and systems can look up, trust, and communicate with.

Think of ANS as a combination of a phone book, an ID card issuer, and a security guard — all rolled into one service.

**What ANS Actually Stores**

At its core, ANS maintains a registry of agents. Each registered agent gets a record that includes:

- A unique name (3–64 characters, alphanumeric with hyphens, underscores, and dots)
- A public key for cryptographic verification
- One or more endpoints (addresses where the agent can be reached, with protocol, address, port, and health status)
- A list of capabilities the agent advertises
- A certificate that binds the agent's name to its public key
- Metadata fields for arbitrary additional context
- Timestamps for creation, last update, and expiration
- A status field (active, suspended, revoked, etc.)

This maps closely to how TLS certificates work on the web: a certificate authority vouches that a particular public key belongs to a particular domain. ANS does the same for agents.

**The Certificate Layer**

Every registered agent receives a certificate. This certificate is not just a label — it's a cryptographically signed document that lets any other party verify the agent is who it claims to be. The certificate schema tracks the subject (the agent), the issuer (ANS itself), validity windows (not_before and not_after), the public key, a fingerprint, and a status.

When an agent presents itself to another system, that system can validate the certificate against ANS. If someone tampers with the certificate — changing the agent name, swapping the public key, or altering capabilities — the signature check fails. The `certificate_verification` example in the repository specifically demonstrates this: it checks both a legitimate certificate and a deliberately tampered one, showing how the validation catches the forgery.

**Registration Flow**

Registering an agent is a multi-step process with validation gates:

1. The caller submits an agent name, metadata, optional IP address, and domain.
2. ANS validates the name format (length, allowed characters).
3. ANS checks rate limits — you can't flood the registry with registrations.
4. If validation passes, ANS generates a key pair and certificate for the agent.
5. The agent record is written to the database, linking the agent to its certificate and endpoints.
6. The caller receives back the agent record plus its certificate.

The `validateAgentDetails` workflow step in the codebase enforces these rules explicitly, collecting all validation failures into an `issues` array rather than stopping at the first error — so callers get complete feedback in one round trip.

**Resolution and Caching**

Looking up an agent by name follows a cache-first pattern: ANS checks an in-memory cache before hitting the database. If the cache misses, it queries the database, then updates the cache for future lookups. This is the same pattern CDNs use — serve from the edge when possible, fall back to origin when necessary.

The resolution flow also validates the incoming request (is the name well-formed? are the options valid?) before doing any database work, failing fast on bad inputs.

**Protocol Support**

ANS isn't tied to a single communication protocol. The `protocols.ts` module provides formatters for both A2A (Agent-to-Agent) and MCP (Model Context Protocol), meaning the same registry can serve agents that speak different languages. When you resolve an agent, you can get its endpoint formatted for whichever protocol your system uses.

**Batch Operations**

For systems that need to register or resolve many agents at once, ANS supports batch operations. The batch example also demonstrates security filtering — when resolving a batch, you can filter out agents whose certificates are invalid or whose status is not active, so your system only works with verified, healthy agents.

**Running the Examples**

The repository ships with six runnable examples covering the full feature surface:

- `basic_registration.ts` — register one agent, inspect its certificate
- `certificate_verification.ts` — validate legitimate and tampered certificates
- `batch_operations.ts` — register and resolve multiple agents with security filtering
- `custom_configuration.ts` — tune name validation rules and rate limits
- `usage.ts` — a comprehensive walkthrough of all features
- `quiet_examples.ts` — same features with minimal log output, useful for CI environments

Each runs with `npx ts-node examples/<filename>.ts`, requiring no build step.

In short, ANS gives the multi-agent ecosystem the same foundation the web has relied on for decades: a trustworthy, queryable registry that lets participants verify identity before they communicate.

title: ANS Security Architecture: Threat Modeling, Security Events, and Certificate Integrity
content:
A name service is only as useful as it is trustworthy. If an attacker can register a fake agent, forge a certificate, or flood the registry with junk entries, the whole system breaks down. ANS addresses this through three interlocking security layers: certificate integrity, security event tracking, and an active threat modeling integration.

**Layer 1: Certificate Integrity**

Every agent in ANS is bound to a cryptographically signed certificate. The certificate records the agent's name, public key, issuer, and validity window. The fingerprint field provides a short, unique identifier derived from the certificate content.

The critical property is tamper-evidence. If any field in the certificate changes after issuance — the agent name, the public key, the validity dates — the signature no longer matches. ANS's certificate validation step catches this immediately. This is why the `certificate_verification` example tests both a clean certificate and a deliberately modified one: the modified one fails validation, demonstrating that the system cannot be fooled by a copy-and-edit attack.

Certificates also have a `status` field (active, revoked, expired). A certificate that has been revoked — because the agent was compromised or decommissioned — will fail validation even if the signature is technically intact. This mirrors how certificate revocation works in web PKI.

**Layer 2: Security Event Logging**

ANS maintains a `SECURITY_EVENTS` table in its database. Every significant action — registrations, certificate operations, resolution attempts, authentication events — can generate a security event record. Each record captures:

- A timestamp
- An event type and severity
- Source and target identifiers
- A description of what happened
- Whether a mitigation was applied, and what it was

The event source schema is notably detailed. Sources are typed into categories like `AGENT_ACTIVITY`, `CERTIFICATE_OPERATION`, `DIRECTORY_ACCESS`, `API_GATEWAY`, `AUTHENTICATION_SERVICE`, `NETWORK_MONITOR`, `THREAT_INTELLIGENCE`, `SYSTEM_MONITOR`, `AGENT_SELF_REPORT`, `USER_REPORT`, and `AUTOMATED_SCAN`. This taxonomy matters because it lets downstream analysis distinguish between, say, an agent reporting its own anomalous behavior versus an external network monitor flagging unusual traffic patterns.

Each event also records the outcome of the triggering action: `SUCCESS`, `FAILURE`, `BLOCKED`, or `UNKNOWN`. This makes the event log useful not just for forensics but for real-time alerting — a spike in `BLOCKED` outcomes from `CERTIFICATE_OPERATION` sources is a signal worth investigating.

**Layer 3: Threat Model Integration via Mastra.ai**

Beyond passive logging, ANS integrates with Mastra.ai for active threat modeling. The `ThreatModelService` class manages this integration. On initialization, it:

1. Connects to the database service
2. Authenticates with the Mastra.ai API using an API key and endpoint (configurable via environment variables)
3. Registers the ANS service instance with Mastra.ai so it appears in the broader threat model
4. Initializes typed threat handlers — each `ThreatType` gets a dedicated handler function
5. Schedules periodic security posture assessments

The periodic assessment is important. Rather than only reacting to events as they happen, ANS proactively evaluates its own security posture on a schedule. This is analogous to a security team running regular vulnerability scans rather than only responding to incidents.

The repository includes both a full Mastra integration (`mastra.ts`) and a simplified fallback (`mastra-simple.ts`). The fallback exists for environments where the full Mastra.ai connection isn't available — the system degrades gracefully rather than failing entirely.

**Rate Limiting as a First Line of Defense**

Before any of the cryptographic machinery runs, ANS enforces rate limits at the registration step. The `validateAgentDetails` workflow checks whether the caller has exceeded their allowed registration rate. This prevents a simple denial-of-service attack where an adversary floods the registry with registrations to exhaust resources or obscure legitimate entries.

Rate limiting is configurable via the custom configuration options (demonstrated in `custom_configuration.ts`), so operators can tune thresholds to match their deployment environment.

**Defense in Depth**

The security design follows a defense-in-depth philosophy: no single layer is expected to stop all attacks. Rate limiting stops floods. Name validation stops malformed entries. Certificate signing stops forgery. Revocation stops compromised agents from continuing to operate. Event logging provides visibility. Threat modeling provides proactive assessment. Each layer assumes the others might be bypassed and adds its own check.

For teams building multi-agent systems, this architecture provides a template: identity infrastructure for agents needs the same rigor as identity infrastructure for humans and services.

title: ANS Database Schema: How Agent Identity Is Persisted
content:
Understanding how ANS stores data helps you reason about what queries are fast, what relationships matter, and how the system scales. The schema is relational, normalized, and designed around the idea that agents, their endpoints, their capabilities, and their certificates are distinct concerns that happen to be linked.

**The Core Tables**

The `AGENTS` table is the center of gravity. Each row represents one registered agent and holds its name, public key, a foreign key to its certificate, a pointer to its default endpoint, version, description, timestamps, status, and owner. The `status` field is particularly important operationally — it's the primary way to disable an agent without deleting its record.

The `CERTIFICATES` table stores the full certificate for each agent: subject, issuer, validity window (not_before, not_after), public key, the raw certificate string, a fingerprint, status, and creation timestamp. Certificates are linked to agents via the `certificate_id` foreign key on the `AGENTS` table. This separation means you can query certificate status independently of agent status — useful when a certificate expires but the agent record should be preserved for audit purposes.

**Endpoints as First-Class Records**

Rather than storing endpoint information as a JSON blob inside the agent record, ANS gives endpoints their own table. Each `ENDPOINTS` row records the agent it belongs to, the protocol (A2A, MCP, HTTP, etc.), address, port, health status, when it was last checked, and a health message.

This design pays off when you need to:
- Query all unhealthy endpoints across all agents
- Add a new endpoint to an existing agent without touching the agent record
- Track health check history over time
- Support agents that are reachable via multiple protocols simultaneously

The `default_endpoint_id` on the `AGENTS` table points to whichever endpoint should be used when a caller doesn't specify a protocol preference.

**Capabilities via a Junction Table**

Capabilities are stored in a normalized many-to-many structure. The `CAPABILITIES` table holds unique capability names. The `AGENT_CAPABILITIES` junction table links agents to capabilities. This means:

- The same capability name (e.g., `text-summarization`) is stored once, not duplicated across every agent that has it
- Querying "which agents have capability X" is a simple join, not a JSON search
- Adding or removing a capability from an agent is a single row insert or delete in the junction table

**Flexible Metadata**

Both agents and certificates have associated metadata tables (`AGENT_METADATA` and `CERTIFICATE_METADATA`). These use a key-value structure: each row stores an agent or certificate ID, a key string, and a value string. This is the escape hatch for information that doesn't fit the fixed schema — custom tags, deployment environment labels, integration identifiers, and so on.

The tradeoff is that key-value metadata is harder to query efficiently than typed columns. ANS uses this pattern deliberately for extensibility: the core schema stays stable while operators can attach arbitrary context without schema migrations.

**Security Events as an Audit Log**

The `SECURITY_EVENTS` table functions as an append-only audit log. It records what happened, when, to whom, from where, and whether a mitigation was applied. The `mitigation_applied` boolean plus `mitigation_details` text column means the log captures not just incidents but responses — useful for compliance reporting and post-incident review.

**Schema Design Principles at Work**

A few patterns are worth noting for teams designing similar systems:

1. **Soft deletes via status fields** — agents and certificates have status columns rather than being physically deleted. This preserves history and supports audit trails.
2. **Timestamps as integers** — `created_at`, `updated_at`, `expires_at`, and `last_checked` are stored as integers (Unix timestamps) rather than database-native datetime types. This makes them portable across database engines and easy to compare arithmetically.
3. **Separation of identity from reachability** — the agent record holds identity (name, key, certificate); the endpoints table holds reachability (where to actually send messages). These change at different rates and for different reasons, so separating them reduces unnecessary updates.
4. **Foreign key discipline** — every relationship is expressed as an explicit foreign key, making the data model self-documenting and enabling referential integrity enforcement at the database level.

This schema is compact enough to run in SQLite for development and testing, while being structured well enough to migrate to PostgreSQL for production deployments without redesign.

title: open-claude-code v2 Architecture: Eight Layers That Power an AI Coding Agent
content:
When you type a question into open-claude-code and watch it read files, run shell commands, and edit code, you're seeing eight distinct layers working in concert. Understanding how they stack helps you reason about where things happen, why they're separated, and how to extend the system.

Think of the architecture like a restaurant kitchen. The customer (you) talks to the front-of-house (Terminal UI). Orders flow to the head chef (Agent Loop). The head chef dispatches prep cooks (Tools). The kitchen manager enforces health codes (Permission system). A timer tracks how long each dish takes (Context Manager). And a separate team handles special dietary requests from external suppliers (MCP Client).

**Layer 1 — Terminal UI (Ink/React + 40 Slash Commands)**
The outermost layer is a React-based terminal interface built with Ink. It handles keyboard navigation and exposes 40 slash commands. These commands are your control panel: `/model` switches the AI mid-conversation, `/compact` triggers context compression, `/undo` rolls back the last file edit, and `/doctor` checks API health. This layer is purely presentational — it translates your intent into structured requests.

**Layer 2 — Agent Loop (Async Generator, 13 Event Types)**
The agent loop is the brain. It's implemented as an async generator, meaning it yields events one at a time as they arrive from the model. Thirteen distinct event types flow through it: text tokens, tool calls, tool results, errors, usage stats, and more. The loop is recursive — when a tool spawns a subagent, that subagent runs its own nested agent loop. This is how complex multi-step tasks decompose into parallel workstreams.

**Layer 3 — Tool System (25+ Tools)**
Tools are the hands. Each tool lives in its own module with a `validateInput` function and a `call` function. The registry enforces this interface. Notable tools include `bash.mjs` (sandboxed shell with timeout and background process support), `edit.mjs` (file editing with uniqueness validation to prevent ambiguous replacements), `agent.mjs` (spawns subagents in isolated git worktrees), and `notebook-edit.mjs` (Jupyter notebook manipulation). The tool gap analysis in the codebase is instructive: early versions used shell `grep` and `find`; production-quality versions bundle ripgrep and the `fast-glob` npm package for correctness and speed.

**Layer 4 — Permission System (6 Modes)**
Before any tool executes, the permission layer decides whether it's allowed. Six modes range from fully sandboxed (read-only) to fully autonomous. This is the safety valve — it's why the system can run in CI pipelines without accidentally deleting production files.

**Layer 5 — Hooks Engine (6 Events)**
Hooks let you inject custom logic at six points in the agent lifecycle. Think of them as middleware: before a tool runs, after it completes, when the session starts, and so on. This is how you'd add logging, cost tracking, or custom approval workflows without modifying core code.

**Layer 6 — Context Manager (Token Tracking + Compaction)**
Large language models have finite context windows. The context manager tracks token usage in real time (visible via `/tokens`) and triggers compaction when the window fills. Compaction summarizes older conversation turns to free space while preserving the essential thread of the task. The `/compact` slash command lets you trigger this manually.

**Layer 7 — MCP Client and Settings Chain**
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) client connects to external tool servers over stdio, SSE, WebSocket, or streamable HTTP. This is how the agent integrates with databases, APIs, and custom enterprise tools without baking them into the core. The settings chain has five layers — defaults, global config, project config, environment variables, and runtime flags — each overriding the previous.

**Layer 8 — Infrastructure (Streaming, Caching, Rate Limiting, Providers)**
At the bottom sits the plumbing: an SSE streaming handler that processes three modes of server-sent events, a prompt caching layer that reduces costs on repeated context, a rate limiter that handles 429 and 529 errors with exponential backoff, and a providers module supporting five AI backends. The scheduler module adds cron-style task execution for automated workflows.

The key architectural insight is separation of concerns at every level. The agent loop doesn't know about terminals. Tools don't know about permissions. The context manager doesn't know about tools. This modularity is what makes the system extensible — you can swap a provider, add a tool, or change the permission model without touching unrelated code.

title: The Nightly Verified Release Pipeline: How open-claude-code Automates Safe Upgrades
content:
Keeping an AI coding tool up to date with its upstream model provider is tricky. Update too eagerly and you ship broken integrations. Update too slowly and users miss improvements. open-claude-code solves this with a nightly CI/CD pipeline that runs at 03:00 UTC every day and only publishes a new release if every gate passes.

Think of it like a quality control line in a factory. Raw material (a new npm package version) enters one end. It passes through four inspection stations. Only if it clears all four does it get boxed and shipped. If any station rejects it, the line stops and an alert goes out.

**Phase 1: Detect**
The pipeline queries the npm registry for `@anthropic-ai/claude-code` and compares the latest version against a file called `last-known-claude-version.txt` stored in the repository. If the versions match, there's nothing to do and the pipeline exits cleanly. If a new version exists — or if someone manually triggered the workflow with `force_release=true` — the pipeline advances to verification.

This version-file pattern is simple but effective. It creates an auditable record of what version was last processed, survives across pipeline runs, and can be manually edited to force a re-check of any version.

**Phase 2: Verify — Four Gates**
Verification runs four checks in sequence, and all four must pass:

1. **Test Suite (903+ tests)** — The full test suite runs against the new version. 903 tests is a substantial coverage floor; a regression in any tested behavior fails the gate here rather than in production.

2. **npm audit (no high/critical vulnerabilities)** — The dependency tree is scanned for known security vulnerabilities. High and critical severity findings block the release. This catches supply-chain issues introduced by the upstream package's own dependencies.

3. **Lint (syntax validation)** — Code is linted to confirm syntactic validity. This is a fast, cheap check that catches obvious breakage before slower tests run.

4. **Smoke Test (CLI boots)** — The CLI is actually launched and confirmed to start successfully. This end-to-end sanity check catches runtime failures that static analysis misses — missing files, broken imports, environment assumptions.

**Phase 3: AI-Powered Change Analysis**
If all four gates pass, the pipeline optionally uses Claude Sonnet 4.6 to analyze what changed between versions. This produces human-readable release notes describing new features, behavior changes, and potential breaking points. The `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret is optional — if absent, the pipeline skips this step and publishes without AI-generated notes.

This is a clever use of the tool itself: the AI coding assistant uses an AI model to explain its own upstream changes.

**Phase 4: Publish**
Only after all gates clear does the pipeline publish a verified release with the generated notes. The release is tagged and documented, giving users confidence that what they're installing has been tested against the project's own standards, not just the upstream publisher's.

**Manual Override**
The pipeline supports manual triggering via GitHub Actions:
```bash
gh workflow run nightly.yml -f force_release=true
```
This is useful when you want to re-run verification on the current version — for example, after fixing a flaky test or updating the test suite itself.

**The Design Principle**
The pipeline embodies a principle worth generalizing: *trust but verify, automatically*. Rather than manually reviewing every upstream update or blindly auto-merging, it defines a machine-checkable quality bar and enforces it on every candidate. The 03:00 UTC schedule means verification happens during off-hours, results are ready when developers start their day, and the system doesn't compete with daytime CI load.

For teams building on top of rapidly-evolving AI APIs, this pattern — detect, verify with multiple gates, analyze changes, publish only on full pass — is a reusable template for any dependency that updates frequently and carries integration risk.

title: Mastering open-claude-code's REPL: 40 Slash Commands and When to Use Each
content:
The open-claude-code REPL isn't just a chat interface — it's a control panel for a running AI agent. The 40 slash commands give you real-time visibility and control over the agent's state, cost, model, and behavior. Knowing which command to reach for in which situation makes the difference between a smooth session and a runaway context window.

Here's a mental model: imagine you're co-piloting a plane with an AI. The slash commands are your instrument panel. Some instruments tell you the plane's current state (altitude, fuel). Others let you adjust course. A few are emergency controls. You don't need all of them constantly, but you need to know where they are.

**Observability Commands — Know What's Happening**

`/tokens` shows current token usage against the context window limit. Check this when a session has been running for a while and responses start feeling slower or less coherent — you may be approaching the limit.

`/cost` shows the estimated API spend for the current session. Useful for budget-conscious work or when you've been running many tool calls and want to know the damage before continuing.

`/memory` shows memory usage. Relevant when running large file operations or many parallel subagents.

`/config` dumps the current settings — which model, which permission mode, which hooks are active. When behavior seems unexpected, this is your first diagnostic step.

`/permissions` shows the current permission mode. There are six modes ranging from read-only to fully autonomous. If the agent is refusing to write files or run commands, check here first.

`/hooks` lists active hooks — custom logic injected at lifecycle events. If something unexpected is happening before or after tool calls, hooks are the likely cause.

**Control Commands — Adjust Course Mid-Flight**

`/model <name>` switches the AI model without ending the session. This is powerful: start a session with a capable model for complex reasoning, then switch to a faster/cheaper model for mechanical tasks like formatting or renaming.

`/fast` toggles fast mode, which switches to Claude Haiku. One-keystroke version of `/model` for the common case of wanting speed over capability.

`/effort <level>` sets reasoning depth: `low`, `medium`, `high`, or `max`. Lower effort is faster and cheaper; higher effort produces more thorough analysis. Adjust based on task complexity.

`/compact` manually triggers context compaction — summarizing older turns to free window space. Use this proactively when `/tokens` shows you're getting close to the limit, rather than waiting for automatic compaction.

`/clear` wipes conversation history entirely. Use when you want to start a fresh task without the context of the previous one, but don't want to exit and restart.

**Session Management — Save, Resume, Navigate**

`/sessions` lists saved sessions with their IDs and timestamps.

`/resume [id]` loads a previous session, restoring conversation history and context. This is how you pick up a long-running task across days without re-explaining the codebase.

The combination of `/sessions` and `/resume` enables a workflow pattern: start a session for a feature branch, save it, work on something else, come back and resume exactly where you left off.

**Agent and Skill Discovery**

`/agents` lists custom agents defined in your configuration. Custom agents are pre-configured personas with specific tools, models, and system prompts.

`/skills` lists available skills — reusable task templates. Think of skills as macros: common workflows you've encoded so the agent can execute them consistently.

**Diagnostics and Recovery**

`/doctor` checks API connectivity and overall health. Run this first when something seems broken — wrong API key, network issue, or provider outage.

`/undo` rolls back the last file edit. This is your safety net when an edit went wrong. It works because the tool system maintains file checkpoints before every write.

`/tools` lists all available tools with their descriptions. Useful when you're not sure whether the agent can do something — check if the relevant tool exists before asking.

`/mcp` shows MCP server status — which external tool servers are connected and healthy.

**Practical Workflow**
A typical productive session might look like: start with `/doctor` to confirm connectivity, use `/permissions` to verify the right mode for the task, monitor `/tokens` and `/cost` periodically, run `/compact` before the window fills, and use `/undo` if an edit misfires. For long tasks, `/resume` means you never lose progress to a terminal restart.

title: dynamo-mcp Architecture: How Templates, Environments, and the MCP Server Work Together
content:
dynamo-mcp is a system that lets AI agents (or any MCP-compatible client) create real software projects from templates — automatically, programmatically, and in isolated environments. To understand how it works, it helps to think of it like a professional kitchen: the Template Registry is the recipe book, the Environment Manager is the prep station that keeps ingredients separate, and the MCP Server is the head chef taking orders and coordinating everything.

**The Three-Layer Architecture**

At the top sits the API layer (`dynamo_mcp/api/`). This contains two components: the MCP server (`mcp_server.py`) and an SSE transport layer (`sse_transport.py`). The MCP server exposes tools that clients can call — things like `list_templates`, `add_template`, `create_project`, and `get_template_variables`. The SSE (Server-Sent Events) transport layer handles the real-time communication channel between the server and clients, allowing the server to stream updates back as long-running operations (like project generation) proceed.

Below the API layer is the core layer (`dynamo_mcp/core/`). This is where the real work happens. Five components live here:

- **Template Registry** (`template_registry.py`): Manages a catalog of project templates stored as JSON files in a `templates/` directory. It knows how to list, add, update, remove, and discover templates. Each template is represented as a `TemplateInfo` object with metadata and version tracking.
- **Environment Manager** (`environment_manager.py`): Creates and manages isolated Python virtual environments (stored under `venvs/`). When a template requires specific dependencies, the environment manager ensures those are installed in a clean sandbox, preventing conflicts between different templates.
- **Interface Generator** (`interface_generator.py`): Inspects a template and generates the interface description — essentially figuring out what variables a template needs before you can use it.
- **Project Generator** (`project_generator.py`): The execution engine. Given a template name, an output directory, and a set of variable values, it actually runs the template (typically via cookiecutter or a similar tool) inside the appropriate virtual environment.
- **Models** (`models.py`): Shared data structures used across the system.

The bottom layer is utilities (`dynamo_mcp/utils/`): configuration, database access, custom exceptions, and database initialization helpers. The database (initialized from `sql/schema.sql`) stores persistent state — which templates are registered, environment metadata, and so on.

**Data Flow: From Client Request to Generated Project**

Here's what happens when an AI agent calls `create_project`:

1. The MCP client sends a tool call to the MCP server over HTTP (or stdio for local use).
2. The MCP server receives the request and routes it to the Project Generator.
3. The Project Generator asks the Template Registry: "Do we have a template called `python-package`?"
4. The Template Registry looks up the template in its JSON store and returns the template's location and metadata.
5. The Project Generator asks the Environment Manager: "Is there a ready virtual environment for this template?"
6. If not, the Environment Manager creates one, installs the required dependencies, and caches it under `venvs/`.
7. The Project Generator executes the template inside that virtual environment, passing in the user-supplied variables.
8. The result (success, errors, output path) is returned to the MCP server, which sends it back to the client.

**Two Transport Modes**

dynamo-mcp supports two ways for clients to connect. The SSE transport (`sse_transport.py`) is used when the server runs as an HTTP service — clients connect to `http://localhost:8000` and communicate over a persistent event stream. The stdio transport (tested in `test_mcp_stdio.py`) is used when the server is launched as a subprocess and communicates over standard input/output — the pattern used by tools like Claude Desktop when spawning local MCP servers.

**Why This Design Makes Sense**

The separation between the Template Registry and the Environment Manager is deliberate. Templates are just descriptions (JSON metadata + a URL or path to the actual cookiecutter template). Environments are the runtime context needed to execute them. By keeping these separate, you can register dozens of templates without paying the cost of creating virtual environments for all of them upfront — environments are created lazily, only when a template is actually used.

The database layer adds durability. If the server restarts, it doesn't lose track of which templates have been registered or which environments have been built. The `init_db.py` and `init_db_from_sql.py` scripts give operators two ways to initialize the schema: programmatically or directly from the `schema.sql` file.

This architecture makes dynamo-mcp well-suited for agentic workflows where an AI needs to scaffold new projects as part of a larger task — without requiring a human to manually run cookiecutter commands.

title: Using dynamo-mcp as an MCP Client: Registering Templates and Generating Projects
content:
dynamo-mcp exposes a set of MCP tools that any compatible client — an AI agent, a script, or a developer tool — can call to manage project templates and generate new codebases. This entry walks through the core workflow using the client API pattern shown in the repository's examples.

**Connecting to the Server**

The server runs at `http://localhost:8000` by default. A client connects and then calls tools by name, passing arguments as a dictionary. The interaction looks like a remote procedure call: you name the tool, provide inputs, and get a result back.

```python
client = MCPClient("http://localhost:8000")
```

**Step 1: List Available Templates**

Before creating anything, you can ask the server what templates are already registered:

```python
templates = await client.call_tool("list_templates")
```

This returns the current contents of the Template Registry — a list of `TemplateInfo` objects describing each registered template, including its name, source URL, and version metadata.

**Step 2: Register a New Template**

Templates are typically cookiecutter-compatible repositories. To add one:

```python
template = await client.call_tool("add_template", {
    "url": "https://github.com/audreyfeldroy/cookiecutter-pypackage",
    "name": "python-package"
})
```

The server fetches the template definition, stores its metadata as a JSON file in the `templates/` directory, and registers it in the database. The `name` you provide becomes the handle you use in all future calls. You can also update or remove templates using `update_template` and `remove_template`.

**Step 3: Inspect Template Variables**

Before generating a project, you need to know what inputs the template expects. The `get_template_variables` tool introspects the template and returns its variable schema:

```python
variables = await client.call_tool("get_template_variables", {
    "template_name": "python-package"
})
```

This is handled internally by the Interface Generator component, which reads the template's `cookiecutter.json` (or equivalent) and returns the list of variables with their names, types, and default values. This step is especially useful for AI agents that need to dynamically discover what information to collect before proceeding.

**Step 4: Generate a Project**

Once you know the variables, you can create a project:

```python
result = await client.call_tool("create_project", {
    "template_name": "python-package",
    "output_dir": "my-new-project",
    "variables": {
        "project_name": "My Amazing Package",
        "project_slug": "amazing_package",
        "version": "0.1.0"
    }
})
```

Behind the scenes, the Project Generator checks whether a virtual environment for this template already exists. If not, the Environment Manager creates one and installs the template's dependencies. The generator then executes the template inside that environment, writing the output to the specified directory. The result object tells you whether the operation succeeded and where the files were written.

**Practical Notes for Agentic Use**

This workflow is designed to be called programmatically inside larger agent pipelines. An agent tasked with "scaffold a new Python library called `dataflow`" can:
1. Call `list_templates` to check if a suitable template exists.
2. Call `add_template` if it doesn't.
3. Call `get_template_variables` to learn what inputs are needed.
4. Gather or infer those inputs from context.
5. Call `create_project` to produce the actual files.

All five steps are tool calls — no shell access, no manual file manipulation. The MCP interface keeps the agent's interaction clean and auditable.

For local development or testing, dynamo-mcp also supports stdio transport, where the server is launched as a subprocess and communicates over stdin/stdout. This is the mode used by tools like Claude Desktop. The `test_mcp_stdio.py` test file demonstrates this pattern.

title: dynamo-mcp Repository Layout: What Each Module Does and Why It's Organized That Way
content:
Understanding a codebase starts with understanding why it's organized the way it is. dynamo-mcp follows a clean separation of concerns across four top-level packages inside `dynamo_mcp/`. Here's a map of what lives where and the reasoning behind the structure.

**`api/` — The Public Interface**

This package contains everything related to how the outside world talks to dynamo-mcp:

- `mcp_server.py`: Defines the MCP tools (the callable functions that clients invoke). This is where tool names like `list_templates` and `create_project` are registered and their handlers are wired up.
- `sse_transport.py`: Implements the Server-Sent Events transport, which keeps an HTTP connection open so the server can push updates to the client as operations complete. This is one of two supported transports; the other (stdio) is used when the server runs as a subprocess.

Keeping transport concerns in `api/` means the core logic doesn't need to know or care how it's being called — HTTP, stdio, or any future transport can be added without touching the business logic.

**`core/` — The Business Logic**

This is the heart of the system. Five modules handle the actual work:

- `template_registry.py`: CRUD operations for templates. Stores template metadata as JSON files and tracks them in the database. Supports discovery (scanning a directory for templates) in addition to manual registration.
- `environment_manager.py`: Creates and caches Python virtual environments keyed to templates. Ensures each template runs with its own dependency set, preventing version conflicts.
- `interface_generator.py`: Reads a template's variable schema and returns it in a structured format. Powers the `get_template_variables` tool.
- `project_generator.py`: Orchestrates project creation — looks up the template, ensures an environment exists, runs the template engine, and returns the result.
- `models.py`: Shared Pydantic (or dataclass) models used across all modules. Centralizing models here prevents circular imports and keeps data contracts explicit.

**`utils/` — Infrastructure Support**

- `config.py`: Loads configuration (paths, database URL, server settings) from environment variables or a config file. Centralizing config here means other modules import from one place rather than reading environment variables directly.
- `database.py`: Database connection and query helpers. Abstracts away the raw SQL so core modules work with Python objects.
- `exceptions.py`: Custom exception classes. Having named exceptions (e.g., `TemplateNotFoundError`, `EnvironmentCreationError`) makes error handling in the API layer precise — you can catch specific failures and return meaningful error messages to clients.
- `init_template_db.py`: Programmatic database initialization logic, used by the scripts.

**`scripts/` and `sql/` — Operational Tooling**

- `scripts/init_db.py`: A runnable script that initializes the database programmatically.
- `scripts/init_db_from_sql.py`: An alternative that applies `sql/schema.sql` directly. Useful when you want the schema definition to be the single source of truth and don't want to maintain a parallel Python migration.
- `sql/schema.sql`: The authoritative database schema. Having this as a plain SQL file means it can be reviewed, version-controlled, and applied by any SQL tool — not just through Python.

**`tests/` — Four Levels of Testing**

The test suite is organized by scope:

- `test_basic.py`: Smoke tests — does the package import? Do the core objects instantiate?
- `test_database.py`: Tests database operations in isolation.
- `test_mcp_stdio.py`: Tests the full MCP protocol over stdio transport, simulating how a tool like Claude Desktop would interact with the server.
- `comprehensive_test.py`: End-to-end tests covering the full workflow from template registration through project generation.

**The Design Principle**

The overall structure follows a dependency rule: `api/` depends on `core/`, `core/` depends on `utils/`, and nothing in `utils/` depends on `core/` or `api/`. This one-way dependency graph means you can test and reason about each layer independently. It also means the MCP interface is a thin shell over well-defined core logic — swapping out the transport or adding a new API (REST, CLI) would only require changes in `api/`, leaving everything else untouched.

title: How Swarm Agents Think: The Three Forces of Flocking Behavior
content:
Imagine you're at a concert, moving through a crowd. Without thinking, you avoid bumping into people (separation), drift in the same general direction as those around you (alignment), and stay loosely grouped with your friends (cohesion). This is exactly what Craig Reynolds described in 1986 with his 'Boids' model — and it's the foundation of every swarm simulation in the swarm-world system.

The `SwarmAgent` class in Unity implements this with three weighted forces that combine every frame into a single steering decision.

**Separation** pushes agents away from neighbors that are too close. Think of it as personal space — each agent wants a bubble around itself. In the code, `separationWeight = 1.5f` is set slightly higher than the other two, meaning agents prioritize not colliding above all else. This prevents the swarm from clumping into a single point.

**Alignment** nudges an agent's velocity toward the average velocity of its neighbors. If everyone around you is heading northeast at moderate speed, you gradually start heading northeast too. This is what gives a flock its sense of unified direction — no leader required.

**Cohesion** pulls agents toward the center of mass of their local group. It's the social glue. Without it, separation would scatter everyone apart permanently. With it, the swarm stays loosely together even while individuals move freely.

These three forces are calculated each frame in `CalculateSteering()`, summed as a `Vector3 acceleration`, and applied to the agent's velocity:

```csharp
velocity += acceleration * Time.deltaTime;
velocity = Vector3.ClampMagnitude(velocity, maxSpeed);
transform.position += velocity * Time.deltaTime;
```

Notice `Vector3.ClampMagnitude` — this is the speed limiter. No matter how strong the combined forces are, the agent never exceeds `maxSpeed`. This prevents jittery, unrealistic movement.

**Perception radius** is the key parameter tying everything together. Each agent only 'sees' neighbors within a sphere of radius `perceptionRadius` (default 5 units). This is checked using Unity's `Physics.OverlapSphere`, which returns all colliders on the `agentLayer` within that radius. Agents outside this bubble simply don't exist to the agent — which is both realistic and computationally efficient.

The emergent result is striking: hundreds of agents following only local rules produce globally coherent, lifelike group behavior. No central controller tells anyone where to go. The flock is a property of the interactions, not of any individual.

To tune your own swarm, start with the BasicFlocking scene (100 agents) and adjust the three weights. Raising `separationWeight` creates a looser, more scattered flock. Raising `cohesionWeight` pulls agents into tight clusters. Raising `alignmentWeight` makes the group move in more synchronized waves. The sweet spot depends entirely on what behavior you're simulating — fish schools behave very differently from starling murmurations.

title: Scaling Swarms to 5000+ Agents: CPU vs GPU Architecture
content:
There's a hard wall you hit when simulating swarms on the CPU. With 100 agents, each checking 99 potential neighbors every frame, you have roughly 10,000 neighbor checks per frame — trivial. Scale to 5,000 agents and that becomes 25 million checks per frame. Your frame rate collapses.

The swarm-world system addresses this with two complementary strategies: spatial partitioning on the CPU side, and full GPU compute offloading for massive simulations.

**Spatial Partitioning (CPU path)**

The `SpatialPartition.cs` utility divides the world into a grid of cells. Instead of checking every agent against every other agent, each agent only checks agents in its own cell and immediately adjacent cells. If your perception radius is 5 units and your cell size matches that, you go from O(n²) comparisons to roughly O(n × k) where k is the average agents per cell — often just 5-20 even in dense swarms. This alone can handle hundreds of agents smoothly.

**GPU Compute Path (MassiveSwarm scene)**

For 5,000+ agents, `GPUSwarmManager` moves the entire simulation onto the GPU using Unity's Compute Shaders. The key insight is that GPU cores are designed for exactly this kind of embarrassingly parallel work — thousands of agents all running the same calculation simultaneously.

The setup involves three compute buffers:
- `agentBuffer`: stores position, velocity, and acceleration for every agent as a flat array of structs
- `spatialGridBuffer`: a GPU-side spatial hash grid
- `spatialKeysBuffer` / `spatialValuesBuffer`: sorted indices for fast neighbor lookup

The cell size is derived directly from the perception radius:
```csharp
cellSize = perceptionRadius * 2f;
gridDimensions = Mathf.CeilToInt(worldSize.x / cellSize);
```

This ensures that any two agents who could possibly perceive each other are guaranteed to be in adjacent grid cells — so the GPU kernel never needs to search further.

Two kernels run each frame: `BuildSpatialHash` constructs the neighbor lookup structure, then `UpdateSwarm` runs the full boids calculation for every agent in parallel.

**An important gotcha: GPU struct padding.** The `Agent` struct on the GPU side must match the memory layout expected by the compute shader. The comment in the source (`// Note: GPU struct padding considerations`) flags this — if your C# struct has 3 floats for position, 3 for velocity, and 3 for acceleration, the GPU may expect 4-float alignment. Mismatched padding causes subtle, hard-to-debug corruption where agents fly to infinity.

**When to use which approach:**
- Under 200 agents: plain `SwarmAgent` with `Physics.OverlapSphere` is fine
- 200–1000 agents: add `SpatialPartition` and consider Unity's Job System via `SwarmJobSystem.cs`
- 1000+ agents: move to `GPUSwarmManager` with compute shaders

The `SwarmPerformanceMonitor` component gives you real-time FPS, agent count, and average neighbor count — the last metric is especially useful. If average neighbors spikes above 30-40, your spatial partitioning cell size may be too large and agents are doing unnecessary work.

title: Pheromone Maps: How Ant-Style Stigmergy Works in Code
content:
Most swarm behaviors are reactive — agents respond to what they see right now. Pheromone-based systems are different: agents respond to what previous agents *left behind*. This is called stigmergy, and it's how real ant colonies solve complex problems like finding the shortest path to food without any individual ant understanding the global solution.

The `PheromoneMap` class in swarm-world implements a 2D grid-based pheromone system with two separate chemical channels: `foodPheromones` (laid when an ant is carrying food home) and `homePheromones` (laid when an ant is searching for food). The separation matters — ants follow food pheromones when hungry and home pheromones when loaded, creating two-way traffic that reinforces the best routes.

**The grid as chemical memory**

The map is a 2D float array (`gridWidth × gridHeight`), where each cell holds a concentration value from 0.0 (none) to 1.0 (saturated). Agents deposit pheromone by incrementing the cell at their current grid position. The grid is the shared memory of the entire colony.

**Two physical processes keep the system honest**

Evaporation (`evaporationRate = 0.01f`) reduces every cell's concentration each frame. This is crucial — without it, pheromone trails from old, suboptimal paths would persist forever and mislead future agents. Evaporation creates a natural 'forgetting' that biases the system toward recently-used, currently-relevant paths.

Diffusion (`diffusionRate = 0.1f`) spreads pheromone from high-concentration cells to neighbors. The implementation averages each cell with its 8 surrounding neighbors using a `tempGrid` buffer to avoid reading-while-writing artifacts:

```csharp
float sum = 0;
for (int dx = -1; dx <= 1; dx++)
    for (int dy = -1; dy <= 1; dy++)
        sum += pheromones[x + dx, y + dy];
tempGrid[x, y] = sum / 9f;
```

Diffusion widens trails slightly, making them easier for agents to detect and follow. Without it, a single-cell-wide trail would be nearly impossible to navigate reliably.

**The emergent result**

Short paths get reinforced faster than long ones — ants traveling a short route complete round trips more frequently, depositing more pheromone per unit time. Longer routes evaporate before they accumulate competitive concentrations. The colony collectively discovers shortest paths through pure chemical feedback, with no agent ever 'knowing' the map.

This pattern appears in the PredatorPrey and Robot Swarms example scenes, where pheromone maps coordinate search behavior across large areas. For your own implementations, the key tuning parameters are the ratio of evaporation to deposition rate (too fast and trails vanish before being useful; too slow and the map saturates into noise) and cell size relative to agent speed (agents should cross roughly 1-3 cells per second for smooth gradient following).

title: Air-Gapped AI Deployments: Running Claude-Flow Without Internet Access
content:
Sometimes the most sensitive work happens in environments that are deliberately cut off from the internet — think classified government systems, hospital networks handling patient data, or financial institutions with strict data residency requirements. An air-gapped network is exactly what it sounds like: a system physically isolated from external networks, like a room with no doors. Claude-Flow is designed to operate fully within these constraints.

Imagine a submarine. Everything the crew needs must be loaded before they dive — food, fuel, charts, tools. Once submerged, there's no resupply from the surface. An air-gapped Claude-Flow deployment works the same way: all the components are loaded and configured before isolation, and then the system operates entirely on its own.

**The Core Components Inside the Air Gap**

A fully air-gapped Claude-Flow stack includes four main pieces, all running locally:

1. **Local LLM (Ollama or vLLM)** — Instead of calling out to Anthropic's API, the system runs a language model directly on local hardware. Ollama and vLLM are two popular runtimes for hosting open-weight models like Llama, Mistral, or Qwen on your own servers. No tokens leave the building.

2. **Ruvector + Local Postgres** — This is the vector database layer, responsible for storing and searching embeddings. In a standard deployment, this might connect to a managed cloud database. In air-gapped mode, Postgres runs on a local machine within the secure perimeter.

3. **Claude-Flow Memory (SQLite)** — Agent memory and conversation history are stored in SQLite, a lightweight file-based database that requires zero external infrastructure. It's the simplest possible persistence layer — just a file on disk.

4. **Agent Swarm (local execution)** — The orchestration layer that coordinates multiple agents runs entirely on local compute. Agents spawn, communicate, and complete tasks without any external API calls.

**The Data Diode: One-Way Only**

Here's where it gets interesting. A true air gap means nothing goes in or out — but that creates a practical problem: how do you ever update the system? The answer is a **data diode**.

A data diode is a hardware or software mechanism that enforces one-way data flow. Think of it like a one-way valve in plumbing — water (data) can flow in, but it physically cannot flow back out. In the Claude-Flow architecture, the data diode sits between the air-gapped network and an external update server.

Updates — new model weights, security patches, knowledge base refreshes — are prepared on the external server and transferred inward through the diode. The air-gapped system can receive these updates, but it cannot send anything back out. This means even if an attacker somehow compromised the internal system, they couldn't exfiltrate data through the update channel.

In practice, many organizations implement this with manual transfer procedures: an operator downloads updates to a write-once USB drive, carries it physically into the secure facility, and loads it into the system. The "manual transfer" label in the architecture diagram reflects this reality.

**Why This Architecture Matters**
