The beauty of this design is that it doesn't require you to choose between capability and security. You get the full power of a multi-agent AI system — memory, vector search, tool use, swarm coordination — without any of the data leaving your controlled environment.

For compliance-heavy industries, this is often non-negotiable. HIPAA, FedRAMP, and various defense regulations may prohibit sending certain data to third-party APIs, no matter how secure those APIs claim to be. An air-gapped deployment sidesteps the question entirely: the data never leaves, so there's nothing to regulate in transit.

**Tradeoffs to Understand**

Air-gapped deployments come with real costs. Local LLMs are typically less capable than frontier models like Claude 3.5 Sonnet — you're trading raw intelligence for isolation. Hardware requirements are significant: running a capable local LLM requires substantial GPU resources. And updates are slow and operationally complex compared to a cloud service that updates transparently.

The right question isn't "is air-gapped better?" but "does my threat model and compliance requirement demand it?" For most use cases, a well-secured cloud deployment is both safer and more capable. But when the answer is yes — when the data truly cannot leave the building — Claude-Flow's air-gapped architecture provides a complete, production-ready path forward.

title: Defining Tools for Claude-Flow Agents: Structure, Parameters, and Best Practices
content:
When you give an AI agent a tool, you're not just handing it a function — you're writing a contract. The agent reads your tool definition to understand what the tool does, what inputs it needs, and what's optional versus required. Getting this contract right is the difference between an agent that uses tools confidently and one that fumbles, hallucinates parameters, or refuses to act.

Think of it like writing a job posting. A vague posting — "help with stuff" — attracts confusion. A precise one — "manage inbound customer emails, categorize by urgency, draft responses using approved templates" — gives a new hire everything they need to succeed on day one. Tool definitions work the same way.

**The Anatomy of a Tool Definition**

Every tool in Claude-Flow follows a consistent JSON structure with three key fields:

- **`name`** — A short, snake_case identifier. This is what the agent calls when it wants to use the tool. Keep it descriptive and unambiguous: `search_database` is better than `search` or `db`.

- **`description`** — A plain-English explanation of what the tool does. The agent reads this to decide *whether* to use the tool. Be specific about scope: "Search the product database" tells the agent this is for products, not customers or orders.

- **`parameters`** — A JSON Schema object describing the inputs. This is where precision really matters.

Here's a concrete example from the Claude-Flow codebase:

```javascript
{
  name: 'search_database',
  description: 'Search the product database',
  parameters: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      query: { type: 'string', description: 'Search query' },
      limit: { type: 'number', description: 'Max results' }
    },
    required: ['query']
  }
}
```

Notice that `query` is in the `required` array but `limit` is not. This tells the agent: you must provide a search query, but the result limit is optional. The agent can make a sensible call without knowing how many results you want, but it can't search without knowing what to search for.

**The `send_email` Tool: A Richer Example**

The second tool in the example handles email:

```javascript
{
  name: 'send_email',
  description: 'Send an email to a customer',
  parameters: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      to: { type: 'string' },
      subject: { type: 'string' },
      body: { type: 'string' }
    },
    required: ['to', 'subject', 'body']
  }
}
```

Here, all three parameters are required — and rightly so. You can't send an email without a recipient, subject, and body. The agent will never attempt to call this tool unless it has all three pieces of information, which prevents half-formed emails from being sent.

**Writing Better Descriptions**

The description field is often underestimated. Agents use it for tool selection — when multiple tools are available, the agent reads descriptions to pick the right one. Ambiguous descriptions lead to wrong tool choices.

Compare these two descriptions for the same tool:
- Weak: "Get data"
- Strong: "Retrieve a customer's order history by customer ID, returning the last 90 days of transactions"

The strong version tells the agent exactly when to use this tool and what it returns. This reduces errors and makes agent behavior more predictable.

**Required vs. Optional Parameters**

A common mistake is marking everything as required. Optional parameters give agents flexibility — they can call a tool with minimal information and let defaults handle the rest. The `limit` parameter in `search_database` is a good example: the tool works fine without it (perhaps defaulting to 10 results), so there's no reason to force the agent to always specify it.

Conversely, don't make critical parameters optional. If your email tool silently uses a default recipient when `to` is missing, you'll send emails to the wrong people. When in doubt, ask: "Can this tool do something useful and safe without this parameter?" If yes, it can be optional. If no, mark it required.

**Putting It Together**

Well-defined tools make agents dramatically more reliable. The investment in clear names, precise descriptions, and thoughtful required/optional distinctions pays off every time the agent needs to decide what to do next. Treat your tool definitions as first-class documentation — because for your agents, they are.

title: Configuring DreamFactory with Nginx on Ubuntu
content:
When you deploy DreamFactory on a Linux server, you need a web server to act as the front door — receiving HTTP requests from clients and routing them to the PHP application running behind the scenes. Nginx is a popular choice for this role because of its performance and straightforward virtual-host configuration model. Think of Nginx as a hotel concierge: it greets every incoming guest (HTTP request) and directs them to the right room (application process).

This guide covers the setup steps for Nginx 1.6.x on Ubuntu 14.04, though the concepts apply broadly to other Ubuntu versions with minor path adjustments.

**Step 1 — Copy the Nginx site configuration files**

DreamFactory ships with pre-built Nginx configuration files inside the repository under `config/external/nginx/`. You do not need to write these from scratch. Copy the virtual-host definition files into the standard Ubuntu location where Nginx looks for available sites:

```bash
sudo cp config/external/nginx/etc/nginx/sites-available/* /etc/nginx/sites-available/
```

Think of `sites-available` as a filing cabinet of every site Nginx *could* serve. Nothing is live yet — you are just registering the configuration.

**Step 2 — Copy the supplemental conf.d files**

Additional global settings (such as PHP FastCGI parameters or upstream definitions) live in `conf.d`. Copy those as well:

```bash
sudo cp config/external/nginx/etc/nginx/conf.d/* /etc/nginx/conf.d/
```

**Step 3 — Create the sites-enabled directory if it does not exist**

Ubuntu's Nginx uses a two-folder pattern: `sites-available` holds all configurations, while `sites-enabled` holds only the ones that are actually active. If the `sites-enabled` directory is missing, create it:

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /etc/nginx/sites-enabled
```

**Step 4 — Activate the DreamFactory site with a symlink**

Rather than copying the file a second time, you create a symbolic link from `sites-enabled` pointing back to the file in `sites-available`. This is the standard Unix pattern — it means you only maintain one copy of the config, and toggling the site on or off is as simple as adding or removing the symlink:

```bash
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/dsp.single.local /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/dsp.local
```

After creating the symlink, reload or restart Nginx to apply the changes:

```bash
sudo service nginx restart
```

**Configuring PHP variables for DreamFactory**

DreamFactory also requires specific PHP runtime settings (memory limits, upload sizes, execution timeouts, etc.) that differ from the defaults. These are packaged in a file called `dreamfactory.ini` inside `config/external/php/etc/php5/mods-available/`.

On Ubuntu with PHP 5, the `mods-available` system lets you drop an `.ini` file into a known directory and then enable it with a single command — similar to how `sites-available` works for Nginx.

1. Copy the ini file into place:
   ```bash
   sudo cp config/external/php/etc/php5/mods-available/dreamfactory.ini /etc/php5/mods-available/
   ```

2. Enable the module:
   ```bash
   sudo php5enmod dreamfactory
   ```

3. Restart your web server so PHP picks up the new settings:
   ```bash
   sudo service nginx restart
   ```

**Other operating systems**

CentOS and Red Hat Enterprise Linux use a similar virtual-host pattern, typically placing configuration files under `/etc/nginx/conf.d/` rather than the `sites-available/sites-enabled` split. The included configuration files can be adapted with minimal changes — primarily adjusting file paths and user/group settings to match the distribution conventions.

**Key takeaway**

DreamFactory's repository includes ready-made server configuration files so you do not have to configure Nginx or PHP from scratch. The workflow is always the same: copy the provided files to the correct system directories, activate them using the platform's standard mechanism (symlinks for Nginx, `php5enmod` for PHP), and restart the web server. This approach keeps your custom configuration version-controlled alongside the application code, making deployments repeatable and auditable.

title: Understanding DreamFactory's Release Versioning and Community Resources
content:
Every mature open-source project needs a clear way to communicate what changed between releases, where to get help, and how to track the project's history. DreamFactory handles all three of these concerns in ways that are worth understanding, especially if you are evaluating the platform, planning an upgrade, or troubleshooting an issue.

**Semantic versioning and the changelog pattern**

DreamFactory follows semantic versioning (SemVer), where version numbers take the form `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. Looking at the changelog links in the repository, you can see a long history of releases: 2.6.0, 2.7.0, 2.8.0 … all the way through 7.0.0 and 7.1.0 (released May 2025). Each entry in the changelog is a GitHub comparison URL, meaning you can click any version pair and see the exact commits, pull requests, and file diffs that make up that release. This is a powerful auditing tool — before upgrading from, say, 7.0.0 to 7.1.0, you can review every change that will land in your environment.

The `[Unreleased]` entry at the top of the changelog always points to the diff between the latest stable release and the current `HEAD` of the main branch. This tells you what is being developed right now but has not yet been tagged as a release.

**Reading recent commit history**

The commit log reveals how the team works. You will notice a pattern of feature branches (named things like `DP-666` or `DP-657`, which are internal ticket numbers) being merged into a `develop` branch, which is then periodically merged into `main` and tagged as a release. This is a classic Gitflow-style workflow.

A few notable recent changes visible in the log:
- **Version 7.0.0** landed in February 2025, representing a major milestone.
- **Version 7.1.0** followed in May 2025 with bug fixes.
- A specific fix ensured `$version` is always included when rendering the `firstUser` template — a small but important detail that would have caused errors during initial setup if missing.
- The `AuthServiceProvider` location was changed in late 2024, which is relevant if you have any custom authentication extensions that reference that class path.

When you are debugging an unexpected behavior after an upgrade, scanning the commit log for the version range you upgraded across is often the fastest way to identify what changed.

**Where to get help**

DreamFactory maintains several support channels, each suited to different needs:

- **Stack Overflow** — Tag your question with `dreamfactory`. This is best for specific, reproducible technical questions where a public answer benefits the broader community. The tag has an active following.

- **Official documentation** — Three distinct resources exist:
  - `docs.dreamfactory.com` — Reference documentation for APIs, configuration options, and features.
  - `wiki.dreamfactory.com` — Community-maintained knowledge base with how-to articles.
  - `guide.dreamfactory.com` — Tutorials and worked examples, good for learning workflows end-to-end.

- **Community forum** — `community.dreamfactory.com` is the place for broader discussions, feature requests, and questions that do not fit the Stack Overflow format.

**Practical upgrade advice**

Before upgrading DreamFactory in a production environment:
1. Check the changelog comparison URL for your current version to the target version.
2. Scan commit messages for anything touching authentication, database migrations, or configuration file formats — these are the most likely sources of breaking changes.
3. Test in a staging environment first, paying particular attention to custom scripts or service overrides you may have added.

Understanding the versioning scheme and knowing where to look for change information transforms upgrades from a risky unknown into a manageable, informed process.

title: Running Open UI with Ollama: Local LLM Inference Without the Cloud
content:
Most AI-powered tools assume you have an OpenAI API key and a credit card ready to go. Open UI breaks that assumption by supporting Ollama — a runtime that lets you pull and serve large language models entirely on your own machine or in a cloud development environment. Understanding how these two pieces fit together is key to getting the most out of a local-first AI workflow.

**What Ollama Does**

Think of Ollama as a local model server — the same way a web server like nginx sits between your browser and your application code, Ollama sits between Open UI and the actual model weights. It handles downloading models, loading them into memory, and exposing a consistent API endpoint that Open UI can talk to. When you run `ollama serve`, you're starting that local server. When you run `ollama pull llava`, you're downloading a specific model (in this case, LLaVA, a vision-capable model) into Ollama's local registry.

**The Codespaces Shortcut**

If you're using GitHub Codespaces with the Open UI repository, most of the setup happens automatically on boot. The devcontainer configuration installs Ollama and pulls the `llava` model before you even open a terminal. You can verify everything is working with:

```bash
ollama list
```

If that command fails or returns nothing, it usually means the Ollama server process isn't running. Open a new terminal and start it manually:

```bash
ollama serve
```

Once it's running, `ollama list` should show `llava` in the output. From there, Open UI's settings modal (accessible via the gear icon in the upper left) will automatically surface any models Ollama knows about. Pull additional models with `ollama pull <model-name>` and they'll appear in the settings list without any restart required.

**The OPENAI_API_KEY Quirk**

Here's a detail that trips up nearly every new user: even if you have zero intention of using OpenAI and only want to run local Ollama models, Open UI still requires the `OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable to be set. This is a validation artifact in the current codebase — the variable must exist, but its value doesn't matter for Ollama-only usage. The workaround is simple:

```bash
OPENAI_API_KEY=xxx python -m openui
```

Setting it to `xxx` or any non-empty string satisfies the check. This is a common pattern in tools that started OpenAI-first and added local model support later — the original validation logic wasn't updated to account for the new code path.

**Docker as an Alternative**

If you'd rather not manage a Python environment, Docker provides a clean encapsulation. From the `/backend` directory:

```bash
docker build . -t wandb/openui --load
docker run -p 7878:7878 -e OPENAI_API_KEY wandb/openui
```

Note that `-e OPENAI_API_KEY` passes the variable from your host shell into the container. If it's set to `xxx` in your shell, that value carries through. Port 7878 is where Open UI's backend listens by default — the frontend will be accessible at `http://localhost:7878` once the container is running.

**Development Mode**

For contributors or anyone who wants live-reload behavior while modifying the backend, install the package in editable mode first, then pass `--dev`:

```bash
pip install -e .
OPENAI_API_KEY=xxx python -m openui --dev
```

The `--dev` flag enables file watching so changes to Python source files trigger an automatic reload — the same experience you'd get from `nodemon` in a Node.js project or `flask run` with debug mode on.

**Key Takeaways**

- Ollama acts as a local model server; `ollama serve` starts it, `ollama pull` downloads models
- GitHub Codespaces auto-installs Ollama and pulls `llava` on boot — verify with `ollama list`
- `OPENAI_API_KEY` must be set even for Ollama-only usage; use `xxx` as a placeholder
- Docker deployment maps port 7878 and passes the API key via `-e OPENAI_API_KEY`
- Use `pip install -e . && python -m openui --dev` for live-reload development

title: Installing and Running Open UI: Three Deployment Paths Compared
content:
Open UI is a UI generation tool backed by LLMs, and it supports three distinct ways to get running: direct Python installation, Docker, and cloud development environments like GitHub Codespaces or Gitpod. Each path has different tradeoffs around setup complexity, isolation, and iteration speed. Knowing which to choose — and what each one requires — saves significant debugging time.

**Path 1: Direct Python Installation**

This is the lowest-overhead option for developers who already have Python and pip set up. Clone the repository, navigate to the backend directory, and install:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/wandb/openui
cd openui/backend
pip install .
```

Then run with your API key:

```bash
OPENAI_API_KEY=your_key python -m openui
```

If you're using Ollama instead of OpenAI, set the key to any non-empty placeholder like `xxx`. The application starts a local server you can access through your browser. This path gives you the fastest iteration loop and the most direct access to logs and process management, but it requires managing your own Python environment and any system dependencies.

**Path 2: Docker**

Docker trades some iteration speed for environment isolation and reproducibility. Build the image from the `/backend` directory:

```bash
docker build . -t wandb/openui --load
docker run -p 7878:7878 -e OPENAI_API_KEY wandb/openui
```

The `--load` flag ensures the built image is loaded into your local Docker daemon rather than just cached in the build context. The `-p 7878:7878` flag maps the container's internal port to your host machine, and `-e OPENAI_API_KEY` passes the environment variable from your shell into the container at runtime. This means you don't hardcode credentials into the image — a security best practice.

Docker is the right choice when you want a clean, reproducible environment that matches what you'd deploy to production, or when you're sharing the setup with teammates who may have different local configurations.

**Path 3: Cloud Development Environments**

GitHub Codespaces and Gitpod both offer browser-based development environments that eliminate local setup entirely. The Open UI repository includes preconfiguration for both:

- **Codespaces**: Automatically installs Ollama and downloads the `llava` model on boot. No manual setup required. Verify Ollama is running with `ollama list`; if it's not, run `ollama serve` in a new terminal.
- **Gitpod**: Preconfigured with OpenAI integration. Requires a valid `OPENAI_API_KEY` to be set in your Gitpod environment variables.

Cloud environments are ideal for quickly evaluating the tool, contributing without touching your local machine, or working from devices where you can't install software. The tradeoff is that you're dependent on network connectivity and the cloud provider's resource limits.

**Choosing the Right Path**

| Scenario | Recommended Path |
|---|---|
| Quick evaluation | Codespaces or Gitpod |
| Active development with live reload | Direct Python (`pip install -e . && --dev`) |
| Team onboarding / consistent environments | Docker |
| Local-only LLM inference | Direct Python or Codespaces with Ollama |

**The One Universal Requirement**

Regardless of which path you choose, `OPENAI_API_KEY` must be present in the environment. For Ollama-only setups, `OPENAI_API_KEY=xxx` satisfies this requirement without making any actual OpenAI API calls. This is worth documenting prominently in any team runbook, as it's the most common source of startup failures for new contributors.

title: What Is the Swagger-ChatGPT-Plugin-Creator and Who Should Use It?
content:
Imagine you run a restaurant and you want your menu listed on every major food delivery app. Instead of manually re-entering all your dishes on each platform, you use a tool that reads your existing menu and automatically formats it for each app. The Swagger-ChatGPT-Plugin-Creator works on a similar principle — it reads your existing API description (written in Swagger/OpenAPI format) and helps you package it as a ChatGPT plugin, so ChatGPT users can interact with your API through natural language.

ChatGPT plugins are extensions that allow the ChatGPT model to reach outside its training data and call real, live APIs. This means a user could type 'What is the current weather in Tokyo?' and ChatGPT, equipped with a weather API plugin, would fetch that live data and respond intelligently. The Swagger-ChatGPT-Plugin-Creator is a tool designed to make building those plugins easier.

**Who is this tool for?**

There are three main groups of people who benefit from this project:

1. **API developers** — If you have already built an API and documented it with Swagger (OpenAPI), this tool helps you expose that API to ChatGPT users without rebuilding everything from scratch. Your existing Swagger spec becomes the foundation for the plugin.

2. **API providers** — Companies or individuals who offer API services (weather data, financial data, translation services, etc.) can use this tool to expand their reach. Instead of only serving developers who write code to call their API, they can now serve ChatGPT users who interact through plain English.

3. **ChatGPT power users** — People who want to extend what ChatGPT can do by connecting it to third-party services. If you want ChatGPT to look up your calendar, query a database, or interact with a SaaS tool, plugins are the mechanism — and this tool helps create them.

**The core idea: bridging two worlds**

Swagger (now formally called OpenAPI) is the industry-standard way to describe REST APIs. It defines what endpoints exist, what parameters they accept, and what responses they return — all in a structured, machine-readable format. ChatGPT plugins also require a structured description of what the plugin can do, written in a specific format OpenAI defines.

The Swagger-ChatGPT-Plugin-Creator acts as a translator between these two worlds. It takes the Swagger spec you already have and helps generate the plugin manifest and configuration that ChatGPT needs to understand and use your API.

This dramatically reduces the manual work involved. Without such a tool, a developer would need to read OpenAI's plugin documentation, manually write a plugin manifest, ensure the descriptions are clear enough for the language model to understand, and handle the plumbing between ChatGPT and the API. This tool automates or simplifies much of that process.

**Getting started**

The installation is straightforward for anyone comfortable with a terminal. You clone the repository from GitHub, navigate into the project directory, and follow the setup steps. The project is Python-based, which means it fits naturally into the ecosystem most API developers already work in.

```
git clone https://github.com/ruvnet/Swagger-ChatGPT-Plugin-Creator.git
cd chatgpt-plugin-creator
```

From there, the tool provides a UI layer (as noted in the commit history, UI improvements were part of the development cycle) to help guide you through the plugin creation process.

**Why this matters for the broader AI ecosystem**

ChatGPT plugins represent a significant shift in how AI models interact with the world. Instead of being limited to knowledge baked in during training, a plugin-enabled ChatGPT can act as an intelligent interface to any API. This turns ChatGPT from a static knowledge base into a dynamic agent capable of taking actions and retrieving live information.

For API providers, this is a new distribution channel. For developers, it is a new way to make their services accessible to non-technical users. And for end users, it means a more capable, connected AI assistant.

The Swagger-ChatGPT-Plugin-Creator lowers the barrier to entry for all three groups by automating the translation between the API world (Swagger specs) and the ChatGPT plugin world (OpenAI plugin manifests). It is an early but important tool in the growing ecosystem of AI-native integrations.

title: How to Set Up the Swagger-ChatGPT-Plugin-Creator: Installation and Project Structure
content:
Setting up the Swagger-ChatGPT-Plugin-Creator is the first practical step toward turning any Swagger-documented API into a ChatGPT plugin. Think of it like installing a translation app on your phone — once it is there, you can start converting content between two languages. In this case, the two languages are Swagger/OpenAPI specifications and ChatGPT plugin manifests.

This entry walks through the installation process, explains what you are setting up, and gives context for what to expect as you get started.

**Prerequisites**

Before cloning the repository, make sure you have the following in place:

- **Git** installed on your machine (to clone the repository)
- **Python** installed (the project is Python-based, as confirmed by the commit history referencing Python updates)
- A terminal or command-line interface you are comfortable using
- A Swagger/OpenAPI specification for the API you want to expose as a ChatGPT plugin (this is your raw material)

If you do not yet have a Swagger spec, you will need to create one first. Swagger specs are typically written in YAML or JSON and describe your API's endpoints, parameters, authentication, and responses.

**Step 1: Clone the repository**

Open your terminal and run:

```
git clone https://github.com/ruvnet/Swagger-ChatGPT-Plugin-Creator.git
```

This downloads the full project to your local machine. Cloning rather than downloading a ZIP file is recommended because it preserves the Git history, making it easier to pull future updates.

**Step 2: Navigate into the project directory**

```
cd chatgpt-plugin-creator
```

This puts you inside the project folder where all the relevant files live. From here, you will install dependencies and run the tool.

**Step 3: Install dependencies**

The project is Python-based, so you will typically install dependencies using pip. While the exact command depends on the project's setup file, the standard approach is:

```
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

This installs all the Python libraries the tool needs to parse Swagger specs, generate plugin manifests, and run the UI.

**What the project contains**

Based on the development history, the project includes several components that evolved over its early commits:

- **A parser** — reads and interprets Swagger/OpenAPI specifications
- **A generator** — produces the ChatGPT plugin manifest and related configuration files
- **A UI layer** — provides a user interface to guide you through the plugin creation process without requiring you to manually edit configuration files
- **Python utilities** — helper scripts for processing and transforming API descriptions

The commit history shows rapid iteration: the project went from an initial commit to UI improvements, Python parsing updates, and bug fixes within about ten days. This is typical of early-stage developer tools where the core workflow is being refined based on real usage.

**What you get at the end**

After running the tool against your Swagger spec, you should have the files needed to register your API as a ChatGPT plugin. This typically includes:

- A plugin manifest file (`ai-plugin.json`) that describes your plugin to ChatGPT
- An OpenAPI spec formatted to meet ChatGPT's plugin requirements
- Configuration for how ChatGPT should authenticate with your API

These files are then hosted alongside your API (or on a separate server) so that ChatGPT can discover and use your plugin.

**A note on stability**

The commit history includes an honest note: 'updated. Needs some major fixes.' This is a reminder that early-stage open source tools are works in progress. If you encounter issues, check the repository's issues page on GitHub, and consider contributing fixes back to the project. The tool is functional enough to be useful, but may require some manual adjustment depending on the complexity of your Swagger spec.

**Next steps after installation**

Once installed, your workflow will be: provide your Swagger spec as input, run the tool, review the generated plugin files, host them appropriately, and register the plugin with ChatGPT. Each of those steps has its own considerations, but installation is the necessary foundation — and it is designed to be quick and accessible for any developer already working with APIs.

title: What is ai-gist and Why Does a Unified LLM Interface Matter?
content:
Imagine you are a chef who needs ingredients from a dozen different grocery stores, but every store has its own ordering system, its own phone number, and its own way of packaging deliveries. You would spend most of your time learning store procedures rather than actually cooking. That is exactly the problem developers face when working with multiple large language model (LLM) providers — OpenAI has one API format, Anthropic has another, Hugging Face has yet another. The ai-gist project solves this by acting as a universal translator between your code and all of those providers.

ai-gist is an open-source Python library built around a single core idea: one consistent input/output format that works across 100+ LLMs. Whether you want to call GPT-4 from OpenAI, Claude from Anthropic, or a model hosted on Hugging Face, your code looks exactly the same. You write it once, and ai-gist handles the translation behind the scenes.

The project is structured cleanly. At its heart is the `aigist/app/lite_llm.py` module, which manages the actual communication with LLM providers. Supporting it are `models.py` for data structures, `services.py` for business logic, and `database.py` for persistence. The `main.py` entry point ties everything together, and the test suite in `tests/` ensures reliability.

Why does this matter in practice? Consider a team evaluating which LLM provider gives the best results for their use case. Without a unified interface, switching from OpenAI to Cohere means rewriting API calls, adjusting response parsing, and debugging new edge cases. With ai-gist, switching providers is a configuration change, not a code rewrite. This dramatically reduces the cost of experimentation and lets teams make data-driven decisions about which model actually performs best for their specific task.

Cost optimization is another concrete benefit. Different providers charge very different rates, and the best model for a task is not always the most expensive one. A unified interface lets you route different types of requests to different providers based on cost and capability, without maintaining separate codebases for each.

The open-source nature of ai-gist means the community continuously adds support for new providers and models as the LLM landscape evolves. You are not locked into a vendor's roadmap.

title: Automatic Error Handling and Streaming in Multi-Provider LLM Systems
content:
Two of the most painful problems when building production applications on top of LLMs are reliability and memory management. ai-gist addresses both directly through built-in error handling with automatic retries and streaming support.

Think of error handling in a multi-provider system like having a backup generator. When your primary power source fails, you do not want to manually flip a switch — you want the system to detect the failure and switch automatically. ai-gist does exactly this for LLM calls. If a provider returns an error, is rate-limiting your requests, or goes temporarily offline, ai-gist automatically retries and can fall back to an alternative provider. From your application's perspective, the call either succeeds or fails gracefully — you are not writing custom retry logic for every provider's specific error codes and rate limit headers.

This matters enormously in production. LLM APIs are not perfectly reliable. Rate limits, transient network errors, and provider outages are all real events that happen regularly. Without automatic handling, each of these becomes an incident your team has to respond to. With ai-gist's retry mechanism, many of these events become invisible to end users.

Streaming is the second major reliability feature. When you ask an LLM to generate a long document, a detailed code review, or an extended analysis, the model may take 30 seconds or more to produce the full output. Without streaming, your application has to hold that entire response in memory and wait for completion before doing anything with it. For large outputs, this is both slow from the user's perspective and expensive in terms of memory usage.

Streaming solves this by delivering the model's output in chunks as it is generated, similar to how video streaming services send your movie in small pieces rather than downloading the entire file before playback begins. Your application can start processing or displaying content immediately, and memory usage stays flat regardless of how long the final output is.

In ai-gist's architecture, the `lite_llm.py` module handles both of these concerns at the provider communication layer, meaning the rest of your application code does not need to think about them. The `services.py` layer can call LLM functionality and trust that retries and streaming are handled correctly underneath.

For teams building customer-facing products on LLMs, these two features — automatic failover and streaming — are often the difference between a prototype and a production-ready system. ai-gist packages them as defaults rather than features you have to build yourself.

title: How ai-gist Reduces Complexity When Working Across Multiple LLM Providers
content:
One of the most underappreciated costs in AI development is not compute or API fees — it is cognitive overhead. Every time a developer has to context-switch between different provider documentation, different authentication schemes, and different response formats, they lose time and introduce bugs. ai-gist is designed specifically to eliminate this overhead.

The core architectural decision in ai-gist is standardization at the interface level. Rather than exposing the quirks of each provider's API, ai-gist defines a single input format for sending prompts and a single output format for receiving responses. This is the same philosophy behind standards like USB-C: instead of carrying a different cable for every device, you carry one cable that works everywhere.

In practical terms, this means a developer learning to use ai-gist learns one API, not one hundred. The knowledge transfers completely when switching providers. A prompt that works with OpenAI's GPT-4 will work with Anthropic's Claude or a Cohere model using identical code — only the model identifier changes.

The project's file structure reflects this philosophy. The `lite_llm.py` module is the abstraction layer that speaks each provider's native language internally while presenting a clean, consistent interface externally. The `models.py` file defines the shared data structures that flow through the system. This separation of concerns means that adding a new provider requires changes in one place, not throughout the entire codebase.

For teams, this has a compounding benefit over time. New team members can become productive quickly because there is only one interface to learn. Code reviews are simpler because LLM calls all look the same. Testing is more straightforward because you can mock a single interface rather than multiple provider-specific clients.

The flexibility benefit is also significant for research and experimentation. When evaluating which model performs best for a specific task, you can run the same prompt through multiple providers in a loop, collect results, and compare — all with minimal code. This kind of systematic evaluation is difficult when each provider requires different integration code.

ai-gist's open-source community model ensures that as new providers emerge and existing ones update their APIs, the library stays current. Contributors maintain the provider-specific translation layer so that users of the library do not have to track every API change across the industry.

For anyone building on LLMs beyond a single-provider prototype, ai-gist represents a practical architectural choice: invest in a unified interface early, and avoid paying the complexity tax every time the LLM landscape shifts.

title: What Is Micro Agent and Why Does It Exist?
content:
Writing code with an AI assistant often feels like asking a contractor to build you a deck and then discovering they left out the stairs. The first draft looks promising, but it doesn't quite work. You go back and forth, explaining what's wrong, waiting for a new attempt, testing again. This loop can eat hours.

Micro Agent is a tool built to automate that loop. Instead of you manually checking whether the AI's code works and then re-prompting it, Micro Agent does the checking for you — repeatedly — until the code actually passes.

Here's the core idea in plain English: you point Micro Agent at a source file and either a test file or a design screenshot. Micro Agent then calls an LLM to write or fix the code in that file, runs your tests (or compares the output to your screenshot), and if things still aren't right, it feeds the failure information back to the LLM and tries again. It keeps doing this until the tests pass or the visual output matches closely enough.

Think of it like a very patient intern who never gets frustrated. You give them a task and a rubric (the tests or the screenshot), and they keep revising their work and checking it against the rubric until they get a passing grade — without you having to supervise each attempt.

The package is available on npm as `@builder.io/micro-agent`, so you can install it into any Node.js project. It was built by the team at Builder.io and has been actively developed with contributions from the open-source community.

**Two modes of operation**

Micro Agent supports two distinct feedback mechanisms:

1. **Test-driven mode**: You provide a test file (for example, a Vitest or Jest spec). Micro Agent runs the tests after each code generation attempt. The test output — including error messages and stack traces — becomes the feedback that gets sent back to the LLM. This is powerful because test failures are precise: they tell the model exactly what went wrong and where.

2. **Screenshot mode**: You provide a reference image of what the UI should look like. Micro Agent renders the component or page, takes a screenshot, and compares it to your reference. The visual diff becomes the feedback signal. This is useful when you're building UI components and want the output to match a design mockup.

**Why tests make such a good feedback loop**

LLMs are probabilistic — they generate plausible-looking code, not guaranteed-correct code. The gap between "looks right" and "is right" is exactly where developers lose time. Tests are a formal, executable specification of what "right" means. When you give an LLM a failing test and its error output, you're giving it a very specific, unambiguous signal about what needs to change. This is far more effective than vague re-prompting like "that didn't work, try again."

Micro Agent essentially turns your test suite into a training signal for a single-task optimization loop. Each iteration, the model gets smarter about your specific problem because it sees exactly how its previous attempt failed.

**What Micro Agent is not**

It's worth being clear about scope. Micro Agent is not a general-purpose coding assistant that browses your whole codebase and makes sweeping architectural decisions. It's deliberately narrow: one file, one test (or screenshot), iterate until passing. This constraint is a feature, not a limitation. By keeping the scope small, the feedback loop stays tight and the results stay predictable.

It also doesn't replace the need to write good tests. If your tests are vague or incomplete, Micro Agent can produce code that passes them without actually doing what you intended. Garbage in, garbage out — but with more automation.

**Practical takeaway**

If you find yourself in a cycle of "ask AI for code → test it → it's broken → explain the error → repeat," Micro Agent is designed to handle that cycle automatically. You write the test that defines what success looks like, and the agent handles the iteration. Your job shifts from debugging AI output to writing clear, precise tests — which is a much better use of your time.

title: Test-Driven Iteration: How Micro Agent Uses Failing Tests as LLM Feedback
content:
One of the most powerful patterns in AI-assisted development is using automated test output as a feedback signal for code generation. Micro Agent implements this pattern in a clean, practical way that's worth understanding deeply — because the underlying idea applies far beyond this one tool.

**The problem with one-shot code generation**

When you ask an LLM to write a function, it produces something that looks syntactically correct and semantically plausible. But "plausible" and "correct" are different things. Edge cases get missed. Assumptions about data shapes are wrong. Off-by-one errors slip through. The model has no way to know it made a mistake because it never actually ran the code.

This is the fundamental limitation of one-shot generation: the model is flying blind. It produces output based on pattern matching over training data, not based on execution feedback.

**Closing the loop with tests**

The insight behind Micro Agent is simple: tests are a machine-readable specification of correctness. When a test fails, the error message, stack trace, and assertion output contain precise, structured information about what went wrong. That information is exactly what an LLM needs to make a targeted fix.

Here's the loop Micro Agent runs:

1. Send the current file contents and the test file to the LLM, ask it to write or fix the implementation.
2. Write the LLM's output to the file.
3. Run the tests.
4. If tests pass, done. If tests fail, collect the failure output.
5. Send the failure output back to the LLM along with the current file state, ask it to fix the issues.
6. Go to step 2.

This is a closed feedback loop. Each iteration gives the model more information than the last. The model isn't just guessing — it's responding to concrete evidence about what its previous attempt got wrong.

**Why this works better than manual re-prompting**

When a developer manually re-prompts an LLM after a failure, they typically summarize the problem in natural language: "the function returns null when the input is empty." This is lossy. The actual error output might contain a stack trace pointing to a specific line, an assertion showing the expected versus actual value, and context about which test case triggered the failure. All of that precision gets lost in the human summary.

Micro Agent passes the raw test output directly. No information is lost. The LLM sees exactly what a developer would see in their terminal, and it can reason about that output directly.

**The Angular component example**

The repository includes an illustrative example involving Angular component introspection. Given a component class like this:

```ts
import { Component, Input } from '@angular/core';
type Foo = number;

@Component({ selector: 'my-component' })
export class MyComponent {
  @Input() num: Foo;
}
```

The expected output is a structured metadata object:

```ts
{
  name: 'MyComponent',
  selector: 'my-component',
  inputs: [{ name: 'num', type: 'number' }],
}
```

Notice that `Foo` is a type alias for `number` — the correct output resolves the alias to its underlying type. This is a non-trivial transformation. A test that asserts the output must equal `{ type: 'number' }` (not `{ type: 'Foo' }`) gives the LLM a precise, unambiguous target. If the model returns `Foo` instead of `number`, the test fails with a clear diff, and the next iteration can fix exactly that issue.

**Writing tests that make good feedback signals**

Not all tests are equally useful as feedback. Tests that produce informative failure messages work best. Assertion libraries that show expected versus actual values (like Vitest's `expect(result).toEqual(expected)`) give the LLM rich information. Tests that just throw a generic error without context are less useful.

The practical advice: write your tests to be as explicit as possible about what the correct output looks like. The more specific the assertion, the more targeted the LLM's correction can be. Think of your test as a conversation with the model — the failure message is what the model hears when it gets something wrong.

**Broader applicability**

This pattern — use executable specifications as feedback for generative models — is one of the most reliable techniques for getting consistent, correct output from LLMs on coding tasks. Micro Agent packages it into a convenient CLI tool, but the underlying principle can be applied manually or built into other workflows. Any time you can express "correct" as a runnable check, you can build a feedback loop.

title: Core Capabilities of the ChatGPT OpenAI API Plugin
content:
The ChatGPT OpenAI API plugin is best understood as a Swiss Army knife for language-based tasks. Rather than doing one thing well, it packages a broad set of natural language capabilities into a single, extensible interface. Understanding what each capability does — and when to reach for it — is the foundation for building effective AI-powered applications.

**Text Generation** is the most fundamental capability. You provide a prompt, and the model (GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo, or others) returns coherent, contextually appropriate text. Think of it like giving a highly literate assistant a starting sentence and asking them to continue. The quality of the output depends heavily on how well you craft the prompt.

**Conversational AI** builds on text generation but adds memory of the exchange. Instead of a single prompt-response pair, you maintain a thread of messages — user turns and assistant turns — that the model uses as context. This is how chatbots and virtual assistants are built. The model doesn't have persistent memory between sessions by default, so the conversation history must be passed explicitly each time.

**Language Translation** leverages the model's multilingual training to convert text between languages with high accuracy. Unlike rule-based translation systems, the model understands nuance, idiom, and context, making translations feel more natural. This also powers **Multilingual Applications**, where you can generate content or interact with users in their native language without maintaining separate models per language.

**Code Generation** is one of the most practically valuable capabilities. You can describe a problem in plain English and receive working code in Python, JavaScript, SQL, or dozens of other languages. This is useful for prototyping, automating repetitive coding tasks, or helping developers who are unfamiliar with a specific language's syntax.

**Content Summarization** takes long documents, articles, or conversation logs and condenses them into concise summaries. Imagine having a research assistant who can read a 50-page report and hand you a one-paragraph brief. This is particularly useful in enterprise workflows where information overload is a constant challenge.

**Creative Writing** extends text generation into literary territory — poems, short stories, dialogues, scripts. You can control the tone (formal vs. casual), the style (minimalist vs. elaborate), and the level of detail. This makes the plugin useful not just for technical teams but for content creators and marketers as well.

**Data Augmentation** is a less obvious but powerful use case. Machine learning models need large, diverse datasets to train well. When real data is scarce, you can use the language model to generate synthetic examples that mimic the distribution of real data. This is especially valuable in specialized domains like medical or legal NLP where labeled data is expensive to produce.

Taken together, these capabilities cover the full spectrum from raw text manipulation to domain-specific intelligence, making the plugin a versatile foundation for a wide range of AI applications.

title: Advanced Patterns: Recursive Workflows, Chain of Thought, and External Data Integration
content:
Beyond the standard prompt-response pattern, the ChatGPT OpenAI API plugin supports several advanced techniques that unlock significantly more powerful behavior. These patterns treat the language model not as a simple question-answering machine, but as a reasoning engine that can iterate, branch, and reach outside itself for information.

**Recursive Workflows** are one of the most creative applications. Instead of generating a single response and stopping, you feed the model's output back in as new input, repeating the process across multiple cycles. Think of it like a writer who drafts a paragraph, reads it back, revises it, reads again, and revises again — each pass refining the result. In practice, this is used for exploring narrative branches in storytelling ("what if the character made a different choice?"), generating multiple candidate solutions to a problem, or building conversation trees where each branch represents a different dialogue path. The key insight is that the model's output at step N becomes the context for step N+1, allowing complex, multi-stage reasoning to emerge from simple building blocks.

**Chain of Thought** is a prompting technique that instructs the model to reason step by step before arriving at a final answer. Rather than asking "What is the answer to X?", you ask "Think through this carefully, step by step, then give me the answer to X." This dramatically improves performance on tasks that require multi-step logic, arithmetic, or causal reasoning. The analogy is the difference between asking someone to shout out an answer versus asking them to show their work. Showing the work forces more careful reasoning and catches errors that would otherwise slip through. Chain of Thought is particularly effective when combined with few-shot examples — showing the model two or three worked examples before presenting the actual problem.

**Integration with External Data** addresses one of the language model's fundamental limitations: its knowledge is frozen at training time. By connecting the plugin to external data sources — web content, databases, Wolfram Alpha for mathematical computation, APIs, and more — you can give the model access to current, domain-specific, or proprietary information it would otherwise lack. This is the architectural pattern behind retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): retrieve relevant documents or data at query time, inject them into the prompt as context, and let the model reason over fresh information rather than relying solely on what it memorized during training.

**Model Fine-Tuning** takes a different approach to specialization. Instead of injecting domain knowledge at inference time, you retrain the model on domain-specific examples so the knowledge becomes part of the model's weights. The plugin supports fine-tuning for specialized domains like legal, medical, or financial applications. The trade-off is cost and complexity: fine-tuning requires curated training data (the repository includes a `training_data.jsonl` file as a starting point) and compute time, but the resulting model can be faster and more consistent for narrow tasks than a general model guided by prompts alone.

These advanced patterns — recursion, chain of thought, external data integration, and fine-tuning — are not mutually exclusive. The most sophisticated applications combine them: a recursive workflow that uses chain of thought reasoning at each step, retrieves external data to ground its outputs, and runs on a fine-tuned model optimized for the target domain. Understanding each pattern individually is the prerequisite for combining them effectively.

title: Choosing Between Prompt Engineering, Fine-Tuning, and Retrieval Augmentation
content:
One of the most common decision points when building with the OpenAI API is choosing how to specialize the model for your use case. The ChatGPT OpenAI API plugin supports three distinct approaches, and picking the right one depends on your data, latency requirements, and how stable your domain knowledge is.

**Prompt Engineering** is always the starting point. You shape the model's behavior entirely through the text you send it — instructions, examples, constraints, and context all live in the prompt. This requires no training, no infrastructure beyond the API call, and can be iterated on in minutes. The `prompt.txt` file in this repository is an example of a carefully crafted system prompt that defines the model's persona and behavior. The limitation is that prompts have a finite context window: you can only fit so much information before you hit the token limit, and the model can only "see" what's in the current prompt.

**Retrieval Augmentation (RAG)** solves the context window problem by fetching only the most relevant information at query time and injecting it into the prompt. Instead of trying to cram an entire knowledge base into a single prompt, you store documents in a searchable index, retrieve the top-N most relevant chunks when a query arrives, and include those chunks as context. The model then reasons over fresh, specific information rather than relying on general training knowledge. This is the right choice when your knowledge base is large, frequently updated, or contains proprietary information that was never in the model's training data. The plugin's external data integration capability is the practical expression of this pattern.

**Fine-Tuning** goes deeper: you actually update the model's weights by training on domain-specific examples. The `training_data.jsonl` file in the repository illustrates the format — pairs of prompts and ideal completions that teach the model the patterns, vocabulary, and reasoning style of a specific domain. Fine-tuning is appropriate when you need consistent stylistic behavior that's hard to enforce through prompting alone, when you're making thousands of API calls and want to use a smaller, cheaper model that performs like a larger one for your specific task, or when your domain has highly specialized terminology that the base model handles poorly.

A practical decision framework: start with prompt engineering. If you hit context limits or need current information, add retrieval augmentation. If you need consistent behavior at scale or the base model fundamentally lacks domain knowledge, consider fine-tuning. These approaches also compose — a fine-tuned model can still use retrieval augmentation and carefully crafted prompts. The repository's inclusion of both `prompt.txt` and `training_data.jsonl` reflects this layered philosophy: prompt engineering and fine-tuning are complementary tools, not competing alternatives.

The cost of getting this decision wrong is real but recoverable. Prompt engineering is cheap to experiment with and easy to change. Fine-tuning is expensive to redo if your requirements shift. When in doubt, exhaust prompt engineering and retrieval augmentation before committing to a fine-tuning run.

title: How Agentic Report Systems Decompose Complex Queries into Subqueries
content:
When you ask a research assistant to write a report on a broad topic like 'the future of AI in smart cities,' the assistant faces a fundamental problem: no single search will capture everything worth knowing. Agentic report systems solve this by breaking the original question into a set of focused subqueries, each targeting a specific angle of the topic. Think of it like sending a team of specialist researchers to different sections of a library simultaneously, rather than having one generalist wander the stacks alone.

In the agentic-reports system, this decomposition is driven by a dedicated `subqueries_prompt`. This prompt instructs the language model to generate a configurable number of diverse, targeted search queries (`num_subqueries`) that collectively cover the topic's surface area. For a query about AI in smart cities, the system might generate subqueries like 'AI traffic management systems 2024,' 'energy efficiency machine learning urban infrastructure,' and 'public safety surveillance AI ethics.' Each subquery is then dispatched to a search API independently and in parallel.

The key insight here is separation of concerns. The model is not asked to research and write at the same time. Instead, the pipeline has distinct phases: decompose, search, retrieve, synthesize. This mirrors how expert human researchers work — you outline your research questions before you start pulling sources, not while you're writing.

Once all subqueries return results, the system aggregates the retrieved content and passes it to a final `report_prompt`. This prompt instructs the model to synthesize everything into a coherent, structured report. Crucially, the report prompt can include formatting instructions — for example, requiring inline citations using footnote notation like `[2]`, followed by a `References` section listing URLs and publication dates. This keeps the output both readable and verifiable.

Date filtering is another important lever. The system accepts `start_published_date` and `end_published_date` parameters, ensuring that retrieved sources fall within a relevant time window. For fast-moving fields like AI, a report drawing only on sources from the past six months is far more useful than one mixing 2018 blog posts with 2024 research papers.

The practical takeaway for builders: when designing agentic pipelines that produce long-form outputs, resist the temptation to collapse everything into a single mega-prompt. A prompt that says 'search the web and write a report' is asking the model to do too many things at once. Instead, decompose the task into explicit stages — query generation, retrieval, and synthesis — and give each stage its own focused prompt. This makes the system easier to debug, easier to improve incrementally, and more likely to produce high-quality outputs.

title: Prompt Architecture in Agentic Pipelines: Primary, Subquery, and Report Prompts
content:
A well-designed agentic pipeline doesn't rely on a single monolithic prompt. Instead, it uses a layered prompt architecture where different prompts govern different stages of the workflow. The agentic-reports system is a clean example of this pattern, using three distinct prompt types: the `primary_prompt`, the `subqueries_prompt`, and the `report_prompt`. Understanding what each one does — and why they are kept separate — is essential for anyone building research or report-generation agents.

**The Primary Prompt** defines the overall intent and scope of the report. It tells the system what the report is about, what aspects to focus on, and what the expected output should look like at a high level. For example: 'Generate a detailed report on the future of AI in smart cities, focusing on traffic management, energy efficiency, and public safety. Include analysis of current technologies, ongoing projects, challenges, and future prospects.' This prompt is not used for searching — it's used to orient the entire pipeline and can be passed as context to later stages.

**The Subqueries Prompt** is a meta-prompt: it instructs the model to generate search queries rather than to answer a question directly. This is a subtle but powerful distinction. Instead of asking 'what do you know about AI in smart cities?', you're asking 'what would you search for to learn about AI in smart cities?' The model's output here is a list of strings that get fed directly into a search API. The prompt can constrain the number and diversity of queries, ensuring broad coverage without redundancy.

**The Report Prompt** governs the final synthesis step. By this point, the pipeline has retrieved real-world source material. The report prompt tells the model how to use that material: what structure to follow, what tone to adopt, how long the output should be, and how to handle citations. Separating citation instructions into this prompt — rather than the primary prompt — keeps concerns clean. The model doesn't need to think about citation format while it's generating search queries.

This three-prompt architecture maps onto a general principle in agentic system design: each prompt should have exactly one job. A prompt that tries to simultaneously define scope, generate queries, and format output will produce muddled results. When prompts are focused, they are easier to tune independently. If your subqueries are too narrow, you adjust the subqueries prompt without touching the report prompt. If your citations are malformatted, you fix the report prompt without risking changes to query generation.

For teams building similar pipelines, a useful exercise is to audit your existing prompts and ask: is this prompt doing more than one thing? If so, consider splitting it. The overhead of managing multiple prompts is small compared to the improvement in output quality and system maintainability.

title: Controlling Search Scope in Agentic Research Pipelines with Date Filtering and Result Shaping
content:
One of the most underappreciated aspects of building agentic research systems is controlling what information the agent is allowed to see. An agent that can search the entire web without constraints will often surface outdated, irrelevant, or low-quality content. The agentic-reports system addresses this through a combination of date filtering and result-shaping parameters that give developers precise control over the retrieval stage.

**Date Filtering** is implemented via `start_published_date` and `end_published_date` fields in the request configuration. These parameters are passed to the underlying search API to restrict results to a specific publication window. For a report on AI in smart cities covering developments through mid-2024, you'd set `start_published_date` to `2024-01-01` and `end_published_date` to `2024-06-03`. This ensures the synthesized report reflects the current state of the field rather than mixing in historical content that might contradict or dilute recent findings.

Date filtering is especially important in fast-moving domains. A report on large language models that draws on sources from 2021 will describe a fundamentally different landscape than one restricted to 2024. Without date constraints, the model may confidently synthesize contradictory information from different eras, producing a report that sounds authoritative but is internally inconsistent.

**Result Shaping** controls how retrieved content is presented to the model. The `highlights` parameter, for example, specifies `num_sentences` — how many sentences from each source should be extracted as highlights. Setting this to 5 means the system pulls the five most relevant sentences from each retrieved document rather than dumping the entire article into the context window. This is analogous to a researcher reading only the abstract and key findings of a paper rather than the full text — it keeps the context window lean and forces the retrieval layer to do meaningful summarization work before synthesis begins.

The `text` parameter with `include_html_tags: false` is a small but important detail. Raw web content is full of navigation menus, cookie banners, and markup noise. Stripping HTML tags before passing content to the model reduces token waste and prevents the model from being distracted by irrelevant structural elements.

Taken together, these parameters form a retrieval hygiene layer. The lesson for pipeline builders is that retrieval quality is as important as model quality. A powerful language model fed noisy, outdated, or poorly scoped retrieval results will produce a poor report. Investing in clean retrieval — through date filtering, content extraction, and result shaping — pays dividends at every downstream stage of the pipeline.

title: Deploying Open Interpreter as an AWS Lambda Function with Docker
content:
Open Interpreter is a powerful library that lets an LLM write and execute code on your behalf — think of it as giving an AI a terminal and letting it solve problems hands-on. Deploying it as a serverless AWS Lambda function unlocks on-demand, scalable AI code execution without managing servers. Here's how the agileagents pattern works and what you need to understand to do it right.

**The Core Architecture**

Because Open Interpreter has heavy dependencies (it bundles a Python runtime, code execution sandbox, and LLM client), it exceeds Lambda's standard 250MB deployment package limit. The solution is to package everything into a Docker container image and push that image to Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry), then point Lambda at it. This is the 'repository_name + image_tag' pattern you see in the config — `open-interpreter:latest` is the Docker image that Lambda will run.

**The Lambda Handler Pattern**

There's a subtle but important architectural detail in the script worth understanding. The Open Interpreter call happens *outside* the `lambda_handler` function:

```python
response = interpreter.chat('What is the capital of France?')
with open('/tmp/response.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write(response)

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    with open('/tmp/response.txt', 'r') as f:
        response = f.read()
    return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': json.dumps({'response': response})}
```

This means the interpreter runs at *container initialization time*, not per-invocation. The result is written to `/tmp/response.txt`, and the handler simply reads it back. Think of it like a chef who preps the meal before the restaurant opens — the work is done ahead of time, and the waiter (the handler) just serves what's ready. This is useful for pre-computed responses but means the query is hardcoded at build time, not dynamic per request. For production use, you'd move the `interpreter.chat()` call inside the handler and pass the query from `event`.

**Configuration Parameters That Matter**

The deployment config specifies `memory_size: 1024` (1GB RAM) and `timeout: 900` (15 minutes, the Lambda maximum). These are not arbitrary — Open Interpreter can spin up subprocesses, install packages, and run multi-step reasoning chains that take significant time and memory. Skimping on either will cause silent failures or timeout errors. For LLM-backed agents doing real work, always start generous with resources and tune down after profiling.

**Secrets Management**

The `OPENAI_API_KEY` is passed as a Lambda environment variable. In the script, it's retrieved with `os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY']` and injected into the interpreter: `interpreter.llm.api_key = api_key`. Never hardcode API keys in your Docker image or script. For production, replace the plain environment variable with an AWS Secrets Manager reference or Parameter Store integration — Lambda supports fetching secrets at runtime through the AWS SDK, keeping your keys out of environment variable logs.

**The /tmp Filesystem**

Lambda provides a writable `/tmp` directory with up to 10GB of ephemeral storage (as of recent AWS updates). This is the only place you can write files during execution. The pattern of writing results to `/tmp/response.txt` and reading them back is a common Lambda idiom for passing data between initialization code and the handler. Just remember: `/tmp` is ephemeral and not shared between concurrent Lambda instances.

**When to Use This Pattern**

This architecture makes sense when you want to expose AI code execution as a microservice endpoint — for example, a backend API that accepts natural language tasks and returns results. The serverless model means you pay only for actual execution time, and Lambda's concurrency model handles bursts of requests automatically. The tradeoff is cold start latency: Docker-based Lambda functions can take several seconds to initialize on first invocation.

title: Dynamic Code Execution in AWS Lambda Using Virtual Environments
content:
One of the more advanced patterns in the agileagents repository is a Lambda function that accepts arbitrary Python code as input, executes it in an isolated virtual environment, and returns the result. This is the foundation for building AI agent systems where the LLM generates code that needs to run safely in the cloud. Understanding how this works — and why each step exists — is essential for building robust agent infrastructure.

**The Problem: Lambda's Immutable Runtime**

AWS Lambda functions run in a frozen execution environment. You can't install new packages after deployment. But AI agents often generate code that requires libraries you didn't anticipate at build time. The solution in this pattern is to use Python's `venv` module and `pip` at *runtime* inside the `/tmp` directory, creating a fresh virtual environment for each execution.

Think of it like a hotel room with a kitchenette: the room itself is fixed, but you can bring in your own groceries and cook whatever you need during your stay.

**Step-by-Step Execution Flow**

The handler follows a clear pipeline:

1. **Extract code from the event**: `code = event.get('code')` — the caller sends Python code as a string in the Lambda invocation payload.

2. **Set up a temp directory**: `os.makedirs('/tmp/deployment', exist_ok=True)` creates a working directory in Lambda's writable filesystem.

3. **Write the script to disk**: The code string is written to `/tmp/deployment/script.py` so it can be executed as a file.

4. **Write requirements**: A `requirements.txt` is written (currently empty in the base version, but extensible for agent-generated dependency lists).

5. **Create a virtual environment**: `subprocess.run(['python3', '-m', 'venv', 'venv'], cwd=temp_dir)` creates an isolated Python environment inside `/tmp/deployment/venv/`.

6. **Install dependencies**: `venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt` installs any required packages into the venv, not the system Python.

7. **Execute the script**: The script runs using the venv's Python interpreter, keeping it isolated from the Lambda runtime.

**Why Virtual Environments Matter Here**

Without a venv, installing packages with pip inside Lambda would attempt to write to system directories, which are read-only. The venv creates a self-contained Python installation under `/tmp` where everything is writable. It also prevents dependency conflicts if multiple agent tasks run sequentially in the same warm Lambda container — each gets a clean slate.

**Error Handling Pattern**

The code checks `result.returncode != 0` after the pip install and returns a structured error response with both stdout and stderr. This is critical for debugging agent-generated code: when an LLM writes code that requires a package that fails to install, you need the full pip output to diagnose whether it's a network issue, a version conflict, or a nonexistent package name.

**Security Considerations**

Executing arbitrary code sent via an API is inherently risky. This pattern should always be paired with: (1) strict IAM permissions on the Lambda role — give it only what it needs, nothing more; (2) input validation before execution; (3) network isolation via VPC configuration to prevent the executed code from making unexpected outbound calls; and (4) resource limits to prevent runaway processes. Lambda's built-in timeout (set to 900 seconds in this config) acts as a hard kill switch.

**Extending This Pattern**

To make this production-ready for AI agents, you'd extend it to parse LLM-generated requirements from the code (e.g., scanning for `import` statements and mapping them to pip packages), stream execution output back to the caller, and cache the venv between warm invocations to reduce overhead. This pattern is the engine room of any cloud-based code-executing AI agent.

title: How the Hacker League CLI Routes Commands to Agents and Sandboxes
content:
A command-line interface is like a switchboard operator from the old telephone era — someone sits at the center, listens for a request, and then patches the call through to the right department. The Hacker League CLI works exactly this way. When you run the interactive menu, it presents numbered options and waits for your input. Depending on what you type, it hands control off to one of several specialized modules: authentication, templates, sandboxes, or AI agents.

Let's walk through what each category does.

**Authentication (Options 1–2)**
Options 1 and 2 call `auth.login()` and `auth.logout()`. These are the front door of the system. Before you can do anything meaningful — build templates, spawn sandboxes, or invoke agents — you need to be authenticated. Keeping auth as a separate module means the rest of the system doesn't need to know how credentials work; it just trusts that the auth module handles it.

**Template Management (Options 3–5)**
Templates are reusable project blueprints. Option 3 initializes a new template, option 4 builds it (compiles or packages it), and option 5 lists what's available. Think of templates like cookie cutters — you define the shape once, then stamp out as many instances as you need. This pattern is common in developer tooling where you want reproducible environments.

**Sandbox Management (Options 6–7)**
Sandboxes are isolated execution environments. Option 6 lists all running sandboxes, and option 7 kills a specific one by ID. The kill operation asks you to type a sandbox ID, which gets passed directly to `sandbox.kill_sandbox(sandbox_id)`. Sandboxes are important for safely running untrusted or experimental code — if something goes wrong inside a sandbox, it doesn't affect the host system.

**Agent Commands (Options 8–10)**
This is where things get interesting. Options 8, 9, and 10 invoke AI agents, but notice the clever trick used to pass arguments: `type("Args", (), {...})`. This dynamically creates a throwaway class with attributes set to whatever the user typed. It mimics the `argparse.Namespace` object that command-line argument parsers normally produce. This means `agent.handle_agent_command(args)` doesn't need to know whether it was called from a menu or a terminal flag — it just reads attributes off the args object either way.

- **Option 8 (Code Agent):** Takes a natural language prompt and routes it to the code generation agent. You describe what you want built, and the agent writes the code.
- **Option 9 (Data Agent):** Handles data file operations. You specify an operation (`load`, `describe`, or `plot`), a file path, and optional column names. This is a lightweight data analysis pipeline triggered from a menu.
- **Option 10 (Employee Agent):** Manages lifecycle of role-based worker agents. You name a role, then decide whether to start or stop that employee. This hints at a multi-agent architecture where different "employees" handle different ongoing tasks.

**The Bigger Pattern**
What makes this CLI design clean is separation of concerns. Each module (auth, template, sandbox, agent) owns its own logic. The menu is just a thin routing layer — it collects input and dispatches. This makes the system easy to extend: adding option 11 means writing one new `elif` block and implementing the handler in the appropriate module.

The dynamic `type()` trick for creating args objects is worth remembering. It's a Pythonic shortcut that lets you reuse functions designed for argparse without actually going through argparse. It's not something you'd use in production library code, but for internal CLI tooling it's pragmatic and readable.

title: Streaming LLM Responses Over HTTP with OpenRouter and httpx
content:
When you ask a large language model a question, it doesn't compute the entire answer and then send it all at once — it generates tokens one at a time, like a person typing. Streaming lets your application receive and display those tokens as they arrive, rather than waiting for the full response. This dramatically improves perceived responsiveness, especially for long outputs.

The `stream_openrouter_response` function in NOVA demonstrates how to implement this correctly using Python's `httpx` library with async streaming.

**The Basic Setup**
The function is `async`, meaning it runs inside an event loop and doesn't block other work while waiting for network data. It uses `httpx.AsyncClient` as a context manager, which handles connection pooling and cleanup automatically. The key call is `client.stream(...)`, which opens a persistent HTTP connection that stays alive while the server pushes data.

**The Request**
The POST request goes to `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions`. OpenRouter is a unified API gateway that lets you call many different LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google) through a single endpoint. The headers include:
- `Authorization`: Bearer token from your `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` environment variable
- `HTTP-Referer` and `X-Title`: Optional metadata OpenRouter uses for routing and analytics

The JSON body sets `"stream": True`, which tells the server to use Server-Sent Events (SSE) format instead of returning a single JSON blob. `temperature: 0.7` controls randomness — lower values make outputs more deterministic, higher values more creative.

**Parsing the Stream**
The response comes back as a series of byte chunks. Each chunk is decoded to a string and checked for the `data: ` prefix — this is the SSE format. The actual JSON payload follows that prefix. The function strips the prefix with `chunk_str[6:]` and parses the JSON.

There's a special sentinel value `[DONE]` that signals the stream has ended. Every other chunk follows the OpenAI chat completions delta format: `choices[0].delta.content` contains the new token(s) to append to the output.
