Always-On Agents: Building Systems That Never Sleep
content:
Most people think of AI agents like a calculator — you press a button, it gives you an answer, and then it sits idle waiting for the next question. But rUv's coaching sessions point toward a fundamentally different model: agents that run perpetually, like a security guard who never clocks out.

Think of always-on agents the way you'd think about a thermostat versus a thermometer. A thermometer tells you the temperature when you ask. A thermostat watches the temperature constantly and acts the moment something drifts out of range. Always-on agents are thermostats — they don't wait to be queried. They monitor, learn, and respond on their own schedule.

**What Makes an Agent 'Always-On'?**

An always-on agent is assigned a specific slice of a system to watch. Rather than one giant agent trying to understand everything, you deploy focused agents — each responsible for a narrow domain. One agent watches database query latency. Another monitors API error rates. A third tracks user behavior patterns. Each one runs a tight feedback loop: observe, compare against known baselines, decide, act.

This specialization is critical. A broad agent trying to monitor everything becomes slow and noisy. A narrow agent watching one thing becomes genuinely expert at that thing. Over time, through tightly packed learning algorithms, it builds a model of what 'normal' looks like in its domain and gets better at spotting anomalies.

**Industrial Control Systems as a Mental Model**

rUv specifically mentioned industrial control systems as a use case, and it's a useful mental model. In a factory, you don't have a human engineer manually checking every valve and sensor every few minutes. You have automated systems watching those sensors continuously, ready to trigger an alarm or shut down a process the moment something goes wrong. The cost of missing an event — a pressure spike, a temperature anomaly — is too high to rely on periodic checks.

Software systems have the same problem. A memory leak that starts at 2 AM and crashes your service by 4 AM won't be caught by a monitoring job that runs every 30 minutes. An always-on agent watching memory allocation in real time catches it early, logs the pattern, and can even trigger a remediation workflow before humans wake up.

**Orchestration Over Line-by-Line Reading**

A key insight from the Agentix Foundation sessions reinforces this: modern AI-assisted development is about orchestration, not reading code line by line. The same principle applies to always-on agents. You're not building a system that understands every detail of your codebase in real time. You're building a system that manages agents — each of which understands its own narrow domain deeply.

This is the difference between a conductor and a musician. The conductor doesn't play every instrument. They coordinate specialists, each of whom is expert in their part. Your orchestration layer coordinates always-on agents, each expert in their slice of the system.

**Learning by Themselves**

The phrase rUv used — 'learn by themselves through tightly packed algorithms' — points to something important. These agents aren't static rule engines. They adapt. An agent monitoring API response times doesn't just check 'is this over 500ms?' It builds a rolling model of typical response times, accounts for time-of-day patterns, and adjusts its alerting thresholds accordingly. What counts as 'slow' at 3 AM during low traffic is different from 'slow' at noon during peak load.

This self-learning behavior is what separates always-on agents from traditional monitoring scripts. A cron job runs the same logic every time. An always-on agent gets smarter with every cycle.

**Practical Deployment Considerations**

When deploying always-on agents, a few principles matter:

- **Scope narrowly.** Each agent should own one concern. Resist the temptation to add 'just one more thing' to an existing agent.
- **Define the action space clearly.** What can the agent do on its own? What requires human approval? An agent that can restart a crashed microservice autonomously is useful. An agent that can delete production data autonomously is dangerous.
- **Build in observability.** Always-on agents need to be watched too. Log their decisions, their confidence levels, and their actions. You need to be able to audit what they did and why.
- **Plan for graceful degradation.** If an always-on agent itself fails, the system it monitors shouldn't fail with it. Design agents to fail safely and alert loudly.

Always-on agents represent a shift from reactive to proactive system management. Instead of humans responding to problems after they surface, you build agents that catch problems as they form — or prevent them entirely. The goal isn't to replace human judgment on complex decisions, but to free human attention for the decisions that actually require it.

title: Orchestration-First Development: Managing Agents Instead of Reading Code
content:
There's a mental model shift happening in how experienced developers think about building software with AI, and it's worth understanding clearly: the goal is no longer to read and write every line of code yourself. The goal is to orchestrate agents that do that work for you.

This came up explicitly in the Agentix Foundation sessions, where the emphasis was on 'building and managing agents rather than reading code line by line.' It sounds simple, but it represents a genuine change in what a senior developer's job looks like.

**The Old Model: Craftsperson**

In the traditional model, a developer is a craftsperson. They understand every line of code in their system. They can trace a bug from a user-facing error message down through the call stack to the specific function that misbehaved. Their value comes from deep, detailed knowledge of the codebase.

This model works well for small systems. It breaks down at scale. No human can hold a million-line codebase in their head. No human can simultaneously monitor performance, review pull requests, write new features, and respond to incidents. Something always gets dropped.

**The New Model: Conductor**

The orchestration-first model treats the developer more like a conductor than a craftsperson. The conductor doesn't play every instrument — they set the tempo, coordinate the sections, and ensure the overall piece sounds right. Individual musicians (agents) handle the detailed execution.

In practice, this means:
- A code review agent reads pull requests and flags issues
- A documentation agent keeps docs in sync with code changes
- A testing agent generates and runs tests for new functions
- A monitoring agent watches production and alerts on anomalies

The developer's job shifts to defining what each agent should do, setting the quality bar, reviewing agent outputs, and intervening when agents get stuck or make mistakes.

**Tools That Enable This Approach**

The sessions referenced several tools that support orchestration-first development: Cloud Code, Gemini CLI, Codex by OpenAI, and Claude Flow. What these tools share is an agentic interface — you describe what you want accomplished, and the tool figures out the steps.

Claude Flow, discussed in the London Chapter session, is a good example. It's not tied to a single AI model — you can run it with Gemini, Ollama, or other backends. The platform's value isn't the underlying model; it's the orchestration layer that coordinates multiple agents working on a problem together. One agent might browse the web for context, another might write code, a third might run tests. The orchestration layer sequences their work and passes outputs between them.

This composability is key. You're not building one giant AI that does everything. You're building a pipeline of specialized agents, each good at one thing, coordinated by an orchestration layer.

**What This Means for How You Build**

Orchestration-first development changes several practical habits:

**Define interfaces, not implementations.** When you're orchestrating agents, you care about inputs and outputs, not the internal logic. Define clearly what each agent receives and what it should return. The agent figures out the how.

**Invest in prompt engineering as architecture.** The instructions you give agents are architectural decisions. A vague instruction produces inconsistent results. A precise, well-structured prompt produces reliable, repeatable behavior. Treat your agent prompts with the same care you'd give a function signature.

**Build feedback loops.** Agents make mistakes. Build systems where agent outputs are reviewed — either by humans or by other agents — before they have irreversible effects. A code-writing agent whose output goes directly to production without review is a liability. The same agent whose output goes to a staging environment and gets reviewed is an asset.

**Embrace tool integration.** The sessions mentioned Playwright for browser automation alongside Claude Flow. The pattern here is important: agents become more powerful when they have tools — the ability to browse the web, run code, query databases, call APIs. An agent with no tools can only generate text. An agent with tools can take actions in the world.

**The Skill That Remains Human**

Orchestration-first development doesn't eliminate the need for technical skill — it redirects it. The valuable skill becomes system design: understanding how to decompose a problem into agent-sized pieces, how to define clear interfaces between them, how to build in the right checks and balances, and how to debug when the orchestration goes wrong.

The developers who thrive in this model are the ones who can think at the system level — who can look at a complex workflow and see how to break it into coordinated, specialized agents working in concert.

title: Building a News Curator with AI: A Practical Pattern for Content Pipelines
content:
One of the most instructive examples from the rUv coaching sessions is a news curator platform built by the London Chapter team. It's a concrete, real-world application that illustrates several important patterns for building AI-powered content pipelines — and it's simple enough to understand completely while being complex enough to be genuinely useful.

**What the System Does**

The news curator platform solves a specific problem: technical articles are written for technical audiences, but many organizations need to share that information with non-technical stakeholders. The platform takes articles from RSS feeds or individual URLs, rewrites them using Claude Haiku for non-technical audiences, and then routes them through a human approval workflow before publishing.

Breaking that down into components:
1. **Ingestion** — RSS feeds and individual URL scraping bring raw content into the system
2. **Transformation** — Claude Haiku rewrites the content for a different audience
3. **Review** — Human curators approve or reject transformed articles
4. **Publication** — Approved articles go out to the intended audience

This four-stage pipeline is a pattern that appears in dozens of AI content applications. Understanding it well means you can adapt it to many different use cases.

**Why Claude Haiku Specifically?**

The choice of Claude Haiku (rather than a more powerful model) is worth noting. Haiku is faster and cheaper than larger models, which matters when you're processing potentially hundreds of articles per day. For a rewriting task — where the goal is clear, the input is structured, and 'good enough' is genuinely good enough — a smaller, faster model is the right tool.

This is a general principle: match model capability to task complexity. Don't use a sledgehammer to crack a nut. Reserve your most capable (and expensive) models for tasks that genuinely require deep reasoning. Use lighter models for high-volume, well-defined transformation tasks.

**The Human-in-the-Loop Design**

The approval/rejection workflow is the most important architectural decision in this system. The AI does the heavy lifting of rewriting, but a human curator makes the final call on what gets published. This design reflects a mature understanding of where AI is reliable and where human judgment is still essential.

AI is reliable at: transforming text from one register to another, summarizing long content, maintaining consistent tone, processing high volumes quickly.

AI is less reliable at: judging whether a piece of content is appropriate for a specific organizational context, catching subtle factual errors introduced during rewriting, understanding the political or social nuances of what should or shouldn't be shared.

The human curator handles the second category. They don't have to read every word of every article — the AI has already done the transformation work. They're making a higher-level judgment: is this worth sharing with our audience?

**RSS Feeds and URL Scraping as Input Sources**

Supporting both RSS feeds and individual URL scraping gives the system flexibility. RSS feeds handle the ongoing, automated ingestion of content from known sources. URL scraping handles one-off additions — a curator finds an interesting article and drops the URL in manually.

This dual-input pattern is worth copying. Fully automated pipelines are efficient but brittle — they only capture what they're configured to capture. Adding a manual input path gives human curators a way to inject content the automated system would miss.

**Extending the Pattern**

The news curator pattern generalizes well. Consider these variations:

- **Internal knowledge base curator**: Ingest internal documents, transform them into standardized formats, route through subject matter expert review before adding to a knowledge base
- **Competitive intelligence pipeline**: Ingest competitor announcements and press releases, transform into structured summaries, route to relevant team members
- **Customer feedback processor**: Ingest support tickets and reviews, transform into categorized summaries, route to product teams

In each case, the four-stage structure holds: ingest, transform, review, publish. The AI handles the transformation at scale. Humans handle the judgment calls that require context the AI doesn't have.

**Tooling Considerations**

The session mentioned Playwright as a browser automation framework alongside this work. For URL scraping, Playwright is a strong choice — it handles JavaScript-rendered pages that simpler HTTP-based scrapers miss. Many modern news sites render their content dynamically, so a scraper that only fetches raw HTML will get incomplete content. Playwright runs a real browser, waits for the page to fully render, and then extracts the content.

The combination of Playwright for ingestion, a lightweight LLM for transformation, and a simple approval UI for review gives you a complete, production-ready content pipeline with relatively modest engineering effort. It's a good example of what's possible when you pick the right tool for each stage rather than trying to solve everything with a single system.

title: The 5-Phase Decompiler Pipeline: How Rudevolution Reconstructs Readable Code from Minified Bundles
content:
When JavaScript ships to production, it is typically minified — variable names become single letters, whitespace vanishes, and multiple modules are smashed into one giant file. Rudevolution's decompiler reverses this process through a carefully ordered five-phase pipeline. Understanding each phase helps you reason about both the output quality and the performance characteristics you will observe.

**Phase 1: Parse**
The pipeline begins with a single-pass scanner written in Rust. Rather than building a full abstract syntax tree (which is expensive), the parser uses `memchr` SIMD acceleration to scan for declarations, extract string literals, and map which symbols reference which other symbols. Think of this as quickly reading a book and underlining every proper noun and every sentence that mentions another proper noun — you are not analyzing meaning yet, just cataloguing relationships.

**Phase 2: Graph Construction**
The extracted declarations become nodes in a reference graph. Every time symbol A calls or references symbol B, an edge is drawn between them, weighted by how frequently that reference occurs. High-frequency edges indicate tight coupling; low-frequency edges suggest loose or optional dependencies. This graph is the structural skeleton of the original module system, reconstructed purely from usage patterns.

**Phase 3: Partition**
With the graph built, the pipeline must decide where one module ends and another begins. For bundles with fewer than 5,000 nodes, an exact MinCut algorithm finds the mathematically optimal split points — the cuts that sever the fewest high-weight edges. For larger bundles, the Louvain community detection algorithm runs instead, trading exactness for O(n log n) scalability. Once partitions are identified, each module is named based on the dominant string literals found inside it, giving you human-readable filenames rather than `module_0042.js`.

**Phase 4: Infer**
Naming individual functions and variables is harder than naming modules. Phase 4 applies a GPU-trained transformer model alongside a corpus of 210 domain-specific patterns stored in `claude-code-patterns.json`. The model considers string context, property access chains, and calling conventions to propose names, then assigns a confidence level — HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW — to each inference. This is analogous to a translator who knows the grammar of a language but is guessing proper nouns from context clues.

**Phase 5: Witness**
The final phase is about trust. Every output module is hashed with SHA3-256, and those hashes are chained into a Merkle tree. The pipeline then verifies that the output is a strict subset of the input — nothing was invented, only reorganized. This cryptographic witness chain means you can independently verify that the decompiler did not hallucinate code. The result is a readable source file, a V3 source map for debugger integration, the witness chain itself, and a confidence report.

The full pipeline completes in roughly 26 seconds for a typical production bundle, making it practical for iterative analysis workflows.

title: Rudevolution Frontend Architecture: How the Browser-Side Tooling Is Organized
content:
The Rudevolution web interface is a React application that mirrors the capabilities of the Rust backend in a form accessible through a browser tab. Understanding how it is structured helps you extend it, debug it, or simply understand which file to open when something behaves unexpectedly.

**Entry Points and Routing**
The application starts at `main.tsx`, which mounts the React tree. `App.tsx` owns the router, the top-level data loader, and the toast notification system — the three concerns that need to be available everywhere. If you are chasing a bug related to navigation or global data fetching, start here.

**Pages**
There are three top-level pages. `Explorer.tsx` is the version browser; it lets you browse historical versions of a package and compare them side by side using diff view. `Decompiler.tsx` is the interactive decompiler interface where you paste or fetch an npm package and receive reconstructed source. `RvfViewer.tsx` inspects RVF container files, showing manifest details like dimensions, vector count, distance metric, and file identifiers.

**Components**
The component layer is deliberately granular. `CodeViewer.tsx` handles syntax highlighting via highlight.js. `DiffViewer.tsx` renders side-by-side diffs using the `diff` library. `ModuleTree.tsx` renders the file tree with badge annotations showing module metadata. `MetricsCard.tsx` displays aggregate statistics — function count, class count, bundle size. `SearchBar.tsx` provides full-text search across all loaded versions simultaneously. `VersionSelector.tsx` is a dropdown for switching between package versions. `DownloadMenu.tsx` exposes export options in zip, JSON, and raw JS formats.

**Library Layer**
The `lib/` directory contains the logic that would otherwise live on a server. `decompiler.ts` orchestrates the fetch-beautify-split sequence entirely in the browser. `npm-fetch.ts` queries the npm registry and falls back through unpkg and jsDelivr CDNs to retrieve package files. `module-splitter.ts` is a direct browser port of the server-side `module-splitter.mjs` script, meaning the splitting logic is shared conceptually between environments. `beautifier.ts` wraps js-beautify for code formatting. `rvf-parser.ts` reads RVF binary headers and manifests.

**Pre-Built Data**
The `public/data/` directory holds pre-built version data that ships with the application. This means common packages load instantly without a network round-trip — the data was generated at build time and served as static assets.

**Design Philosophy**
The architecture follows a clear separation: pages own layout and user flow, components own rendering concerns, and the lib layer owns data transformation. This makes the codebase approachable — if you want to change how diffs look, you open `DiffViewer.tsx`; if you want to change how packages are fetched, you open `npm-fetch.ts`. There is no ambiguity about where logic lives.

title: Claude Code Permission System: How Tool Access Decisions Are Made
content:
Every time Claude Code wants to use a tool — read a file, run a bash command, make a network request — it passes through a permission check before anything happens. This system is a state machine, and understanding its decision tree helps you configure it correctly and reason about why a particular action was allowed or blocked.

**The Entry Point**
All permission decisions flow through a single function: `canUseTool()`. This function receives the tool name and context, then routes to one of three branches based on the current operating mode.

**The Three Modes**
The first mode is `bypass` or `dontAsk`. In this mode, `canUseTool()` returns ALLOW immediately without consulting any rules. This is appropriate for fully automated pipelines where human confirmation is not possible and the operator accepts full responsibility for tool actions.

The second mode is `default` or `acceptEdits`. This is the standard interactive mode. The function consults a rule set — first checking for explicit ALLOW rules, then for explicit DENY rules. If a matching ALLOW rule exists, the tool runs. If a matching DENY rule exists, the tool is blocked. If neither matches, the system falls through to the third outcome: asking the user in real time.

The third mode is `plan`. In plan mode, `canUseTool()` returns DENY for all tools unconditionally. This mode is used when Claude Code is reasoning about what it would do without actually doing it — a dry-run or preview mode.

**The Rule Matching Layer**
Within default mode, rules are evaluated in order. An ALLOW rule match short-circuits to immediate approval. A DENY rule match short-circuits to immediate rejection. The no-match case is the most interesting: it triggers an interactive prompt, and the user's response can optionally be remembered as a new rule for future sessions.

**Why This Design Matters**
The layered structure means you can tune the system to your risk tolerance. A developer working locally might run in default mode with broad ALLOW rules for file operations. A CI pipeline might run in bypass mode with a carefully audited tool list. A code review assistant might run in plan mode to produce proposals without side effects.

The permission system also integrates with the hooks engine. Pre-tool hooks can run before `canUseTool()` resolves, and post-tool hooks run after a tool completes. This means you can inject logging, auditing, or secondary validation at the boundary of every tool invocation — including WASM-based hooks that execute in under one millisecond.

Understanding this state machine is foundational to deploying Claude Code in any environment where tool access needs to be controlled, audited, or customized.

title: RVM's Three-Tier Proof System: P1, P2, and P3 Explained
content:
When a system needs to verify that an operation is allowed, it has to answer a fundamental question: how much trust do we need, and how much work are we willing to do to establish it? RVM answers this with a three-tier proof system — P1, P2, and P3 — where each tier trades speed for depth of verification.

Think of it like identity checks at different security checkpoints. A gym membership card scan is fast and good enough for the front door (P1). A background check takes longer but is needed for a sensitive role (P2). A full forensic audit with cryptographic evidence trails is reserved for the highest-stakes decisions (P3).

**P1: Constant-Time Capability Check**
P1 is the lightest tier. It verifies that a caller holds a valid capability token — essentially a signed permission slip — using a constant-time comparison to prevent timing side-channels. The `verify_p1()` function in the `rvm-cap` crate handles this. It checks the token against a nonce ring (4096 entries with a watermark) and validates the epoch, ensuring revoked capabilities cannot be replayed. Because it runs in constant time regardless of input, an attacker cannot infer anything about the token by measuring how long verification takes.

**P2: Contextual Rule Verification**
P2 goes deeper. It evaluates the proof against six contextual rules using the `ProofEngine` in `rvm-proof`. These rules examine things like whether the capability was legitimately derived from a parent, whether the requested rights are a subset of what was granted, and whether the current partition context is consistent with the proof's claims. P2 also runs in constant time, making it safe to use in hot paths where timing attacks are a concern. The `ProofContextBuilder` lets callers assemble the context that P2 needs before calling `verify()`.

**P3: Deep Cryptographic Verification**
P3 is the heavyweight tier. It performs SHA-256 hash chain verification, Merkle tree validation, and checks the `WitnessSigner` to confirm that the audit trail backing the proof is cryptographically intact. P3 is used when you need to prove not just that a capability exists, but that the entire history leading to it is tamper-evident. It integrates with the TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) pipeline and supports Ed25519, HMAC-SHA256, and DualHmac signers.

**Important Security Note**
An audit of the codebase identified a critical finding (A-05): in an earlier version, P3 verification did not actually check the cryptographic signature on the `CoherenceCert` payload. The 64-byte signature field was present but never validated, meaning any 64-byte value would pass. This is a canonical example of why security audits matter — the structure looked correct, but the verification step was silently skipped. Developers working with RVM should confirm this is resolved before relying on P3 in production.

**Capability Derivation Trees**
Underpinning all three tiers is the `DerivationTree` in `rvm-cap`. When a capability is granted, it is recorded as a child of the granting capability. The `GrantPolicy` controls what rights can be delegated downward — you can never grant more rights than you hold. This tree structure means revocation is transitive: revoking a parent capability invalidates all descendants automatically.

The key types to know: `CapToken` and `CapRights` live in `rvm-types` and represent the token and its permission bitmask. `CapabilityManager` and `CapabilityTable` in `rvm-cap` manage the runtime state. `ProofTier`, `Proof`, and `ProofEngine` in `rvm-proof` handle the verification logic.

For most operations, P1 is sufficient. Use P2 when the operation crosses partition boundaries or involves delegated rights. Reserve P3 for attestation, audit replay, or any scenario where you need to prove the integrity of the entire capability chain to an external verifier.

title: Witness Records and Audit Trails in RVM: How Every Action Leaves a Cryptographic Footprint
content:
In a system managing partitions, capabilities, and memory across potentially untrusted environments, you need more than just access control — you need an unforgeable record of what happened and when. RVM's witness system provides exactly this: a tamper-evident audit trail where every significant action emits a 64-byte witness record that is chained to all previous records.

**The 64-Byte Witness Record**
The `WitnessRecord` type is exactly 64 bytes — this size is enforced at compile time with a static assertion, not just documented. This constraint matters for performance: 64 bytes fits in a single cache line on most architectures, making reads and writes efficient even in high-frequency logging scenarios. Each record contains an action kind (drawn from ~40 `ActionKind` variants), a timestamp, a partition identifier, and a hash linking it to the previous record in the chain.

**Hash Chains: The Backbone of Tamper Evidence**
The chain works like a blockchain in miniature. Each record includes a hash of the previous record. If anyone modifies a historical record, every subsequent hash in the chain becomes invalid — the tampering is immediately detectable during replay. The primary hash function is SHA-256, with FNV-1a available as a fallback in constrained environments.

However, a critical audit finding (A-01) revealed that an earlier implementation expanded a 64-bit FNV-1a hash to 256 bits through repeated multiplication — a deterministic transform that provides only 64 bits of actual collision resistance. An attacker could forge a witness chain entry in approximately 2^32 operations. A separate finding (A-02) showed that XOR folding of field bytes allowed field-swapping attacks where reordered fields produced identical hashes. These findings illustrate why cryptographic primitives must be used correctly, not just present.

**Signing and the StrictSigner**
Witness records can be signed using HMAC-SHA256. The `StrictSigner` enforces that every record in a session is signed — it will reject any attempt to emit an unsigned record when signing is enabled. This prevents an attacker from injecting unsigned records into a signed audit trail. The `rvm-witness` crate manages a 16MB ring buffer for in-memory storage of recent records.

**Replay and Forensic Queries**
The witness system supports RLE-compressed replay, allowing you to reconstruct a sequence of events from the stored records. This is useful for forensic analysis after an incident — you can replay the witness trail to see exactly what operations occurred, in what order, and whether the chain remained intact throughout. The compression reduces storage overhead for repetitive action sequences without losing any information.

**Querying the Trail**
The `rvm-witness` crate exposes query interfaces for filtering records by action kind, partition, time range, or hash. This makes it practical to answer questions like "show me all capability grants in partition X during the last hour" or "find the first record where this hash chain breaks."

**Where Witnesses Appear Across the System**
Witness records are not isolated to the audit subsystem. They appear in memory management (tier transitions emit records), capability operations (grants and revocations are witnessed), partition lifecycle events, and the boot sequence (the 7-phase measured boot produces an attestation digest built from witness records). The cross-reference index shows witness trail referenced in eight of the seventeen user guide chapters, reflecting how deeply it is woven into the system.

For developers integrating with RVM: emit witness records for any operation that changes system state, use `StrictSigner` in production deployments, and always verify the hash chain before trusting a replayed audit trail.

title: RVM's Crate Architecture: How 13 Crates Stack Into a Hypervisor
content:
RVM is not a monolithic codebase. It is organized into 13 focused crates arranged in a layered dependency graph, where each layer builds on the one below it and no crate reaches upward into a higher layer. Understanding this structure helps you find the right place to make changes, understand what a test failure means, and reason about which parts of the system are affected by a given modification.

**The Four-Layer Stack**
At the bottom sits the hardware abstraction layer (`rvm-hal`), which handles AArch64 EL2 specifics: stage-2 page tables, the PL011 UART, GICv2 interrupt controller, and the ARM generic timer. Nothing above this layer should contain architecture-specific code.

Above HAL sits the foundation layer: `rvm-types` and `rvm-cap`. `rvm-types` defines the shared vocabulary — `WitnessRecord`, `ActionKind`, `CapToken`, `CapRights`, error variants, and other primitives used everywhere. `rvm-cap` implements capability management: the `CapabilityManager`, `CapabilityTable`, `DerivationTree`, and the P1 verifier. These two crates are the most widely imported in the dependency graph.

The middle layer contains the subsystem crates: `rvm-witness` (audit trail), `rvm-proof` (P2/P3 verification), `rvm-memory` (buddy allocator and four memory tiers), `rvm-partition` (lifecycle state machine and IPC), `rvm-sched` (2-signal priority scheduler), and `rvm-coherence` (unified coherence engine with pluggable backends). Each of these is substantial — `rvm-partition` alone has 86 tests covering lifecycle, IPC message queues, device leases, and split/merge operations.

At the top sit `rvm-boot` (7-phase measured boot sequence), `rvm-wasm` (WebAssembly agent runtime), and the integration layer that wires everything together.

**Why Layering Matters for Testing**
Because dependencies only flow downward, you can test each crate in isolation. A failure in `rvm-cap`'s 40 tests tells you something is wrong with capability logic specifically — not with scheduling or memory. The total test count across all crates exceeds 797, with `rvm-memory` carrying the heaviest load at 110 tests (reflecting the complexity of buddy allocation with coalescing, four-tier management, and LZ4-style RLE compression).

**Key Crate Responsibilities at a Glance**
- `rvm-types` (~40 types): shared primitives, no logic
- `rvm-cap` (40 tests): capability lifecycle, nonce ring, epoch revocation
- `rvm-witness` (29 tests): 16MB ring buffer, hash chains, signing, replay
- `rvm-proof` (45 tests): full P1/P2/P3 engine, TEE pipeline, multiple signer backends
- `rvm-partition` (86 tests): the most feature-rich subsystem crate
- `rvm-sched` (49 tests): SMP coordination, VMID-aware context switching
- `rvm-memory` (110 tests): the largest test suite, reflecting allocator complexity
- `rvm-coherence` (59 tests): pluggable MinCut and Coherence backends, edge decay
- `rvm-boot` (26 tests): boot phases, attestation digest, HAL initialization
- `rvm-wasm` (33 tests): 7-state agent lifecycle, `HostContext` trait

**Finding Your Way Around**
The user guide's cross-reference index maps every major type and function to both its crate and the documentation chapter that explains it. For example, `ProofEngine` lives in `rvm-proof` and is explained in chapter 05. `WitnessRecord` lives in `rvm-types` but its usage is covered in chapter 06. When you encounter an unfamiliar type, the cross-reference index is the fastest path to understanding it in context.

The CI pipeline runs all 797+ tests, clippy lints, and `cargo audit` on every dependency update, with benchmark regression checks ensuring that performance-sensitive paths do not silently degrade.

title: How the Cognitum Claude Plugin Connects Claude Code to a Seed Device
content:
The cognitum-claude-plugin is a Claude Code extension that gives Claude a direct line into a physical Cognitum Seed device — a piece of hardware that runs its own cognitive container, vector store, thermal subsystem, and witness chain. Think of it like giving Claude a remote control for a small, self-contained AI appliance sitting on your desk or in a server rack.

The plugin works through two complementary mechanisms: slash commands and an MCP server.

**Slash Commands — Your Quick-Action Toolkit**

Slash commands are short, purpose-built instructions you type directly in Claude Code. Each one maps to a specific operational concern:

- `/seed-pair` — Establishes trust between Claude Code and the device. It posts to `/api/v1/pair`, receives a bearer token, and asks you to save it as `COGNITUM_SEED_TOKEN`. Every subsequent command uses that token for authentication.
- `/seed-status` — Pulls a one-page summary: firmware version, WiFi state, thermal readings, and store statistics. Good for a quick health check.
- `/seed-wifi` — Manages wireless connectivity. You can check current status, scan for networks, or connect to a new SSID with a passphrase.
- `/seed-ota` — Handles over-the-air firmware updates. `check` tells you whether an update is available; `apply` installs it.
- `/seed-thermal` — Reads thermal state and telemetry, or toggles turbo mode on/off.
- `/seed-store` — Interfaces with the device's vector store. You can query by text, retrieve a vector by ID, or walk the graph to find neighbors of a given node.
- `/seed-snapshot` — Captures a full cognitive snapshot: the container state, coherence profile, recent witness entries, and the latest sensor embedding, all bundled into a single JSON file.
- `/seed-cluster` — Inspects multi-device cluster health, lists peer devices with their last-seen timestamps and sync lag, and flags any peer that has drifted more than 10 epochs behind.

**The MCP Server — Tools for Programmatic Access**

Alongside the slash commands, the plugin registers an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server named `cognitum` that connects to `https://cognitum.one/mcpSse` using Server-Sent Events transport. This server exposes eight tools that Claude can call autonomously during a task:

- `health_check` — Simple liveness probe.
- `catalog_browse` — Browse the Cognitum Seed product catalog.
- `lead_subscribe` — Add an email to a waitlist.
- `order_status` — Look up an order by email.
- `contact_send` — Submit a contact form message.
- `security_verify` — Run a security check on an input string.
- `fleet_status` — Read status across a fleet of devices.
- `docs_search` — Search Cognitum documentation.

The MCP tools are cloud-facing (they hit `cognitum.one`), while the slash commands are device-facing (they hit the local Seed over USB or WiFi). The two layers complement each other: use MCP tools for catalog and support workflows, use slash commands for hands-on device management.

**Authentication and Transport**

The plugin supports two physical transports:

1. **USB (link-local)** — The device appears at `http://169.254.42.1`. No token is required because the physical cable is treated as the trust anchor. This is the simplest path and avoids TLS certificate issues entirely.
2. **WiFi/HTTPS** — The device is reachable over your LAN at a configurable IP and port 8443. This mode requires the bearer token (`COGNITUM_SEED_TOKEN`) and may require adding the device's self-signed certificate to your system trust store, since Claude Code may reject it otherwise.

You configure the base URL via the `COGNITUM_SEED_BASE` environment variable. All slash commands read these two env vars, so setting them once unlocks the entire command suite.

**The Full API Surface**

Under the hood, the plugin talks to nine groups of REST endpoints on the device:

- **Pairing** — `/pair`, `/pair/status`, `/pair/clients`
- **System** — `/status`, `/identity`, `/security/status`
- **WiFi** — `/wifi/status`, `/wifi/scan`, `/wifi/connect`
- **Firmware** — `/firmware/status`, `/upgrade/check`, `/firmware/update`, `/upgrade/apply`
- **Thermal** — `/thermal/state`, `/thermal/telemetry`, `/thermal/turbo`
- **Store** — `/store/status`, `/store/query`, `/store/vectors/{id}`, `/store/graph/neighbors/{id}`
- **Cognitive** — `/cognitive/snapshot`, `/cognitive/status`, `/coherence/profile`
- **Witness** — `/witness/chain`, `/witness/verify`
- **Cluster** — `/cluster/health`, `/peers`, `/sync/stats`

Each group maps cleanly to a slash command, so the command surface is essentially a human-friendly wrapper around this REST API.

title: Troubleshooting Missing MCP Tools from cognitum-seed in Claude Code
content:
If you open Claude Code, type `/mcp`, and the tools from `cognitum-seed` simply aren't there, you're looking at one of five root causes. Working through them in order will resolve the issue in almost every case.

**1. The Plugin Is Disabled**

Run `/plugin list` and look at the status indicator next to `cognitum-seed`. A filled circle (●) means active. An empty circle (◯) means disabled. If it's disabled, enable it and restart Claude Code. This is the most common cause and the easiest fix.

**2. Wrong MCP URL in `.mcp.json`**

The plugin's configuration file tells Claude Code where to find the MCP server on the device. The default URL is `http://169.254.42.1/mcp`, which is the USB link-local address. If your Seed is connected over WiFi instead of USB, that address won't resolve.

Fix: export the correct URL before launching Claude Code:
```
export COGNITUM_SEED_MCP_URL=https://<wifi-ip>:8443/mcp
```
The plugin reads this environment variable and overrides the default. Don't edit `.mcp.json` directly — use the env var so your change survives plugin updates.

**3. Self-Signed Certificate Rejected**

When the Seed is accessed over HTTPS (WiFi mode), it presents a self-signed TLS certificate. Claude Code, like most HTTP clients, refuses self-signed certs by default because it can't verify the certificate chain against a known authority.

You have two clean options:
- **Switch to USB mode** — Use `http://169.254.42.1/mcp` (plain HTTP, no TLS). The physical cable is the trust anchor, so no certificate is needed.
- **Add the cert to your system trust store** — Export the Seed's certificate and install it as a trusted root on your machine. The exact steps depend on your OS, but once done, Claude Code will accept the HTTPS connection.

Avoid disabling certificate verification globally — that trades a configuration problem for a security problem.

**4. Pairing Token Not Set**

HTTPS WiFi mode requires a bearer token. The plugin passes it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on every request. If `COGNITUM_SEED_TOKEN` isn't set in your environment, the device will reject the connection with a 401, and Claude Code will see no tools.

Run `/seed-pair` to generate a fresh token, save it, then:
```
export COGNITUM_SEED_TOKEN='<your-token>'
```
Note: USB mode does not require a token. The physical connection is sufficient proof of authorization.

**5. Device Is Offline**

If none of the above apply, the device itself may be unreachable. Test connectivity directly:
```
ping 169.254.42.1        # USB
ping <wifi-ip>           # WiFi
```
If ping fails, the problem is below the API layer — check the USB cable, the device's power state, or your network configuration. No amount of plugin configuration will fix a device that isn't on the network.

**Quick Diagnostic Checklist**

| Check | Command | Expected Result |
|---|---|---|
| Plugin enabled | `/plugin list` | ● next to cognitum-seed |
| Device reachable | `ping 169.254.42.1` | Replies received |
| Token set | `echo $COGNITUM_SEED_TOKEN` | Non-empty string |
| Base URL set | `echo $COGNITUM_SEED_BASE` | Correct URL |
| Identity responds | `curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $COGNITUM_SEED_TOKEN" $COGNITUM_SEED_BASE/api/v1/identity` | JSON with device UUID |

If the identity endpoint returns a valid JSON response, the plugin should register its tools correctly on the next Claude Code restart.

title: Capturing a Cognitive Snapshot from a Cognitum Seed Device
content:
A cognitive snapshot is a point-in-time capture of everything happening inside a Seed device's mind — its active container state, memory usage, coherence metrics, recent witness log entries, and the latest sensor embedding. Think of it like a core dump for an AI appliance: a frozen cross-section you can inspect, archive, or hand to a developer for debugging.

The `/seed-snapshot` command in the cognitum-claude-plugin automates this capture. Here's what it does under the hood and why each piece matters.

**The Five API Calls**

The snapshot command hits five endpoints in sequence and bundles their responses into a single JSON object:

1. **`GET /api/v1/cognitive/snapshot`** — The main payload. This is the full serialized state of the cognitive container: active concepts, working memory, any pending inference tasks. It's the largest piece of the bundle.

2. **`GET /api/v1/cognitive/status`** — Container resource metrics: how much memory the container is using, how many ticks have elapsed since last update, and when it was last modified. This tells you whether the container is healthy and active or stalled.

3. **`GET /api/v1/coherence/profile`** — Temporal coherence metrics. Coherence measures how internally consistent the device's world model is over time. A dropping coherence score can indicate conflicting inputs, a stalled update cycle, or hardware stress.

4. **`GET /api/v1/witness/chain?limit=20`** — The last 20 entries from the witness chain. The witness chain is an append-only log of significant events the device has observed and recorded. It's the device's version of an audit trail. Reviewing recent entries helps you understand what the device was doing just before a problem occurred.

5. **`GET /api/v1/sensor/embedding/latest`** — The most recent feature embedding produced from sensor input. Embeddings are dense numerical vectors that represent the device's current sensory state in a form its cognitive layer can reason over. Capturing this alongside the snapshot lets you correlate what the device was perceiving with what it was thinking.

**The Output Format**

All five responses are merged into one JSON object:

```json
{
  "captured_at": "<ISO timestamp>",
  "device_uuid": "...",
  "snapshot": {...},
  "container": {...},
  "coherence": {...},
  "witness_recent": [...],
  "sensor_embedding": {...}
}
```

If you pass an output filename to the command (`/seed-snapshot debug-2024-01-15.json`), the bundle is written to disk. Without a filename, it's printed to the Claude Code session.

**When to Use It**

- **Before a firmware update** — Capture the current state so you have a baseline to compare against after the update.
- **After unexpected behavior** — If the device did something surprising, the witness chain and coherence profile often explain why.
- **Routine archiving** — For long-running deployments, periodic snapshots create a history of how the device's cognitive state evolves.
- **Handing off to support** — A snapshot bundle contains everything a developer needs to reproduce the device's state without physical access.

**Authentication**

Like all device-facing commands, `/seed-snapshot` uses the bearer token from `COGNITUM_SEED_TOKEN` and the base URL from `COGNITUM_SEED_BASE`. Both must be set before running the command. If you're on USB, the token requirement is relaxed — the physical connection serves as authentication.

title: Connectome-OS: What Makes It Different From Other Spiking Simulators
content:
Most spiking neural network simulators are built to answer one question: did the neurons fire correctly? Connectome-OS is built to answer a harder question: did the *structure* of the network matter, and can you prove it?

Think of the difference like this. A standard flight simulator tells you whether the plane stayed in the air. Connectome-OS is more like a flight simulator that also monitors the structural integrity of every wing spar in real time, tells you 50 milliseconds before a spar is about to fail, and then lets you surgically remove one rivet to prove that rivet was load-bearing — all while the plane is flying.

Here are the four properties that set it apart:

**1. Live Fiedler coherence detection**

Every 5 milliseconds of simulated time, Connectome-OS computes λ₂ — the second-smallest eigenvalue of the Laplacian of the co-firing graph. This number is called the Fiedler value, and it measures how close the active network is to splitting into disconnected islands. When it drops toward zero, the network is about to fragment.

The system emits a `CoherenceEvent` when this happens, giving downstream code at least 50 ms of simulated lead time on ≥ 70% of constructed-collapse trials. No other spiking simulator ships this signal live. It's the difference between a smoke alarm and a fire investigator's report written after the building burned down.

**2. σ-separation as a causal gate test**

Knowing that a structure *correlates* with behavior is easy. Proving it *caused* the behavior is hard. Connectome-OS operationalizes causality with a concrete protocol:

- Find the load-bearing edges using `ruvector-mincut`
- Cut them
- Rerun the same stimulus
- Measure how much behavior diverges compared to a paired degree-matched *control* cut (same number of edges removed, but chosen randomly)
- Assert the σ-separation between the two conditions

The demo achieves z_cut = 5.55σ — clearing the 5σ SOTA target. The control cut lands at z_rand = 1.57σ. The gap between those two numbers is the honest, falsifiable claim that the structure mattered. This is what computational psychiatry needs for in-silico lesion studies: not "we cut this and behavior changed" but "we cut this, behavior changed by 5.55 standard deviations more than a matched random cut, and here is the paired trial log."

**3. Bit-exact determinism**

Same random seeds produce bit-identical spike traces. This is a contract enforced by the implementation, not a hope. For anyone building a competing simulator or spiking-hardware implementation, this makes Connectome-OS a usable reference baseline. You can diff outputs, not just compare summary statistics.

**4. Honest failure preservation**

The ADR §17 findings table records 20 measurement-driven discoveries, eight of which directly disproved the team's own pre-measurement predictions. None were hidden. No thresholds were relaxed to force green tests. This matters because a simulator that only reports its wins is a marketing document, not a scientific instrument.

title: Twenty Hard-Won Performance Lessons From Building the Fiedler Detector
content:
The Connectome-OS team spent significant effort trying to make the live Fiedler coherence detector fast. The journey produced ten documented findings, most of which disproved the team's own predictions. These lessons generalize well beyond connectome simulation — they apply to any system where you are trying to speed up a measurement loop.

**The most important lesson: change *when* something runs, not *what* it does.**

Finding #6 is the headline. After nine failed or marginal attempts to speed up the detector itself, a 14-line heuristic that changed *how often* the detector ran achieved a 4.29× speedup — the first result to clear the ≥ 2× target. Every structural change to the detector's internals had failed to move the needle meaningfully. The scheduling change beat all of them combined. If you are stuck optimizing a hot path, ask first whether the path needs to run as often as it does.

**Diagnose before you optimize.**

Finding #4: the team believed the simulation kernel was the bottleneck ("kernel-bound"). Measurement revealed the Fiedler detector dominated the saturated benchmark by roughly 450:1. The pre-measurement diagnosis was simply wrong. SIMD work on the kernel (Finding #2) produced a 1.013× gain instead of the ≥ 2× target — because the kernel was not the cost. Profiling is not optional; it is the first step.

**Sparse algorithms have a scale floor.**

Finding #5: switching to a sparse Fiedler computation dropped performance 3× at n=1024 compared to n=96. The sparse path is a win at n ≥ 10,000. At demo scale it is a regression. Algorithmic complexity classes describe asymptotic behavior; they do not tell you where the crossover point is. Measure at your actual scale.

**Algorithmic complexity does not beat constant factors at small scale.**

Finding #9: a BTreeMap-based incremental Fiedler update was 5.8× slower at top-line than the simpler approach. The incremental structure carries overhead that only pays off at sizes the demo never reaches. This is the same lesson as #5 from a different angle: "more sophisticated algorithm" is a hypothesis, not a guarantee.

**Lanczos is not a drop-in eigenvalue solver.**

Finding #7: standard full-reorthogonalization Lanczos converges on λ_max, not λ₂. To get the Fiedler value you need shift-and-invert or deflation. "Use Lanczos" is a reasonable starting point only if you know which eigenvalue it will find.

**OS-zeroed memory beats explicit zeroing for cold allocations.**

Finding #3: reusing observer buffers with an explicit zeroing loop was 3% *slower* than calling `calloc` fresh. The operating system provides pre-zeroed pages for new allocations at essentially no cost. Explicit loop zeroing on cold memory adds cache pressure without benefit. The optimization that looks like it saves work actually adds work.

**Null models that match structure too closely destroy the signal.**

Finding #1: a degree-stratified null for the AC-5 test collapsed entirely at N=1024 on the SBM. The null was so well-matched to the planted structure that it could not be distinguished from the real thing. A null model is supposed to represent "no effect" — if it accidentally represents the effect, the test cannot fire.

**The retrieval gap is corpus structure, not algorithm.**

Finding #8: DiskANN at a 605-window corpus scored 0.551 precision vs brute-force's 0.60. The gap is not an indexing artifact — it exists in brute-force too. Switching to a better approximate-nearest-neighbor index will not close it. The corpus itself does not contain enough repeated structure at that window size to score higher. Diagnose before you optimize the index.

Taken together, these findings form a checklist: profile first, question your scheduling before your algorithm, measure at your actual scale, and treat every optimization as a hypothesis to be falsified.

title: Connectome-OS Application Scaffolding: What You Can Build Today vs. What Requires Phase 3
content:
Connectome-OS ships with scaffolding for several research applications. Understanding which pieces are fully operational versus which are documented stubs saves you from discovering blockers mid-project. Here is a practical map.

**What works today, end-to-end**

*In-silico circuit-lesion studies* are the most complete application. The full pipeline is in-tree: `LesionStudy`, `CandidateCut`, and `LesionReport` in `src/lesion.rs`. You define a candidate cut, run paired trials against a degree-matched control, and get a σ-distance report. The determinism guarantee means your paired trials are reproducible. The AC-5 result (z_cut = 5.55σ) was produced by this exact pipeline on a synthetic SBM. If your research question is "did removing this circuit change behavior, and by how much compared to a matched random removal," you can run that experiment today.

The FlyWire Princeton dataset (115,151 neurons, 2,676,592 synapses) ships under `assets/` and ingests via the streaming CSV reader with zero Python dependencies. You do not need to download or preprocess anything to start a real-scale run.

The live browser UI over SSE is operational. A Vite + EventSource frontend connects to the simulation stream with no mocks — the `witness` counter in the UI proves it is receiving a real event stream, not a replay.

*Embodied fly navigation in VR* is partially scaffolded. The `BodySimulator` trait in `src/embodiment.rs` is defined. `StubBody` runs a deterministic open-loop body today — useful for validating the neural side of the pipeline without a physics engine. The FFI shape for MuJoCo is documented in `MujocoBody` as a panic-stub, meaning the interface contract is written down but the implementation panics if called. You can build and test your neural control logic against `StubBody` now and swap in the real body later.

**What requires Phase 3**

The MuJoCo 3 + NeuroMechFly bridge is explicitly Phase 3. The `cxx` FFI shape is documented but not implemented. Do not plan a demo that requires physical body simulation for the current release.

The visual-system stimulus module is also Phase 3. If your experiment requires the simulated fly to respond to visual input rather than open-loop stimuli, that is a future deliverable.

Cross-species connectome transfer tests are not yet scaffolded at all. The concept is clear — run two connectomes through the same motif-retrieval index and measure shared behavioral vocabulary — but it requires a second heterogeneous connectome ingest path that does not exist yet.

**The practical development pattern**

The recommended approach is to build your experiment logic against the deterministic default implementations today and plan a swap point for the production pieces later. `StubBody` is not a toy — it is a contract-preserving stand-in that lets you validate everything upstream of the physics bridge before the bridge exists. The same pattern applies to the degree-stratified null sampler: the sampler is shipped, but it needs real FlyWire data to be clinically meaningful. You can validate your analysis pipeline on the SBM fixture now.

The key mental model: Connectome-OS distinguishes between *interface complete* (the trait or struct exists, the contract is documented, stubs compile and run), *measurement complete* (the real implementation exists and has passed its acceptance criterion), and *not yet started* (Phase 3 items). Knowing which category each component falls into tells you exactly how far you can get before hitting a wall.

title: obsidian-brain: Turning Your Note Vault into a Semantic Memory System
content:
Most note-taking tools treat search like a library card catalog — you have to know the exact word to find the book. obsidian-brain flips that model. It embeds every note as a vector (a mathematical fingerprint of meaning) and stores those fingerprints in a local vector database. When you search, you're not matching keywords — you're asking "what notes are *about* the same thing as this question?" A note titled "morning clarity ritual" will surface when you search for "how do I focus better," even if those words never appear in it.

Think of it like the difference between a filing cabinet and a knowledgeable colleague. The filing cabinet only finds what you labeled correctly. The colleague understands what you're *really* asking.

**The three-layer stack**

The system has three distinct layers, each with a clear job:

1. **The Obsidian plugin** — lives inside your editor. It intercepts saves, sends note text over local HTTP to the brain, and renders search/Q&A results back to you. It's the thin UI shell.

2. **RuVector brain (on your machine)** — the heavy lifter. It runs a DiskANN vector index, a SQLite store, prompt-injection and PII scanning, and an MCP server so your AI agents can query the same memory. Everything binds to localhost; nothing is exposed to the network by default.

3. **pi.ruv.io (optional, opt-in)** — a shared knowledge base with 12,000+ memories contributed by other users. You pull from it with a command palette action; you need a bearer token to do anything at all. Without the token, those commands simply say "not configured."

The architecture is deliberately layered so that each level can fail independently. If pi.ruv.io is unreachable, your local brain still works. If the local brain is unreachable, the plugin queues your note and indexes it later — nothing is silently dropped.

**What you actually do with it day-to-day**

- **⌘⇧B** opens semantic search. Type a question in plain language; results rank by similarity, not keyword frequency. You can narrow results with `category:project` to filter by tag.
- **⌘⇧K** opens a Q&A modal that stitches together relevant passages from your vault (and pi.ruv.io if configured) and lets you insert or copy the answer directly into your current note.
- The **right sidebar brain icon** shows related notes automatically every time you switch files. Navigate with arrow keys or j/k, open with Enter — no mouse required.
- **Auto-index on save** (off by default) debounces writes so rapid edits don't hammer the brain. Enable it in Settings once you're comfortable with the setup.
- **Graph overlay** colors your Obsidian graph by category, writing reversible groups to `.obsidian/graph.json`. You can clear them anytime without touching your notes.
- **DPO pair export** lets you mark a preferred note and a weaker alternative, then export them as a Markdown table under `Brain/Exports/` — useful if you're fine-tuning a model on your own writing style.

**How it compares to alternatives**

obsidian-brain sits in a different niche than tools like Smart Connections (which runs embeddings in-browser and targets human readers) or obsidian-mind (which targets AI coding agents). The key differentiators are: server-side prompt-injection and PII screening that cannot be bypassed from the plugin side, a shared knowledge base you can pull from, DPO training-data export, and MCP agent access. Smart Connections has none of those; obsidian-mind has MCP but not the safety screening or shared brain.

The tradeoff is that obsidian-brain requires running an external Rust service on your machine, whereas Smart Connections needs nothing beyond the plugin. If you want zero infrastructure, Smart Connections is simpler. If you want your AI agents and your human note-taking to share the same memory with real safety guarantees, obsidian-brain is the right tool.

**The mental model to keep**

Your vault is the source of truth. The brain is a live index of that vault — always derivable from the notes, never the primary store. Bulk sync reads every eligible note, embeds it, and stores the vector; unchanged notes are skipped on re-runs. You can always wipe the brain and rebuild it from scratch. That's an important property: the index is disposable, the notes are not.

title: obsidian-brain Security Model: Localhost-First, Fail-Closed, Non-Bypassable
content:
Security in AI-adjacent tools often gets bolted on as an afterthought — a checkbox in settings that users turn off the moment it causes friction. obsidian-brain takes the opposite approach: the safety guarantees are architectural, not configurable.

**Nothing leaves your machine by default**

Both the brain service and the embedder bind exclusively to localhost. The shipped systemd units enforce this at the OS level with `IPAddressDeny=any` combined with `IPAddressAllow=127.0.0.0/8`. That means even if the application code had a bug that tried to open an outbound connection, the kernel would block it. This is defense in depth — the application policy and the OS policy agree, and neither alone is sufficient to break the guarantee.

There is no telemetry. There are no third-party analytics calls. The plugin communicates with localhost and, if you explicitly configure it, with pi.ruv.io over authenticated HTTPS. Those are the only two destinations.

**Prompt-injection and PII screening: always on, server-side**

Every write to the brain passes through prompt-injection detection and PII scanning before it's stored. Critically, these checks run on the server (the RuVector brain process), not in the plugin. This matters because it means you cannot disable them from the Obsidian settings panel — the plugin simply doesn't have that authority. Even if a malicious plugin update tried to skip the checks, the brain would still run them.

Think of it like a bouncer at a door versus a sign that says "please behave." The sign is advisory; the bouncer is structural.

**Fail-closed, not fail-open**

When the brain service is unreachable — network hiccup, service not started, machine asleep — the plugin does not silently skip indexing and pretend everything is fine. It queues the note locally and retries later. Nothing is ever silently discarded or silently bypassed. This "fail-closed" property means the worst outcome of a connectivity problem is a delayed index, not a corrupted or incomplete one.

The same principle applies to the auto-index-on-save feature: it's debounced (rapid saves don't trigger rapid writes) and it fails closed. The queue is persistent across restarts.

**pi.ruv.io is entirely opt-in**

The shared knowledge base requires a bearer token you paste manually into settings. Without it, the pull and publish commands display "not configured" and do nothing. There is no default token, no anonymous access, no silent fallback to a shared endpoint. The opt-in is explicit and reversible — remove the token and the plugin stops talking to pi.ruv.io immediately.

**One real warning: Obsidian Sync**

Your pi.ruv.io bearer token is stored in `.obsidian/plugins/obsidian-brain/data.json`. If you use Obsidian Sync to replicate your vault across machines, that file travels with it — which means your token travels with it. If you sync to a machine you don't fully control (a shared computer, a cloud VM), your token is on that machine. The mitigation is straightforward: don't use Obsidian Sync on machines you don't trust, or revoke and regenerate your token if you suspect exposure.

**Settings that matter for security**

The settings table includes an "AIDefence scan" toggle, which defaults to on. The documentation is direct: keep it on unless you really know what you're doing. The index minimum characters setting (default: 40) prevents very short notes from being indexed, which incidentally also prevents trivial injection attempts via one-line notes.

**The design philosophy**

The security model reflects a specific belief: safety properties that users can disable aren't really safety properties — they're suggestions. By pushing the critical checks to the server process and enforcing network isolation at the OS level, obsidian-brain makes the safe path the only path. You can opt into more exposure (pi.ruv.io, Obsidian Sync) but you cannot opt out of the baseline protections.

title: obsidian-brain Settings Reference: What Each Knob Actually Controls
content:
Configuration tools are only useful if you understand what each setting actually does — not just what it's called. Here's a plain-English walkthrough of every obsidian-brain setting, why it exists, and when you'd change it.

**Connection settings**

`Brain URL` (default: `127.0.0.1:9876`) and `Embedder URL` (default: `127.0.0.1:9877`) are the loopback addresses of the two local services. You'd only change these if you're running the brain on a non-standard port or (advanced) on a different machine on your local network. For most users, leave these alone.

If you're connecting AI agents to the brain via MCP, use *Vector Brain → Copy MCP endpoint* from the command palette — it drops the correct URL onto your clipboard so you don't have to type it manually.

**Categorization**

`Default category` (default: `obsidian`) is the category tag applied to any note that doesn't have a `brain-category` frontmatter field. Categories matter for two things: filtering semantic search results (`category:project` in the search bar) and controlling what gets pulled from pi.ruv.io. If you have a consistent tagging system in your vault, you may never need to touch this. If you want all your notes to land in a custom category by default, set it here.

**Indexing behavior**

`Auto-index on save` (default: off) is the most consequential toggle for day-to-day use. When enabled, every time you save a note, the plugin debounces the event and sends the note to the brain for embedding. "Debounced" means rapid successive saves (like autosave every few seconds) collapse into a single write — the brain doesn't get hammered. When the brain is unreachable, the note is queued and indexed later. Enable this once you're confident the brain service is stable on your machine.

`Index minimum characters` (default: 40) skips notes shorter than this threshold. This prevents stub notes, empty templates, and one-line scratch files from polluting your vector index. Raise it if you find short notes cluttering search results; lower it if you have intentionally brief notes you want indexed.

**Safety**

`AIDefence scan` (default: on) enables prompt-injection and PII screening on every write. The documentation says to keep it on unless you really know what you're doing — and that's not boilerplate. This is the setting that prevents malicious content embedded in a note from being injected into AI agent queries downstream. Note that even with this toggle, the server-side checks still run; this setting controls an additional layer in the plugin.

**Search and retrieval**

`Search / Related limit` (default: 8) is the top-k value — how many results the semantic search and the related-notes sidebar return. Raise it if you want more candidates to browse; lower it if the sidebar feels noisy. There's a performance tradeoff at very high values, but for typical vault sizes it's negligible.

**Bulk sync**

`Bulk-sync include` (default: whole vault) and `Bulk-sync exclude` (default: `.obsidian,.trash`) are comma-separated folder filters. Bulk sync is the operation that walks your entire vault and indexes everything that hasn't been indexed yet. The exclude list keeps plugin internals and deleted notes out of the brain. Add any folder you don't want indexed — drafts, sensitive personal notes, large attachment folders.

**Training data**

`DPO default direction` (default: `quality`) is the label stored on every preference pair you create. DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) pairs are used to fine-tune language models — you mark one note as preferred over another, and the pair gets exported as training data. The direction label tells the training pipeline what axis the preference is on. `quality` is the right default for most use cases; change it if you're collecting preference data along a different dimension (e.g., `conciseness` or `accuracy`).

**pi.ruv.io connection**

`pi URL` (default: `https://pi.ruv.io`) and `pi token` (default: empty) control access to the shared knowledge base. The token is a bearer token you generate on pi.ruv.io and paste here. Without it, all pi.ruv.io commands are inert. `pi pull limit` (default: 20), `pi pull query`, and `pi pull category` let you scope what gets pulled — how many memories, filtered by a search string or category. Start with a small limit and a specific category to avoid pulling thousands of stubs you don't need.

title: ruOS MacBook Air: What's Included and Why Each Piece Matters
content:
ruOS for the MacBook Air Mid-2012 (model A1466, Ivy Bridge generation) is a purpose-built Linux image that ships with everything pre-configured for DJ performance, music streaming, and running the full ruOS agent stack. Think of it like a restaurant that does mise en place before service — every ingredient is already chopped, measured, and in its place before you even sit down.

Here's a tour of what's baked in and why each choice was made:

**Desktop: XFCE 4.18**
The 2012 MacBook Air ships with 4–8GB of RAM and an Ivy Bridge CPU. XFCE is a lightweight desktop environment that doesn't waste those resources on visual effects. It gives you a full graphical environment without the overhead of GNOME or KDE, which is important when you also need headroom for audio processing and AI agent workloads.

**GPU: Intel HD 4000 with SNA, TearFree, DRI3, and VA-API**
The Intel HD 4000 is a capable integrated GPU for its era. SNA (Sandybridge New Acceleration) is Intel's optimized 2D rendering path. TearFree eliminates screen tearing during video playback without requiring a compositor. DRI3 is the modern direct rendering interface. VA-API hardware decode means H.264 and VP8 video is decoded by the GPU rather than the CPU — important for keeping the CPU free for audio and agent tasks.

**WiFi: Broadcom BCM4360 with broadcom-sta**
The BCM4360 chip in this MacBook requires a proprietary driver (`bcmwl-kernel-source`). This is one of the most common pain points when installing Linux on MacBooks — the driver isn't in the default kernel. ruOS ships with it pre-installed and pre-configured with ruv.net WPA-PSK credentials, so you're on the network immediately.

**Audio: PipeWire with Low-Latency Config**
DJ software like Mixxx requires very low audio latency — the gap between turning a knob and hearing the result must be imperceptible. PipeWire is configured with `rtprio 99` (real-time priority) and `memlock unlimited`, which tells the kernel to treat the audio process as near-highest priority and never swap its memory to disk. This is the same approach professional audio workstations use.

**DJ: Mixxx 2.4 with Pioneer DDJ-200 Mapping**
Mixxx is an open-source DJ application. The Pioneer DDJ-200 is a popular entry-level controller. The mapping file that tells Mixxx how to interpret DDJ-200 knobs, pads, and faders is pre-loaded — no manual MIDI mapping required.

**VPN: Tailscale**
Tailscale creates a mesh VPN (virtual private network) between your devices using WireGuard under the hood. Once you run `tailscale up` and follow the auth URL, this machine joins your tailnet and can securely reach other devices without port forwarding or firewall rules.

**Dev Stack: Node.js 22, Rust, Claude Code**
Node.js 22 and Rust are pre-installed. Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding assistant) is installed automatically on first login via `~/.ruos-first-login.sh` — you don't need to do anything manually.

**ruOS Agent Stack**
Five components form the agent layer: `mcp-brain` (memory and reasoning core), `ruvultra-mcp` (MCP protocol server), `ruvultra-embedder` (vector embedding generation), `ruvultra-profile` (user/agent profiling), and `ruvultra-init` (initialization and orchestration). Together these give the machine a persistent, queryable memory and the ability to run autonomous agent workflows.

**Power: TLP**
TLP is a Linux power management tool. On this MacBook it's configured to run the CPU in performance mode when plugged in and powersave mode on battery, disable CPU boost on battery to extend runtime, and enable WiFi power saving on battery. These are MacBook-specific tunings that wouldn't apply to a generic laptop config.

title: Installing ruOS from a rootfs Tarball: The Chroot Bootstrap Method
content:
Most Linux distributions are installed from a live ISO that boots into a temporary environment and then copies files to disk. ruOS takes a different approach: it ships as a pre-built rootfs tarball that you extract directly onto a formatted partition, then use a chroot to install the kernel and bootloader. Understanding why this works — and how to do it — is useful knowledge for anyone building custom Linux appliances.

**Why Not a Live ISO?**
Ubuntu's `live-build` tool inherits Debian-mode defaults that conflict with Ubuntu Noble (24.04) repositories. It points at `security.debian.org` and uses `debian-archive-keyring` instead of Ubuntu's equivalents. Patching all of this is tedious and fragile. More importantly, a live ISO produces a system you boot and then install — adding a step. The rootfs tarball approach skips the live environment entirely and produces a directly installable system that works offline.

**Step 1: Partition the Target Drive**
You need two partitions: a small FAT32 EFI partition (around 512MB) and an ext4 root partition for everything else. Label them clearly:
```
sudo mkfs.vfat -F 32 -n RUOS-EFI /dev/sdX1
sudo mkfs.ext4 -L ruOS-root /dev/sdX2
```
The `-n` and `-L` flags set human-readable labels, which makes it easier to identify partitions later.

**Step 2: Mount and Extract**
Mount both partitions, then extract the rootfs tarball into the root partition:
```
sudo mount /dev/sdX2 /mnt/ruos-root
sudo mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/ruos-efi
sudo tar xf rootfs.tar -C /mnt/ruos-root/
```
At this point you have a complete Linux filesystem on disk, but no kernel and no bootloader — it can't boot yet.

**Step 3: Set Up the Chroot**
A chroot (change root) lets you run commands as if you're inside the target filesystem, even though you're actually on the host machine. For this to work, the target needs access to the host's device tree, process table, and kernel interfaces. You bind-mount them:
```
sudo mount --bind /dev /mnt/ruos-root/dev
sudo mount --bind /dev/pts /mnt/ruos-root/dev/pts
sudo mount -t proc proc /mnt/ruos-root/proc
sudo mount -t sysfs sysfs /mnt/ruos-root/sys
sudo mount --bind /mnt/ruos-efi /mnt/ruos-root/boot/efi
```
Think of this like giving a house under construction temporary access to the city's water and power grid while the permanent connections are being installed.

**Step 4: Install Kernel and Bootloader Inside the Chroot**
```
sudo chroot /mnt/ruos-root bash -c '
  apt-get update
  apt-get install -y linux-image-generic grub-efi-amd64 efibootmgr initramfs-tools
  grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/boot/efi --removable --no-nvram
  update-grub
'
```
Two flags on `grub-install` deserve attention:
- `--removable`: Writes the bootloader to the EFI fallback path (`EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI`) rather than a machine-specific NVRAM entry. This is essential for USB drives and for machines where you can't or don't want to modify NVRAM.
- `--no-nvram`: Skips writing a boot entry to the machine's UEFI NVRAM. Combined with `--removable`, this makes the installation portable — it will boot on any UEFI machine without leaving traces in that machine's firmware.

**Why This Approach Is Powerful**
The chroot bootstrap method is the same technique used to build embedded Linux systems, container base images, and rescue environments. Once you understand it, you can build a custom Linux appliance for any hardware target, pre-load any software stack, and produce a USB that boots offline with zero first-boot configuration required. The ruOS MacBook image is exactly this: a complete, opinionated environment captured as a tarball and deployed in minutes.

title: MacBook Hardware Quirks on Linux: The ruOS Configuration Reference
content:
Running Linux on Apple hardware requires working around several design decisions Apple made for macOS that don't translate directly to Linux conventions. ruOS pre-configures all of these, but knowing where the config files live and what they control lets you customize or troubleshoot the system confidently.

**Keyboard: Fn Key Behavior and Command/Option Swap**

On a Mac keyboard, the top row of keys defaults to media controls (brightness, volume, Mission Control) with Fn held to get F1–F12. Most Linux software expects F1–F12 as the primary function. ruOS flips this via the `hid_apple` kernel module parameter `fnmode=2`, which makes F1–F12 the default and media controls the Fn-modified behavior.

Additionally, the physical positions of Command and Option on a Mac keyboard are swapped relative to where Linux expects Alt and Super (Windows key). The `swap_opt_cmd=1` parameter corrects this so keyboard shortcuts feel natural.

Config file: `/etc/modprobe.d/hid-apple.conf`

**Trackpad: Tap, Scroll, and Click Behavior**

The MacBook trackpad supports multitouch gestures. ruOS configures `libinput` with three key settings:
- **Tap-to-click**: A single-finger tap registers as a left click, so you don't need to physically press the trackpad.
- **Natural scrolling**: Scrolling direction matches the touchscreen convention (content follows your fingers), consistent with macOS behavior.
- **Clickfinger mode**: A two-finger click or tap registers as a right click. This is more reliable than the alternative (button zones at the bottom of the trackpad).

Config file: `/etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/30-touchpad.conf`
