**GPU: Tearing, Acceleration, and Video Decode**

The Intel HD 4000 uses the `xserver-xorg-video-intel` driver with three important settings:
- **SNA acceleration**: Intel's optimized rendering backend for Sandy/Ivy Bridge. Faster than the older UXA backend for 2D operations.
- **TearFree**: Eliminates horizontal tearing during video playback and window movement by using a shadow framebuffer. Adds a small amount of latency but is worth it for smooth visuals.
- **DRI3**: The modern direct rendering infrastructure. Enables better performance and compatibility with Vulkan and modern OpenGL applications.

For video decode, `intel-media-va-driver` enables VA-API hardware acceleration for H.264 and VP8. This offloads video decoding from the CPU to the GPU's dedicated decode engine — meaningful on a machine where CPU cycles are shared with audio processing and AI agent workloads.

Config file: `/etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/20-intel.conf`

**Power: Battery vs. AC Profiles**

TLP (Thermal and Power management for Linux) applies different CPU and WiFi policies depending on whether the machine is plugged in:

| State | CPU Governor | CPU Boost | WiFi Power Save |
|-------|-------------|-----------|----------------|
| AC | performance | enabled | off |
| Battery | powersave | disabled | on |

The CPU governor controls how aggressively the CPU scales its clock speed. Performance mode keeps it high for responsiveness. Powersave mode scales it down to conserve energy. CPU boost (Intel Turbo Boost) allows the CPU to exceed its base clock for short bursts — useful on AC, but it generates heat and drains battery quickly, so it's disabled on battery.

Config file: `/etc/tlp.d/01-macbook.conf`

**Thermal Management**

`thermald` runs as a background daemon and monitors CPU temperature, applying throttling before the hardware's emergency thermal shutdown kicks in. Ivy Bridge has specific thermal characteristics that thermald handles automatically.

**The Pattern to Remember**

All hardware customization in ruOS follows a consistent pattern: kernel module parameters go in `/etc/modprobe.d/`, X11 input and display configs go in `/etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/`, and power management goes in `/etc/tlp.d/`. If you need to adjust any behavior, find the relevant file in one of these three locations, make your change, and either reboot or reload the relevant service.

title: rvcsi Architecture: How Eight Crates Work Together to Process WiFi CSI Data
content:
Channel State Information (CSI) is the per-subcarrier complex channel response that a WiFi receiver measures every time a packet arrives. Think of it as a detailed fingerprint of how radio waves are bouncing around a room — useful for detecting presence, motion, and even breathing. The rvcsi project turns raw CSI data from commodity hardware into structured, analyzable events, and its architecture is worth understanding because it makes deliberate tradeoffs that keep the system safe, testable, and extensible.

The project is organized as a Rust workspace with eight crates, each owning a distinct slice of responsibility:

**rvcsi-core** is the shared kernel. It defines the normalized data types — `CsiFrame` (one observation at a timestamp), `CsiWindow` (a bounded sequence of frames for analysis), and `CsiEvent` (a semantic interpretation like 'presence started'). It also owns the `CsiSource` plugin trait, identity newtypes, error types, and the frame validation pipeline. Every other crate depends on this one. Crucially, it forbids `unsafe` code entirely.

**rvcsi-dsp** holds reusable signal processing stages: DC removal, phase unwrapping, smoothing, Hampel/MAD outlier filtering, sliding variance, and baseline subtraction. It also computes scalar features like motion energy and presence score. It is also `unsafe`-free.

**rvcsi-events** implements the window aggregation and event detection layer. A `WindowBuffer` collects frames from one `(session_id, source_id)` pair and emits a `CsiWindow` every N frames or T nanoseconds, computing per-subcarrier mean amplitude, phase variance, motion energy, and a logistic presence score. Four state machines — `PresenceDetector`, `MotionDetector`, `QualityDetector`, and `BaselineDriftDetector` — consume windows and emit events. The baseline-drift detector is particularly clever: it measures drift as a fraction of the running baseline's RMS magnitude rather than as an absolute amplitude value. This means the same threshold configuration works whether you are reading raw `int8` ESP32 CSI, `int16`-scaled Nexmon CSI, or baseline-subtracted streams.

**rvcsi-adapter-nexmon** is the one crate that touches hardware-specific formats. It wraps a thin C shim (`rvcsi_nexmon_shim.{c,h}`) compiled via `build.rs` and the `cc` crate. The C code is the only place `unsafe` appears in the entire runtime, and it is confined to a single `ffi` module. The shim itself is allocation-free, global-free, bounds-checked against caller-supplied lengths, never panics, and carries an ABI version number (`0x0001_0001`). It handles two byte formats: the compact self-describing 'rvCSI Nexmon record' (magic `'RVNX'`, version, flags, RSSI, channel, bandwidth, timestamp, then `int16` I/Q samples in Q8.8 fixed-point), and the real nexmon_csi UDP payload used by BCM43455c0, 4358, and 4366c0 chips (an 18-byte header followed by `nsub` `int16` real/imaginary sample pairs, where `nsub = (len − 18) / 4`).

Also in this crate: a dependency-free pure-Rust libpcap reader that handles all four byte-order and timestamp-resolution magic variants, Ethernet/raw-IPv4/Linux-SLL link types, and truncated final records. Parsing the container format in pure Rust avoids vendor-library fragility. A chip registry (`chips.rs`) maps Nexmon chip identifiers and Raspberry Pi models to `AdapterProfile`s, including the Pi 5 mapping to BCM43455c0.

**rvcsi-adapter-file** owns the `.rvcsi` capture format (JSONL: a header line followed by one `CsiFrame` per line), a `FileRecorder`, and a `FileReplayAdapter`.

**rvcsi-runtime** is the composition layer, providing one-shot helpers like `decode_nexmon_pcap`, `summarize_nexmon_pcap`, and `nexmon_profile_for`.

**rvcsi-node** exposes an napi-rs surface for Node.js consumers, and **rvcsi-cli** provides the command-line interface.

The key architectural insight is the strict layering: hardware-specific parsing lives in one adapter crate behind a thin, versioned C shim; signal processing is separated from event detection; and the core schema is shared but never polluted by adapter concerns. `unsafe` is not banned everywhere — that would be impractical — but it is quarantined to the smallest possible surface and documented explicitly. This makes auditing straightforward: you only need to scrutinize one `ffi` module and one C file to reason about memory safety for the entire system.

title: Understanding the rvcsi Ubiquitous Language: From Raw Frames to Semantic Events
content:
One of the most important things a well-designed system does is give its concepts precise names and stick to them. The rvcsi project defines a clear vocabulary that flows from raw hardware data all the way up to human-meaningful events. Understanding this vocabulary makes the codebase, the CLI, and the API surface immediately readable.

**Frame** is the atomic unit. One CSI observation at one timestamp from one source. When your WiFi adapter measures how a packet traveled through the air — which subcarriers were attenuated, which were phase-shifted — that snapshot is a Frame. Frames are normalized into a `CsiFrame` struct by an Adapter, regardless of whether the original data came from a Nexmon-patched Raspberry Pi, an ESP32, or a replay file.

**Source** is anything that produces Frames: a physical NIC capturing live traffic, an ESP32 node sending UDP packets, a PCAP file recorded with `tcpdump`, or a `.rvcsi` replay file. Sources are abstracted behind the `CsiSource` plugin trait so the rest of the system does not care about the origin.

**Adapter** is the translation layer between a source's native format and the normalized `CsiFrame`. The Nexmon adapter, for example, knows how to parse the 18-byte nexmon_csi UDP header and extract `nsub` complex samples. The file adapter knows how to read JSONL capture files. Adapters are the only place where format-specific knowledge lives.

**Window** is a bounded sequence of Frames from one source/session, used for analysis. A single Frame tells you almost nothing useful — you need to see how the channel changes over time. The `WindowBuffer` collects N frames or T nanoseconds worth of data and then emits a Window containing per-subcarrier mean amplitude, phase variance, scalar motion energy, and a logistic presence score.

**Baseline** is the learned normal RF-field state for a space. When a room is empty and undisturbed, the CSI measurements settle into a characteristic pattern. Calibration is the process of observing enough stable Windows to learn this pattern and store it as a `CalibrationProfile`.

**Delta** is the measured difference between the current field and the baseline. A small delta means the room looks normal. A large delta means something has changed — a person walked in, a door opened, or the furniture moved.

**Drift** is slow, gradual movement of the field away from baseline — the kind of change that happens over hours as temperature shifts or objects are rearranged. The `BaselineDriftDetector` tracks an EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) of mean amplitude and flags sustained drift as a `BaselineChanged` event. A sudden large jump in a single window is flagged separately as an `AnomalyDetected` event.

**Event** is a semantic interpretation of one or more Windows: `PresenceStarted`, `PresenceEnded`, `MotionDetected`, `MotionSettled`, `SignalQualityDropped`, `CalibrationRequired`, `BaselineChanged`, `AnomalyDetected`. Events are what the application layer consumes. The four state machines in `rvcsi-events` translate the continuous numerical stream of Windows into these discrete, meaningful signals using hysteresis and debouncing to avoid spurious triggers.

**Quality score** is a confidence value in [0, 1] that a Frame, Window, or signal is usable. Frames that fail validation (out-of-bounds values, non-monotonic timestamps, wrong subcarrier count) are rejected or quarantined rather than silently corrupted. The `QualityDetector` state machine watches for sustained low quality and eventually emits a `CalibrationRequired` event.

**RF memory** is the persisted store of temporal vectors and events for a physical space, kept in RuVector. This is what enables the system to answer questions like 'what does this room normally look like at 3pm on a Tuesday?' or 'has the baseline for this space drifted since last week?'

The value of this vocabulary is that it creates a shared mental model across the C shim, the Rust crates, the CLI commands, the Node.js API, and the documentation. When you run `rvcsi events capture.rvcsi`, you are replaying Frames through the DSP pipeline into Windows, then through the EventPipeline into Events — and every word in that sentence maps directly to a type in the codebase.

title: The rvcsi C Shim Pattern: Safely Crossing the FFI Boundary for Hardware Parsing
content:
Rust's memory safety guarantees are powerful, but they stop at the FFI boundary. The moment you call into C code, you are in `unsafe` territory — the compiler can no longer verify that memory is accessed correctly, that buffers are not overrun, or that global state is not corrupted. The rvcsi project handles this with a pattern worth studying: a thin, carefully constrained C shim that does exactly one job and nothing else.

The shim lives in `native/rvcsi_nexmon_shim.{c,h}` and is compiled by `build.rs` using the `cc` crate. It is the only C code in the entire runtime. The Rust side wraps it in a single `ffi` module, and that module is the only place `unsafe` appears. Everything above that boundary — all eight crates' worth of DSP, event detection, file I/O, and CLI — is `forbid(unsafe_code)`.

**What the shim does.** It parses two binary formats that come off real hardware:

The first is the 'rvCSI Nexmon record' — a compact, self-describing format with a `'RVNX'` magic number, version, flags, RSSI, noise floor, channel, bandwidth, timestamp, and then `int16` I/Q samples in Q8.8 fixed-point format. This is rvcsi's own interchange format.

The second is the real nexmon_csi UDP payload produced by Broadcom chips (BCM43455c0, 4358, 4366c0) running the Nexmon firmware patch. This format has an 18-byte header: magic `0x1111`, RSSI as `int8`, frame control, source MAC, sequence counter, core/stream identifiers, a chanspec word, and a chip version. After the header come `nsub` pairs of `int16` (real, imaginary) samples, where `nsub = (payload_length − 18) / 4`. This is the same format read by CSIKit and `csireader.py`.

The shim also decodes Broadcom's d11ac chanspec encoding: channel number from bits `[7:0]`, bandwidth from bits `[13:11]`, band from bits `[15:14]`, cross-checked against the FFT size implied by the subcarrier count.

**The safety constraints.** The shim enforces four properties that make it safe to call from Rust:

1. **Allocation-free.** The shim never calls `malloc` or any allocator. All output is written into caller-supplied buffers. There is no heap to corrupt and no allocation failure to handle.

2. **Global-free.** No global or static mutable state. Every call is fully self-contained. This means the shim is safe to call from multiple threads without synchronization.

3. **Bounds-checked against caller-supplied lengths.** Every buffer access is validated against a length parameter passed by the caller. The shim never assumes a buffer is large enough — it checks first and returns an error code if not.

4. **Never panics.** C does not have panics, but it can call `abort()` or invoke undefined behavior. The shim avoids both. All error conditions return error codes to the caller.

5. **ABI-versioned.** The shim exports a version constant (`0x0001_0001`). The Rust wrapper checks this at startup. If the compiled C and the Rust expectations diverge — for example, after a format change — the mismatch is caught immediately rather than causing silent data corruption.

**Why a C shim at all?** The nexmon_csi UDP format is a packed binary structure defined by the Broadcom firmware and the Nexmon patch. Parsing it correctly requires exact byte-level control. While this is possible in pure Rust with careful use of `byteorder` and manual offset arithmetic, the shim approach has a practical advantage: the same C code can be validated against reference implementations (CSIKit, `csireader.py`) and tested independently. The ABI version number means the contract between the C and Rust layers is explicit and machine-checkable.

The broader lesson is that `unsafe` is not something to eliminate entirely — it is something to quarantine. By confining all hardware-format parsing to one small, allocation-free, globally-stateless, bounds-checked C file wrapped by one `ffi` module, rvcsi gets the benefits of both worlds: correct hardware parsing and a safe, auditable Rust codebase above it.

title: SkyGraph: How a Browser Dashboard Watches Your Sky with Rust, WASM, and ADS-B
content:
SkyGraph is a real-time all-sky situational awareness dashboard that runs entirely in the browser — no backend server required for the core display logic. It combines live aircraft tracking, satellite propagation, anomaly detection, and weather data into a single polar-projection canvas. Understanding how these pieces fit together reveals a clean architecture pattern for high-performance browser applications built on WebAssembly.

**The polar canvas as a mental model**

Think of the display like looking straight up through a fisheye lens. The center of the circle is directly overhead (zenith), the outer edge is the horizon, and North is always at the top. Elevation rings at 0°, 30°, and 60° give you depth. Every moving object — aircraft, satellite, sun, moon — is projected onto this dome using the same coordinate math: WGS-84 latitude/longitude/altitude → azimuth/elevation/range, handled by the `SkyProjector` WASM module.

**Live aircraft: ADS-B with dead reckoning**

Every 5 seconds, the dashboard polls airplanes.live (falling back to adsb.lol if needed) for all aircraft within 40 nautical miles. Because 5 seconds is a long time on screen, the dashboard applies *dead reckoning* between polls — it extrapolates each aircraft's position using its last known heading and speed, so dots glide smoothly rather than snapping to new positions. Each dot carries metadata: aircraft type, registration, squawk code, wake turbulence category, and climb/descent arrows. Emergency squawks (7500 hijack, 7600 radio failure, 7700 general emergency) trigger a red double-ring and a header alert banner.

**Satellites: SGP4 propagation compiled to WebAssembly**

Satellite positions are computed *per animation frame* using the SGP4 orbital mechanics model, compiled from Rust to WebAssembly for near-native speed. TLE (Two-Line Element) data comes from CelesTrak in three flavors: `visual` (roughly the 150 brightest objects), `stations` (ISS and crewed platforms), and `starlink`. The propagation chain is: TLE → SGP4 → TEME coordinates → GMST-rotated ECEF → geodetic → observer frame. Satellites are drawn as diamonds; a ✦ symbol marks passes where the satellite is sunlit while the sky is dark (sun below −6° elevation) — meaning you can actually see it with the naked eye. A 24-hour pass predictor lists upcoming visible passes with rise/set times, max elevation, and direction, and can fire a browser notification 5 minutes before a pass.

**Anomaly scoring: the dashboard remembers your sky**

Every live aircraft track is converted into a 32-dimensional embedding vector by the `embed_track` WASM function. This vector captures motion statistics — altitude, heading, signal strength, range, elevation, time-of-day patterns — derived by finite differencing the raw position points. These embeddings are stored in IndexedDB (the browser's built-in persistent key-value store), so the system accumulates a rolling memory of your local sky across browser sessions.

When a new track arrives, its embedding is compared against this history using a novelty score. The `AnomalyScorer` then applies the §15 composite formula, which combines the novelty score with rule-based signals (altitude, heading, time of day, signal characteristics) to produce a final anomaly score between 0 and 1. Scores above 0.76 trigger an alert. Crucially, every score comes with mandatory human-readable reasons — you always know *why* something was flagged, not just that it was. Dot and row colors follow a green-to-red band: green is normal, red is a strong anomaly.

**Behavior badges: geometric pattern detection**

Beyond the statistical scorer, four geometric detectors watch for specific flight patterns. `[HOLD]` flags aircraft flying holding patterns (oval racetrack loops). `[GRID]` detects survey-style back-and-forth lawnmower paths. `[GO-AROUND]` catches missed approaches. `[FORM]` identifies pairs of aircraft flying in close formation. These are purely geometric — they look at the shape of the track, not the statistics.

**CPA conflict prediction**

For any two aircraft that are converging, the dashboard computes the Closest Point of Approach (CPA). If two tracks will come within 1 km laterally and 300 m vertically within the next 90 seconds, a dashed alert line connects them on the canvas and a predicted-path cone is drawn. This is a forward-looking collision proximity warning running entirely in the browser.

**No build tooling for the UI**

The canvas dashboard (`ui/dashboard/`) is deliberately vanilla JavaScript and Canvas2D — no React, no bundler, no npm build step. The only compiled artifact is the Rust/WASM package, built once with `wasm-pack build --target web`. An experimental WebGPU path exists for instanced satellite sprite rendering, with automatic Canvas2D fallback for browsers that don't support it yet. This keeps the dashboard deployable as static files with zero infrastructure.

title: Track Embeddings and Anomaly Scoring in SkyGraph: How the Sky Learns What's Normal
content:
One of SkyGraph's most interesting design choices is that it doesn't just display aircraft — it *learns* what your local sky normally looks like and flags deviations. This is done through a pipeline of track embedding, novelty scoring, and composite anomaly formulas, all running in WebAssembly inside the browser. Here's how each step works.

**Step 1: Summarizing a track into a fixed-size vector**

A raw aircraft track is a time series of position pings — latitude, longitude, altitude, heading, speed, signal strength — arriving every few seconds. To compare tracks mathematically, you need a fixed-size representation. SkyGraph's `embed_track` function (in `embed.rs`, compiled to WASM) converts each track into a 32-dimensional vector. Every dimension is documented and deterministic: things like mean altitude, dominant heading, time-of-day bucket, mean signal strength in dBFS, minimum range from the observer, and maximum elevation angle. Per-point motion features (acceleration, turn rate) are derived by finite differencing consecutive position points before being aggregated.

Think of this like a fingerprint. A routine commercial flight at 35,000 feet on a known corridor heading northeast at 6 AM has a very different fingerprint from a slow, low, circling aircraft at 2 AM with no callsign.

**Step 2: Storing fingerprints in IndexedDB**

After each track ends (or at regular intervals), its 32-dim embedding is written to IndexedDB — the browser's built-in persistent storage. This means the system accumulates a rolling history of every track it has ever seen at your location, surviving browser restarts. The dashboard literally remembers your sky across sessions. Over time, this history builds a baseline of what's normal: the morning rush of commuter jets, the afternoon cargo flights, the occasional military transit.

**Step 3: Computing novelty against the rolling history**

When a new track arrives, its embedding is compared against the stored history using the `novelty` function. This is a nearest-neighbor distance in 32-dimensional space — how far is this track's fingerprint from the closest known fingerprints? A track that closely resembles many past tracks scores low novelty (it's familiar). A track with no close neighbors scores high novelty (it's unlike anything seen before). This is the §13 vector novelty score.

**Step 4: The §15 composite anomaly formula**

Novelty alone isn't enough — a new aircraft type might be novel simply because it's rare, not because it's suspicious. The `AnomalyScorer` combines vector novelty with a set of rule-based signals into a composite score. The rules check things like: Is this altitude unusual for this time of day? Is the heading inconsistent with known corridors? Is the signal strength anomalously weak or strong for the reported range? Is the aircraft operating outside normal hours?

Each signal contributes a weighted component, and the weights are configurable via `AnomalyConfig` (defaulting to the §15 specification). The final score is a float between 0 and 1. The alert threshold is 0.76 — above this, the track is flagged red.

**Step 5: Mandatory human-readable reasons**

A key design rule: every anomaly score must be accompanied by human-readable reasons. The system never just says "anomaly score: 0.83" — it says something like "unusual altitude for time of day; heading inconsistent with known corridors; high vector novelty (no similar tracks in history)." This is enforced at the API level of `AnomalyScorer`. The reasons appear in the side panel when you click a flagged track.

**Consistency between browser and native pipeline**

The WASM `AnomalyScorer` reuses the exact same Rust code as the native server-side pipeline (`anomaly::BaselineStats::from_summaries` / `anomaly::score_summary`). There is no separate JavaScript reimplementation of the scoring logic. This means scores computed in the browser are numerically identical to scores computed in the backend pipeline — a property that matters for reproducibility and for the acceptance tests, which verify that anomalous tracks score ≥ 0.76 and corridor traffic scores ≤ 0.55 given the same baseline history.

**Acceptance test coverage**

The acceptance test suite (`tests/acceptance.rs`) includes a dedicated test for this: `acceptance_4_anomaly_scoring_separates_corridor_traffic` proves that the scorer correctly separates an anomalous night track from routine corridor traffic given a seeded baseline. Eight acceptance tests in total cover the full pipeline from coordinate conversion through graph queries to anomaly scoring and explanation citation.

title: SkyGraph's WASM Module Architecture: Four Compiled Rust Structs That Power the Browser
content:
SkyGraph's browser dashboard is powered by four Rust structs compiled to WebAssembly via `wasm-bindgen`. Understanding what each one does — and why the boundary was drawn where it was — is a useful lesson in designing WASM APIs for real-time visualization applications.

**Why compile Rust to WASM for a dashboard?**

Three reasons drive this choice. First, performance: satellite SGP4 propagation runs every animation frame for potentially hundreds of objects; doing this in JavaScript would be too slow. Second, correctness: the anomaly scoring formula needs to be identical between the browser and the native pipeline — sharing the same compiled Rust code guarantees this. Third, persistence math: coordinate projections involve `f64` floating-point chains (WGS-84 → ECEF → ENU → azimuth/elevation) where JavaScript's number handling is fine but having a single authoritative implementation prevents drift.

**`SkyProjector`: coordinate math for the all-sky dome**

`SkyProjector` handles the geometric core: given an observer's location and a target's WGS-84 coordinates, compute azimuth, elevation, range, and bearing. It exposes two modes. `project` handles a single point. `project_batch` takes a `Float64Array` of `[lat, lon, alt]` triplets and returns a `Float64Array` of `[az, el, range, bearing]` quadruplets — this batched form is used for trail rendering, where you need to project dozens of historical positions per track per frame without crossing the JS/WASM boundary repeatedly. `screen_position` applies the polar fisheye mapping: zenith at canvas center, horizon at edge, azimuth 0° = North = up.

**`AnomalyScorer`: the §15 formula in the browser**

`AnomalyScorer` exposes two methods. `baseline_from(tracksJson)` builds a statistical baseline from a JSON array of track summaries. `score(trackJson, novelty)` scores a single track summary against that baseline, returning a composite anomaly score plus human-readable reasons. The track summary schema is: `{icao24, callsign, mean_alt_m, dominant_heading_deg, start_hour, mean_signal_dbfs, min_range_m, max_elevation_deg}`. Because this wraps `anomaly::BaselineStats::from_summaries` and `anomaly::score_summary` directly, the browser scores are numerically identical to native pipeline scores.

**`SatPropagator`: per-frame orbital mechanics**

`SatPropagator` wraps the `sgp4` Rust crate and adds the observer-frame projection chain. The propagation pipeline is: TLE text → SGP4 state vector in TEME frame → GMST rotation → ECEF → Bowring iterative geodetic conversion → observer ENU frame → azimuth/elevation/range. This runs batched for all active satellites every animation frame. The second method, `predict_passes(start, hours, step)`, walks forward through time at a configurable step size and identifies rise, culmination, and set events for each satellite, flagging passes where the satellite is sunlit (using a low-precision Rust sun model) and the sky is dark (sun below −6° elevation). These are the naked-eye-visible passes.

**`embed_track` / `novelty`: the §13 embedding pipeline**

These are functions rather than a struct. `embed_track` takes a sequence of live position points and produces a 32-dimensional `Float64Array` embedding. The per-point motion features (speed change, turn rate) are computed by finite differencing consecutive points before aggregation. `novelty` compares a new embedding against a set of stored embeddings (retrieved from IndexedDB by the JavaScript layer) and returns a distance-based novelty score. The JavaScript side manages IndexedDB persistence; the WASM side handles the math.

**The JS/WASM boundary design principle**

A consistent pattern emerges: WASM owns the compute-heavy, numerically sensitive operations. JavaScript owns I/O (fetch, IndexedDB, Canvas2D drawing calls, DOM updates). Data crosses the boundary as JSON strings for structured objects and `Float64Array` for bulk numeric data. The batched array interfaces (`project_batch`, the per-frame satellite propagation) are specifically designed to minimize boundary crossings, since each crossing has overhead. This is the right pattern for real-time visualization WASM: push loops into WASM, pull results back as typed arrays, draw in JS.

title: The rUv Neural Pipeline: A Six-Layer Tour from Sensor to Cognitive State
content:
The rUv Neural Pipeline is a modular signal-processing chain that takes raw brain measurements and transforms them, step by step, into meaningful cognitive state classifications. Think of it like a factory assembly line where raw ore enters one end and a finished product exits the other — except here, the raw material is electromagnetic brain activity and the finished product is an understanding of what the brain is doing right now.

**Layer 1 — Sensor Layer: Where Data Enters**
The pipeline accepts signals from four source types: NV Diamond magnetometers (quantum-grade magnetic field sensors), Optically Pumped Magnetometers (OPMs), conventional EEG electrodes, or a built-in simulator. This flexibility is intentional — the same downstream pipeline works regardless of how the signal was captured. If you're developing software and don't have a quantum optics bench, the simulator exercises every downstream stage identically.

**Layer 2 — Signal Layer: Cleaning and Transforming**
Raw brain signals are noisy. The Signal Layer applies three key operations. A bandpass filter isolates the frequency bands of interest (e.g., alpha at 8–12 Hz, gamma at 30–100 Hz). Artifact rejection removes eye blinks, muscle noise, and electrical interference. Then the Hilbert transform extracts the instantaneous phase of each signal — imagine tracking not just the height of an ocean wave but exactly where in its cycle (crest, trough, rising, falling) it sits at every moment. Spectral analysis (PSD) also runs here, giving a power-by-frequency fingerprint of the signal.

**Layer 3 — Graph Layer: Mapping Brain Connectivity**
Once signals are clean and phase-tagged, the pipeline asks: which brain regions are talking to each other? Phase-Locking Value (PLV) and coherence metrics measure synchrony between channel pairs. If two regions consistently hit their wave peaks at the same time, they're likely coordinating. The output is a connectivity matrix — a 68×68 grid (one cell per pair of brain regions) where each value represents how tightly coupled those two regions are. This is the brain's functional wiring diagram at that moment.

**Layer 4 — MinCut Layer: Finding Natural Divisions**
The Stoer-Wagner minimum cut algorithm treats the connectivity matrix as a graph and finds the weakest link — the smallest set of connections whose removal would split the brain network into two communities. This reveals natural functional boundaries. The Fiedler decomposition and Cheeger constant provide complementary views of how well-integrated versus compartmentalized the network is. Think of it as finding where a city's road network is most vulnerable to being split in two.

**Layer 5 — Memory Layer: Recognizing Patterns**
The HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) index stores previously seen connectivity patterns as high-dimensional embeddings. When a new pattern arrives, the Memory Layer searches for the closest matches in this index — efficiently, in O(log N) time even with tens of thousands of stored patterns. This is how the system recognizes that the current brain state resembles a previously labeled state like 'focused attention' or 'drowsy'.

**Layer 6 — Decode Layer: Naming the State**
Finally, the Decode Layer uses the retrieved memory matches and current graph features to classify the cognitive state. The output is a human-readable label plus a confidence score.

**The Closed-Loop Extension**
The pipeline doesn't have to be read-only. The `stim`, `biosense`, and `loop` crates extend it into a closed-loop system: stimuli (40 Hz light, audio, haptic) are delivered, biosensors (HRV, respiration, motion) measure the body's response, and a controller adjusts stimulus parameters based on what the brain and body are doing. Every delivered stimulus generates a SHA-256-bound delivery receipt, creating a verifiable audit trail of what was sent and when.

title: NV Diamond Magnetometry: Realistic Hardware Costs and When to Use the Simulator Instead
content:
Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) diamond magnetometry is one of the most exciting sensing technologies in modern neuroscience — it can detect the tiny magnetic fields produced by neural currents, at room temperature, without the liquid helium required by traditional SQUID magnetometers. But it is emphatically not a hobbyist component you can order for $45. Understanding the real cost structure will save you from a frustrating and expensive mistake.

**The Core Sensing Element: The Diamond Itself**
The heart of an NV magnetometer is a diamond crystal with a precisely engineered density of Nitrogen-Vacancy defect centers. These defects are quantum systems whose spin state shifts measurably in the presence of a magnetic field — a phenomenon called Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR).

Research-grade CVD diamonds (e.g., Element Six DNV-B1, 3×3×0.5 mm) run approximately $1,440 and are quote/lead-time items — you can't add them to a cart and receive them next week. They contain ~800 ppb of engineered NV centers, optimized for long spin coherence time (T2), which directly determines magnetic sensitivity.

Budget HPHT diamond plates (e.g., from Adámas Nanotechnologies) cost $200–500 on quote. They have 100–300 ppm nitrogen — much higher density, so they fluoresce brightly and you can definitely see an ODMR dip. But the higher impurity density shortens T2, degrading sensitivity. Fine for learning the physics; not suitable for detecting neural signals.

**The Pump Laser**
NV centers must be excited with 532 nm (green) laser light to read their spin state. This requires 50–150 mW of continuous-wave power. A lab-grade DPSS laser head from Thorlabs costs $1,000–2,000. Budget DPSS 'pointer' modules (Laserlands, ~$30–80) can reach 50–100 mW and will produce a visible ODMR signal, but with poor power stability that adds noise to your measurement. Both are Class 3B laser hazards — permanent eye damage from a momentary direct exposure. Laser safety goggles are mandatory, not optional.

Note: the Thorlabs CPS532 compact module is only 4.5 mW — far too weak for ODMR excitation despite being a convenient 532 nm source.

**The Rest of the Optical Chain**
A long-pass filter (~$120) blocks the green pump light so only the NV fluorescence (red, >650 nm) reaches the detector. A high-NA collection lens focuses that fluorescence onto a photodiode. An amplified photodetector or transimpedance amplifier (TIA) circuit converts photocurrent to a voltage the microcontroller can read. A quality amplified detector runs ~$400; a DIY OPA381/OPA657 op-amp TIA with a bare silicon photodiode can be built for $20–40.

**The Microwave Source**
This is the one genuinely affordable component. An ADF4351-based synthesizer board generates the 2.87 GHz microwave field needed to drive spin transitions. These boards cost $20–35 and work well.

**Honest Cost Summary**
- Cheapest credible single-channel ODMR demo: several hundred dollars (budget diamond, pointer laser, DIY electronics)
- Research-quality single channel: ~$3,000–5,000
- 16-channel NV array: comfortably five figures

**The Practical Recommendation**
If your goal is to develop, test, or demonstrate the rUv Neural Pipeline software, use the EEG input path or the built-in simulator. Both exercise every downstream stage — signal filtering, phase extraction, connectivity matrix computation, HNSW memory, cognitive state decoding — without requiring a quantum optics bench. The NV Diamond sensor path exists for production deployments where sub-picotesla magnetic sensitivity is genuinely required. Don't let hardware cost block software progress.

title: Neural Data Privacy in rUv Neural: Known Gaps and What They Mean
content:
Neural data — recordings of brain activity — is among the most sensitive categories of personal information that exists. It can reveal cognitive states, emotional responses, neurological conditions, and potentially even thoughts. The rUv Neural codebase includes an explicit privacy audit section that honestly documents what is and isn't protected. Understanding these gaps is essential before deploying the system with real subjects.

**What Is Currently Passing**
Error messages are clean. When the pipeline encounters a dimension mismatch, an out-of-bounds index, or a version incompatibility, it reports structural information (sizes, indices, version numbers) — not raw signal values or embedding vectors. This means error logs won't accidentally leak neural data even if they're sent to a centralized logging service.

**Subject and Session IDs: Plaintext PII**
The `EmbeddingMetadata` struct stores `subject_id` and `session_id` as plain `Option<String>` fields. These are directly serialized into HNSW index files and RVF (rUv Vector Format) files via serde. This means any file written to disk, any backup, any transfer over a network carries identifiable subject information in plaintext. In a research context this may be acceptable with appropriate access controls, but in a clinical or consumer context it creates HIPAA/GDPR exposure. The fix is either pseudonymization at ingestion (replace real IDs with opaque tokens before they enter the pipeline) or encryption of the serialized output.

**Memory Store: No Encryption at Rest**
The `NeuralMemoryStore` holds embedding vectors — compressed numerical representations of brain activity patterns — in a plain `Vec<f64>`. There is no encryption-at-rest. If the process memory is dumped (crash report, swap file, memory forensics), embedding data is recoverable. For a research prototype this is a known and accepted limitation. For any deployment handling identifiable subjects, the store should be backed by an encrypted memory region or the embeddings should be encrypted before storage.

**Memory Zeroization: Data Persists After Drop**
When an embedding vector is dropped (freed from memory), Rust's default behavior is to simply mark that memory as available — it doesn't overwrite the bytes. The actual neural data values remain in deallocated memory until something else happens to write over them. This is the same class of vulnerability that led to the `zeroize` crate becoming standard practice for cryptographic keys. The fix is to implement the `Zeroize` trait on embedding types so that sensitive values are explicitly overwritten on drop.

**Logging: Needs Ongoing Vigilance**
The codebase currently has no `tracing::info!` or `tracing::debug!` calls that include data fields — so there's nothing to audit yet. But this is flagged as a future concern: as developers add observability instrumentation, there's a natural temptation to log signal values for debugging. The rule should be enforced in code review: neural signal values, embedding vectors, and subject identifiers must never appear in log output at INFO level or below.

**WASM Boundary: Not Yet Implemented**
The WASM crate is a stub. When implemented, it will create a new trust boundary — code running in a browser sandbox with potential access to external network calls. The audit flags that no neural data should cross this boundary to external services without explicit, informed user consent. This is both an ethical requirement and a legal one in most jurisdictions.

**Practical Guidance**
For software development and testing with synthetic or anonymized data, the current state is acceptable. Before any deployment with real human subjects: pseudonymize IDs at the pipeline boundary, add zeroization to embedding types, consider encrypting RVF files at rest, and establish a logging policy that explicitly prohibits data values in structured log fields. The audit table in the codebase is a good starting checklist — treat every 'NEEDS AUDIT' and 'CONCERN' row as a required ticket before production.

title: RuField's Common Event Grammar: How Eleven Sensor Modalities Speak One Language
content:
Imagine a United Nations assembly where every delegate speaks a different language — WiFi, radar, ultrasound, infrared, quantum magnetic. Without interpreters, nothing gets decided. RuField is that interpreter layer: a common grammar that every ambient sensor modality translates into before any fusion or decision-making happens.

The core insight is that multi-modal sensor fusion has historically been hard not because the physics is incompatible, but because every modality ships its own data format, its own event schema, and its own privacy assumptions. RuField solves this by defining four universal output types that every adapter must produce:

- **FieldEvent** — a timestamped, signed envelope for a single sensor observation
- **FieldTensor** — the actual signal data (shape-validated, axis-labeled)
- **FusionGraph** — a graph of supporting and contradicting evidence across modalities
- **PrivacyClass** — a P0–P5 label that travels with every piece of data, always

The modality registry currently covers 15 signal types: WiFi CSI, WiFi CIR, WiFi beamforming feedback, UWB ranging, Bluetooth Channel Sounding, mmWave radar, ultrasonic, subsonic (structural vibration), infrared thermal, active infrared, LiDAR phase, quantum magnetic (NV diamond / OPM), quantum inertial (atom interferometry), event camera, and synthetic simulation. Each one plugs into the same `FieldAdapter` trait and emits the same event shape.

This is deliberately not a replacement for IEEE 802.11bf, Bluetooth Channel Sounding, UWB, or Matter. Those protocols define the physical and link layers. RuField sits above them — it is the open, privacy-aware, provenance-rich event model that consumes their outputs and makes them fusable.

The practical consequence: a fusion engine written against RuField doesn't need to know whether the motion signal came from a WiFi chip or a quantum magnetometer. It receives a `FieldEvent` with a `FieldTensor`, a `PrivacyClass`, and a `ProvenanceReceipt`. The modality is tagged, but the processing pipeline is uniform. Adding a new sensor type means writing one new adapter, not rewriting the fusion layer.

The `rufield-core` crate implements this grammar: `Modality` (15 variants), `FieldAxis`, `FieldTensor` with shape-to-values validation, `PrivacyClass`, `SensorDescriptor`, `Observation`, `FieldEvent`, `CalibrationReceipt`, `InferenceQuery`, `FieldInference`, and `FieldEmbedding`. The traits `FieldAdapter`, `FieldEncoder`, `FusionEngine`, and `PrivacyGuard` define the contracts every component must satisfy.

The analogy that holds: RuField is to ambient sensors what HTTP is to network communication — a common envelope format that lets wildly different underlying transports interoperate at the application layer.

title: RuField's Privacy and Provenance Model: P0–P5 Classes, ed25519 Signatures, and the Consent Gate
content:
Every piece of data in RuField carries two non-optional properties from the moment it is created: a **PrivacyClass** (P0 through P5) and a **ProvenanceReceipt** (a cryptographic signature). Neither can be stripped or deferred — they are structural fields, not optional metadata.

**The Privacy Class ladder**

P0 is the most sensitive: raw waveform data. By default, P0 events are edge-only — the `DefaultPrivacyGuard` denies network transmission. This means raw WiFi CSI subcarrier amplitudes, for example, never leave the device unless an explicit policy override is in place. P2 is the baseline for processed observations (motion presence, room occupancy) and is allowed by default. P4 covers biometric-adjacent inferences — breathing rate, micro-motion, scratch detection — and requires explicit consent. Without a consent record in the policy, a P4 query returns `RequiresConsent`, not a result. P5 requires identity binding before any output is released.

The `rufield-privacy` crate enforces this with a `DefaultPrivacyGuard` that returns one of three outcomes from `authorize`: `Allow`, `Deny`, or `RequiresConsent`. The acceptance tests are explicit: P0 transmission → Deny; P4 without consent → RequiresConsent; P4 with consent → Allow; P2 → Allow. These are not configuration options — they are the default behavior.

**Provenance receipts and tamper detection**

Every `FieldEvent` is signed with ed25519. The `rufield-provenance` crate computes a real sha256 hash over the event content and signs it with a deterministic key. The `is_fusable` invariant in §11 means: an event that fails signature verification is flagged and **never** fused into a trusted inference. Tampered events are not silently dropped — they are flagged so the system knows something upstream is wrong.

Synthetic events (from the simulator) are also signed, but carry `synthetic = true` in their receipt. This means the fusion engine can distinguish between a real sensor reading and a simulated one at the data level, not just by configuration.

**The security threat model**

RuField's security model addresses six specific threats: raw waveform leakage (mitigated by P0 edge-only default), biometric inference without consent (P4 consent gate), sensor spoofing (signed sensor receipts), replay attacks (nonce + timestamp + hash chain), model drift (calibration expiry and benchmark gates), and silent firmware degradation (firmware hash stored in the receipt).

The replay attack mitigation is worth noting: because each event carries a nonce, a timestamp, and participates in a hash chain, replaying a captured event stream into the fusion engine will produce verification failures — the hash chain won't match the current state.

**The banner honesty contract**

The viewer enforces a three-state banner that is mutually exclusive and visually distinct: amber for SYNTHETIC (simulated sensors, no hardware), green for LIVE (receipt-verified upstream events), and red for DISCONNECTED (live mode selected but upstream unreachable). The system never falls back to synthetic data under a LIVE banner, or vice versa. This is a non-negotiable design constraint, not a UI preference.

title: Understanding RuField's Honesty Tiers: Synthetic, Replay, and the Road to Live-Hardware Validation
content:
One of the most instructive things about RuField is how explicitly it documents what its data is and is not. This is a teaching model for any system that mixes simulated, replayed, and live data — and it's worth understanding the three tiers carefully.

**Tier 1: Synthetic simulation**

The `SyntheticSim` adapter in `rufield-adapters` is a deterministic, seeded simulator. Given the same seed, it produces byte-identical signed event streams with ground-truth labels across three modalities: wifi_csi, mmwave_radar, and infrared_thermal. The v0.1 benchmark numbers — including the §27 acceptance scorecard — are produced entirely by this simulator.

What this proves: the pipeline scores correctly against known ground truth. The latency numbers (p95 ≈ 0.01 ms) are real measurements of in-process computation. The privacy enforcement, provenance signing, and fusion graph construction all work correctly.

What this does not prove: any of this reflects real-world sensor accuracy. The simulator is labeled SYNTHETIC throughout. The benchmark report is deterministic precisely because it is not measuring physical reality.

**Tier 2: Real CSI replay**

The `CsiReplayAdapter` is the first non-synthetic adapter. It parses a `.csi.jsonl` file containing real captured WiFi CSI per-subcarrier amplitudes, calibrates an empty-room baseline using per-subcarrier Welford mean and variance (stored in a `CalibrationReceipt`), and emits one signed `FieldEvent` per frame.

The provenance receipt here is genuinely real: `raw_hash` is a genuine sha256 over the raw subcarrier bytes, signed with a real ed25519 key, with `synthetic = false`. The `FieldTensor` contains real frequency-axis CSI data.

The motion/presence output is a CSI-variance proxy — when variance exceeds the calibrated baseline, the system infers motion or presence. The 199-frame real-CSI fixture drives `RuFieldFusion` to produce `person_present` and `breathing` inferences.

What this proves: the pipeline can ingest real physical signals, produce well-formed signed events, and generate plausible inferences from physically-grounded variance changes.

What this does not prove: accuracy. The recordings are unlabeled — there is no ground truth for what actually happened in the room during capture. The output is explicitly described as a 'physically-grounded CSI-variance proxy, NOT validated accuracy.' It is also replay from a file, not live hardware streaming.

**Tier 3: Live hardware (roadmap)**

Live-hardware streaming and labeled-accuracy validation are documented roadmap items. They do not exist yet. The system is designed to support them — the `FieldAdapter` trait, the provenance receipt structure, and the calibration system are all built with live hardware in mind — but no live adapter currently exists.

**Why this matters as a design pattern**

Most systems blur these tiers. A benchmark run against synthetic data gets cited as accuracy. A replay demo gets described as live. RuField's explicit three-tier model — with different visual banners, different `synthetic` flags in receipts, and explicit documentation of what each tier proves — is a template for honest capability communication in any sensing or inference system. The rule is simple: the banner reflects exactly what is being shown, and the system never silently substitutes one tier for another.

title: WorldGraph: The Typed Belief Graph at the Heart of RuView's Digital Twin
content:
When a building full of sensors is watching people move through it, you end up with a flood of raw signals — WiFi CSI pulses, camera frames, RF echoes. The question is: what do you *do* with all of that? You need a single, coherent map of what's actually happening in the space. In RuView, that map is the `WorldGraph`.

Think of `WorldGraph` as a city map where every landmark, road, and person has a typed identity, and every connection between them has a named relationship. It's not a flat table of sensor readings — it's a living graph of *beliefs* about the world, built on top of Rust's `petgraph` library using a `StableDiGraph` (which means node indices stay stable even as nodes are added or removed).

**Nodes are real things.** The graph holds typed nodes for physical and conceptual entities: `Room`, `Zone`, `Wall`, `Doorway`, `Sensor`, `RfLink`, `PersonTrack`, `ObjectAnchor`, `Event`, and `SemanticState`. A `SemanticState` is a *belief* — a conclusion the system has reached, like "person 3 is in the kitchen" — as opposed to a raw sensor frame.

**Edges are typed relationships.** Connections between nodes aren't generic pointers; they carry meaning. `Observes` links a sensor to what it can see. `LocatedIn` places a person inside a room. `AdjacentTo` connects neighboring spaces. `Supports` and `Contradicts` let beliefs reinforce or challenge each other. `DerivedFrom` traces a conclusion back to its evidence. `PrivacyLimitedBy` marks where privacy constraints apply.

**Where it sits in the pipeline.** `WorldGraph` occupies a precise position: it lives *downstream* of signal fusion (ADR-137) and *upstream* of the semantic/agent layer (ADR-140). Raw sensor data gets fused first; the fused result enters the graph as beliefs. Agents and reasoning layers then query the graph rather than touching raw signals. This separation keeps each layer clean and testable.

**Provenance is not optional.** Every `SemanticState` node must carry a `SemanticProvenance` struct that records the signal evidence, the model that produced the conclusion, the calibration ID used, and the privacy decision applied. This is enforced *structurally* in the type system — you cannot insert a belief without also recording why you believe it. That means auditing is always possible: trace any conclusion back through `DerivedFrom` edges to the original evidence.

**Identity and idempotency.** Every node has a `WorldId`. The `upsert_node` operation is idempotent on that identity, so re-inserting a node with the same ID updates it rather than duplicating it. This makes the graph safe to update from multiple sources without creating phantom duplicates.

**Snapshots and serialization.** At any point you can call `snapshot()` to get a `WorldGraphSnapshot` — a serializable, point-in-time view of the entire graph, bundled with a `PrivacyRollup` that summarizes the privacy posture of the snapshot. The graph serializes to JSON via `to_json` / `from_json`, and a `SCHEMA_VERSION` constant is embedded in every payload. Because the node and edge types use a closed enum model, a reader that encounters an unknown schema version fails immediately rather than silently misinterpreting data — a deliberate design choice that prevents subtle corruption bugs.

**Geospatial grounding.** Coordinates inside the graph use the ENU (East/North/Up) system, measured in meters relative to a `GeoRegistration` origin provided by the `wifi-densepose-geo` crate. This means the local sensor coordinate space can be tied to real WGS84 geographic coordinates, terrain elevation, and OpenStreetMap building data — the digital twin is anchored to a real place on Earth.

In summary, `WorldGraph` is the authoritative, auditable, privacy-aware belief store for a RuView spatial sensing deployment. It turns a stream of fused sensor signals into a queryable, versioned, geospatially grounded graph that downstream agents can reason over with confidence.

title: Forward Prediction with WorldGraph and wifi-densepose-worldmodel
content:
Knowing where people *are* right now is useful. Knowing where they'll *be* in the next few seconds is more useful — it lets a building system pre-position resources, avoid collisions, or flag anomalies before they happen. RuView's `WorldGraph` handles the present; `wifi-densepose-worldmodel` handles the future. Here's how they connect.

**The handoff point.** `WorldGraph` stores `PersonTrack` nodes — each one representing a tracked individual with a position in ENU coordinates (East/North/Up meters). When you want to forecast movement, you extract those positions and hand them to the world model. The bridge between the two is the `OccWorldBridge`, which communicates with the OccWorld service over a Unix socket.

**Rasterizing the scene.** The first step is converting the graph's continuous position data into a discrete occupancy frame — essentially a 3D grid where each voxel is either occupied or empty. The helper function `worldgraph_to_occupancy` does this: you pass it a list of `PersonPosition` structs (each with a `track_id` and ENU coordinates), a `SceneBounds` defining the spatial extent of interest, and a voxel resolution in meters (0.1 m is typical). The output is a single occupancy frame.

**Requesting a prediction.** With an occupancy frame in hand, you send an `OccupancyWorldModelRequest` to the bridge. The request carries the past frame(s), the voxel resolution, the scene bounds, and a `prediction_steps` count. In the example below, 15 steps are requested:

```rust
let bridge = OccWorldBridge::new("/tmp/occworld.sock");
let frame = worldgraph_to_occupancy(&persons, &bounds, 0.1);
let response = bridge.predict(OccupancyWorldModelRequest {
    past_frames: vec![frame],
    voxel_resolution_m: 0.1,
    scene_bounds: SceneBoundsJson { ... },
    prediction_steps: 15,
}).await?;
```

The response contains predicted occupancy grids for each future step, plus trajectory priors that downstream tracking can use to improve its estimates.

**Why this split architecture?** Keeping prediction separate from the belief graph is intentional. `WorldGraph` is a synchronous, auditable record of what the system currently believes. The world model is a probabilistic, forward-looking process that consumes history and emits forecasts. Mixing them would make both harder to test, audit, and replace independently. The pipeline reads cleanly: `fusion → WorldGraph → world model → semantic/agent layer`.

**Practical considerations.** The voxel resolution is a tuning knob: finer resolution (smaller value) gives more spatial detail but increases memory and compute cost. The `SceneBounds` should be set to cover the area of interest without being unnecessarily large — the rasterization step fills the entire bounded volume. For most indoor deployments, a 20m × 20m footprint at 0.1 m resolution is a reasonable starting point.

Paired together, `WorldGraph` and `wifi-densepose-worldmodel` give RuView both a present-tense belief store and a near-future forecast engine — the two things a spatial intelligence system needs to act rather than just observe.

title: Privacy and Trust in WorldGraph: How Provenance and PrivacyRollup Work
content:
A system that tracks people moving through a building carries serious responsibility. RuView's `WorldGraph` is designed so that privacy and auditability aren't features bolted on afterward — they're structural properties of the graph itself. You cannot record a belief without also recording its justification and its privacy status.

**Provenance is mandatory by type.** Every `SemanticState` node (a belief, like "zone A has two occupants") must include a `SemanticProvenance` struct. This struct captures four things: the signal evidence that contributed to the belief, the model that processed that evidence, the calibration ID active at the time, and the privacy decision that was applied. Because this is enforced at the type level in Rust — not by convention or documentation — a belief that lacks provenance simply cannot be constructed. The compiler rejects it.

This is a meaningful guarantee. In many systems, audit trails are maintained by discipline: developers remember to log things, or a middleware layer tries to capture context after the fact. In `WorldGraph`, the audit trail is the data structure. Asking "where did this conclusion come from?" always has an answer because the answer is required to exist before the conclusion can be stored.

**Privacy as a graph relation.** Privacy constraints aren't stored in a separate access-control list — they're edges in the graph. The `PrivacyLimitedBy` edge type connects a belief or entity to the privacy constraint that governs it. This means privacy posture is queryable using the same graph traversal tools used for everything else. You can ask: "which beliefs in this snapshot are subject to a privacy limitation?" and get a direct answer by following edges.

**PrivacyRollup in snapshots.** When you call `snapshot()` on a `WorldGraph`, the resulting `WorldGraphSnapshot` includes a `PrivacyRollup` — a summary of the privacy posture of the entire snapshot. This is useful for downstream consumers that need to know, at a glance, whether a snapshot contains sensitive data before deciding how to handle or transmit it. A consumer can inspect the rollup without traversing every node.

**Schema versioning as a trust mechanism.** Trust also extends to the wire format. Every JSON payload produced by `to_json` embeds a `SCHEMA_VERSION` constant. The node and edge types use a closed enum model, meaning the set of valid types is fixed at compile time. When `from_json` encounters a payload with an unrecognized schema version, it returns an error immediately — it does not attempt to parse the payload and silently produce garbage. This fail-fast behavior is a deliberate trust boundary: a reader that doesn't understand the schema says so, rather than producing subtly wrong beliefs.

**The practical effect.** These design choices mean that a `WorldGraph` instance, or a snapshot derived from it, carries its own justification. An auditor, a regulator, or a downstream agent can inspect any belief and trace it back through `DerivedFrom` edges to the original evidence, through `PrivacyLimitedBy` edges to the applicable constraints, and through the `PrivacyRollup` to the overall posture of the snapshot. The system is designed to be accountable by construction, not by policy alone.

title: How unsorry Validates Mathematical Records: The GB-Code Integrity System
content:
When a swarm of autonomous agents is producing and verifying mathematics, you need a rigorous way to check that every file, claim, and proof is internally consistent. The unsorry project solves this with a numbered set of violation codes — GB001 through GB014 and beyond — each targeting a specific layer of integrity.

Think of it like a building inspection checklist. Before a structure is approved, inspectors check the foundation, then the framing, then the electrical, in a deliberate order. The GB codes work the same way: earlier codes check structural basics, later ones check semantic correctness.

**GB001 — The envelope check.** Every record must be valid UTF-8 and its header line must parse correctly in the form `𝔸<ver>.<type>.<name>@YYYY-MM-DD`. The `γ≔unsorry.<type>` field must also be consistent. If the envelope is malformed, nothing else can be trusted.

**GB002 — Identity agreement.** For goals, translations, and decompositions, the filename, the header, and the embedded `⟦Ω⟧` identity block must all agree. IDs must also conform to the `Id` grammar. This prevents a file from claiming to be one thing while its name says another — a subtle but dangerous inconsistency in a distributed system where agents reference each other by ID.

**GB003–GB005 — Domain and state constraints.** These codes enforce that enum fields stay within their allowed values (`phase`, `status`, `difficulty` 0–5), that the `lean` field is set or cleared correctly depending on phase, and that proved or translated goals carry a valid 64-character lowercase hex SHA.

**GB006 — The proof artifact exists.** When a goal is marked `proved`, the corresponding `.aisp` file must exist at `library/index/<sha>.aisp`, and the filename stem must equal the `sha` field, which must equal the actual SHA-256 of the statement. This triple-lock ensures you cannot mark something proved without a real, retrievable proof artifact.

**GB007–GB009 — Dependency and content checks.** Every dependency reference must point to a real goal ID. Source paths must exist in the tree. And formal blocks must not be overwhelmed by quoted prose — the density of quoted natural language inside formal blocks is capped at 30% of non-whitespace characters. This last rule keeps the formal language honest: a block that is mostly English prose wrapped in quotes is not really a formal statement.

**GB010–GB013 — Claim-specific rules.** Claims (produced by agents asserting they can prove something) have their own integrity layer. The filename must follow `<goal-id>.<agent-id>.aisp` with exactly two dots. The header, `⟦Ω⟧` block, and filename must agree. The `ttl` (time-to-live) must be between 600 and 86400 seconds. And GB013 flags expired claims — if `now > ts + ttl`, the claim is stale and gets consumed by the reaper process.

The practical lesson here is architectural: **layered validation with explicit codes makes debugging tractable in a multi-agent system.** When an agent submits a record and it fails, the violation code tells you exactly which layer broke. You do not have to read the whole file to understand the problem. This is especially important when agents are running autonomously at scale — a human auditing a failure needs a precise signal, not a vague error message.

The GB code system also encodes the project's trust model. Codes GB001–GB002 are about format trust. GB003–GB008 are about semantic trust within a single record. GB009 enforces a stylistic contract that keeps formal mathematics formal. GB010–GB013 enforce the liveness and freshness of agent claims. Together they form a complete integrity surface that a validator can sweep in a single pass.

title: The Decompose-Prove-Recompose Chain: How unsorry Closes Hard Proofs
content:
One of the central ideas in the unsorry project is that a hard mathematical theorem does not need to be proved in one shot. Instead, it can be decomposed into a tree of simpler sub-goals, each sub-goal proved independently, and then the results recomposed upward until the root is closed. This is called the decompose → prove-subs → recompose chain, and it has now been demonstrated end-to-end on a real target.

**The keystone pattern.** A parent goal is marked as blocked until all its sub-goals are proved. Once the last sub-goal closes, the parent becomes provable — it just needs to assemble the pieces. This is analogous to building an arch: every stone is held in place by the others, and the keystone at the top cannot be placed until the two sides meet. In unsorry, the dependency graph encodes this structure explicitly, and the validator (GB007) ensures every dependency reference points to a real, existing goal.

**The Platonic-Schläfli example.** The first real demonstration of this chain was the Platonic-Schläfli core, which closed through a forced depth-3 tree of 13 kernel-verified lemmas, recomposed level by level. The decomposition was forced by a constrained budget — the agent could not prove the whole thing at once, so it had to break it down. This is an important honesty point: the decomposition was not a clever strategic choice, it was a necessity. But the chain still worked.

**Reuse as a compounding mechanism.** The more exciting result came in a follow-up run. A lemma that had already been proved — the triangular closed form, derived from the Nicomachus lemma — was reused by a new goal. The new proof closed in under five minutes by importing and invoking the swarm's own previously verified result. Every recomposing parent in the first run closed the same way. This is the compounding effect the project is designed to produce: the verified commons grows, and future proofs get cheaper because they can stand on already-verified ground.

**What the goal graph looks like in practice.** The backlog currently holds 752 prove-goals, of which 406 are proved and 341 are open. Goals are organized into dependency trees visible in the Mermaid flowcharts embedded in the documentation. A goal like `am-gm-three-cube` sits at the root, with sub-goals `am-gm-three-cube-s1`, `am-gm-three-cube-s2`, and `am-gm-three-cube-s2-s1` beneath it. The color coding — green for proved, orange for blocked, blue for translated — gives an immediate visual read of where the tree stands.

**The honest frontier.** The project is careful to distinguish what has been demonstrated from what remains open. The chain works. Reuse works at depth 1. What is not yet known is whether this scales to genuinely hard, mathlib-absent targets — theorems that are not elementary, that require deep insight, that no existing library touches. The open question is whether a swarm pointed at those targets can grow the verified commons faster than human mathematicians, or whether it stalls at the elementary band. That question is what drives the next phase of development.

For practitioners building similar systems, the key architectural takeaway is this: **explicit dependency graphs with blocked/proved state transitions are the right primitive for compositional proof automation.** They make progress visible, they enable reuse, and they give the system a natural way to parallelize work across agents — each agent can claim and attempt any open leaf node without coordinating with others working on different branches.

title: Known Limitations of unsorry's Statement Matching Engine
content:
The unsorry statement matching engine is deliberately narrow in scope. Understanding what it does not do — and why — is as important as understanding what it does. These are not bugs waiting to be fixed; most are accepted design constraints that reflect a conscious tradeoff between complexity and reliability.

**No semantic equivalence reasoning.** The matcher works on syntax, not meaning. If two statements are logically identical but written differently — `n + 1` versus `Nat.succ n`, or an expression with associativity applied — the matcher will report a MISMATCH. This is intentional. Semantic equivalence reasoning requires a full theorem prover, and embedding one inside the matcher would make it slow, fragile, and hard to audit. The design choice is to keep the matcher fast and deterministic, and route semantic mismatches to a human-flag path for manual review.

The analogy is a diff tool. `git diff` does not know that two functions are semantically equivalent after refactoring — it just shows you the textual difference. That is a feature, not a limitation, because it keeps the tool predictable.

**Canonical-name capture.** The matcher uses `x₁`, `x₂`, and similar subscript-digit names as canonical bound variable names internally. If a statement uses those same names as free identifiers, a collision occurs. The convention is therefore that backlog statements must not use `x<subscript>` as free variable names. Since statements in the backlog are machine-generated, this convention is enforced at the source and does not occur in practice — but it is worth knowing if you are writing statements by hand.

**Alias matching is order-sensitive.** Aliases (digraphs and multi-character symbols) are matched textually before whitespace normalization. This means a digraph split by a space — like `: =` instead of `:=`, or `∃ !` with a space — will not be recognized. Again, because statements are machine-written, this does not arise in practice, but it is a sharp edge if you are feeding hand-authored input.

**ASCII-digit suffixes are not valid identifiers.** The grammar treats `x1` as two tokens, not one identifier. If you want a subscripted variable, use the Unicode subscript digit: `x₁`. This is a deliberate grammar choice that keeps the identifier space unambiguous, but it will silently produce wrong results if you use ASCII digits expecting them to be part of a name.

**Display-width caret alignment.** When the engine produces a human-readable diff with a caret pointing to the mismatch position, it aligns by character count, not by display width. With double-width Unicode glyphs (common in mathematical notation), the caret may appear visually misaligned in a terminal. The printed character index is authoritative — use that, not the visual position of the caret.

**The broader design philosophy.** These limitations share a common thread: the matcher is a precise, auditable tool operating on a well-defined syntactic domain, not a general-purpose semantic reasoner. In a system where autonomous agents are producing and verifying mathematics, predictability and auditability matter more than flexibility. A matcher that sometimes silently accepts semantically equivalent but syntactically different statements would be harder to trust than one that always requires exact syntactic agreement and routes exceptions to humans. The limitations are the price of that trustworthiness.
